Choose the floor:

Option What it takes Notes
1. A new BMW M3 trunk floor (41127895619) with its front reinforcement (51717894229). Recommended Drill the Touring's well out along its factory spot welds and plug-weld the new floor in at the same points New, rust-free steel, and no donor body steel welded into your car, which keeps the floor out of Massachusetts' "reconstructed" title question. BMWPartsDeal lists the floor at $763.61 and the reinforcement at $88.22 (October 2026), both "Ships in 1-3 Business Days", but stock isn't confirmed until you order (floor, reinforcement); eStore-Central, an EU retailer, lists them at €717.97 and €81.79 (eStore-Central). BMW lists the reinforcement as "additionally required" with the floor (ETK). In the UK the floor was about £430 plus VAT in July 2023, one large panel including the battery box; Redish used it on two Tourings (Autoalex – build part 3 (2023), 13:20, Redish – Touring build part 1 (2022), 04:40)
2. The donor's M3 trunk floor As option 1, with the donor's floor cut out with generous margins The same part, used. Coupe and convertible floors both carry the front reinforcement 51717894229, and a convertible's also has two floor supports, 41217021949 and 41217020784 (ETK: coupe, convertible). The right muffler bracket sits on the rail, not the floor, so cut it off the donor separately (see Hangers). M346's Touring took its floor from a 2003 M3 convertible (M346 Projects – Pt 1, M3 part out (2023), 06:40). In Massachusetts, ask the RMV before you weld a donor floor in
3. A flat panel Cut the well out and weld in your own panel Documented once: Calvin's Touring got "a sheet steel one that's been swaged for strength" in 2021 (Calvin's Car Diary – PT10 (2021), 05:00). His mechanic found "nothing wrong with it", but in 2025 it was swapped for a BMW M3 floor section for looks, before the car's exhaust was built (Calvin's Car Diary – PT15 (2025), 22:05). So no flat panel has been published with dimensions or tested under an exhaust; follow the rules below
3b. A bonded composite M3-shape floor Cut the well out inside its flanges and bond and rivet in a carbon panel moulded from an M3 floor One S54 Touring (2026): 16 lb of steel out, 3.5 lb in, 2K non-conductive urethane with sealed stainless rivets over painted steel, M8 bond-in studs for the M3 hangers (the non-M studs are too short) and for the EVAP canister, and a rivet-in hanger bracket placed with jigs taken from an M3. Don't use windshield urethane: its carbon black conducts and invites galvanic corrosion (NAM3 – Black & Tan 332iT #722–#748, #739–#748). No long-term or crash data
4. Keep the well The M3's front exhaust section, with a muffler in the Touring's position: Stromung's bolt-on, which "bolts to factory M3 midpipes and uses stock E46 hangers" (LC's Garage – Stromung (2019), description), Supersprint's rear sections or a welded-on non-M muffler. A US builder of several S54 Tourings says most are done this way (e46fanatics) No floor surgery, but no quad-outlet M3 muffler. Tenza kept its non-M muffler with M3 flanges welded on, since the M3 pipe is 2³⁄₁₆ in against 2 in (Tenza – wagon exhaust (2021), 00:40); Project BMW fitted a ZHP muffler (Project BMW – wagon pulls hard (2021), 04:00). Three S54 swaps on the non-M floor ran a US E36 M3 muffler, one with its necked-down inlet cut off (NAM3 – Kaiv's first S54 Touring #14, NAM3 – Black & Tan 332iT #25); one owner, who had fitted it in place of a loud Stromung, called it "blissfully quiet" (NAM3 – Trent's swap #57). In Massachusetts any of these must be no louder than the car's original equipment, with no gutted or by-passed muffler (Massachusetts checks below). One US S54 wagon whose non-M muffler steps down from 2½ to 2 in "has trouble picking up more speed" near 7,000 rpm (ThaChileanDude – Building an e46 m3 Wagon in 10 days (2024), 33:56)
Note

Massachusetts gives a "reconstructed" title to a car reassembled by "welding together ... the frames or unit bodies of two or more motor vehicles" (c. 90D §20F). We found no ruling on whether a donor's trunk floor counts, so ask the RMV Title Division before you cut the donor's (Massachusetts). A new BMW floor avoids the question.

Record the donor before you cut. No source publishes the muffler's position, the hanger positions, the depth of either well or the factory gaps, so measure them on the donor while its exhaust still hangs, and use them as your pass values on the Touring. Write them on the Floor and exhaust positions worksheet, and photograph each with a tape in frame:

  1. The datum is the midpoint between the bolt centers of the rear subframe's two rear mounts. Measure X rearward from the line through those bolts, and Y left (+) or right (−) of the midpoint. Use the same datum on your Touring, and check that the bolt spacing agrees within 2 mm (our estimate) before you trust the donor's figures. BMW's figure for that spacing is 660 mm (26.0 in) ± 1 mm: dimension F–F, which BMW's top view draws at the front corners of the spare-wheel well, behind the axle (our reading of the drawing) (TIS 41 00).
  2. On level ground at ride height, loaded to BMW's normal position for an M3 (a full tank, 68 kg on each front seat and 14 kg in the trunk; TIS 32 00), at placard tire pressures: the muffler's lowest point above the ground, each tip's center height and its offset from the car's centerline, and the gap from each tip to its bumper cut-out on all four sides (photograph them; the worksheet takes the smallest).
  3. On a lift, exhaust fitted: the muffler to its heat shield at six points (left, center and right, at the front and rear edges); the shield to the floor; the muffler's front face to the diff cover and to the subframe; the closest pipe to the fuel tank, its straps and the V-brace; and the canister cover to the pipes.
  4. The three hangers: X, Y and the length of each body stud, and which bracket it's on: H1 front-left, H2 rear-left or H3 on the right rail, as in Hangers below.
  5. The floor: the depth of the M3's shallow well below its rim, measured from the cargo side; and the canister holder's four studs, photographed, noting whether they're on the floor or the RACP.
  6. The spot welds: mark the donor floor's perimeter spot welds with a paint pen, then count them on each edge and measure their pitch.

On your Touring, in Phase 4, record the same datum, the existing hanger stud plates, the canister and leak-test pump (before they come out), the battery vent-hose exit and ground stud, and the well. One owner measured an E46 well at 62 cm (24.4 in) across (BMW-Syndikat); nobody has published its depth.

Cut rules. The rear subframe mounts sit at the front corners of the well. CMP's access cut removes "the forward most portion of the spare wheel well within 5"/120mm of the chassis rails" to reach their tops (CMP, part 2). That 120 mm (5 in) is the strip CMP cuts away, not a zone to avoid, and every route that takes the well out works inside it. What must survive are the flanges, with their rows of spot welds: along both rails, across the front of the well where the RACP joins it, and at the rear panel. So:

  • Separate the well along those flanges by drilling out its spot welds from the cargo side, through the flange only, with an 8 mm (5/16 in) spot-weld cutter. The holes become your plug-weld holes.
  • If you trim instead, for a partial graft, cut at least 5 mm inboard of the flange, as M346 did (M346 Projects – pt 14 (2024), 02:40).
  • Never torch-cut, and never cut or grind through a rail, RACP or rear-panel flange.
  • Do the topside reinforcement through the opening before you close it (steps 8–13 of the reinforcement procedure).

Fitting the M3 floor (options 1 and 2). This method follows BMW's welding rules (Welding settings and safety) and M346's Touring. Phase 5 has the order of the whole job.

  1. Drill from the cargo side. The well is spot-welded under the rail, RACP and rear-panel flanges. Drill each spot weld from above with the 8 mm cutter, through the flange only, and split the layers from below with a spot-weld chisel. The well drops out downward once it's free (M346 Projects – pt 14 (2024), 02:40). For a donor floor, drill the same welds on the donor; "they all match up" (00:40).
  2. Check what the well was hiding. CMP: "Be sure to check all the spot welds previously hidden beneath this panel for failure. The ones closest to the chassis rails & front of the car commonly let go first and are not visibly failed from beneath the car." Use die penetrant to show hidden cracks. To close a gap at a failed spot weld, drill it out, bolt the layers tight, stitch-weld the flange edge, then fill the holes (CMP, part 2). Then do the topside reinforcement.
  3. Straighten the flanges with a hammer and dolly. Check: a straight-edge shows less than 1 mm (0.04 in) of gap (our target), and no cracks show under die penetrant.
  4. Fit the brackets now, while you can reach both faces (see Hangers below).
  5. Prepare the faces. Take the paint off about 30 mm (1.2 in) around every weld, on both faces, and grind the zinc off in each weld zone (11:00). Coat every mating face with weld-through primer, kept out of the weld spots (I-CAR CRN 503). Strip seam sealer and underbody coating back there too: they burn.
  6. Offer the floor up from below, propped and strapped, and cleco or clamp it at every flange hole (08:20). Check: the layers touch at each hole, with a gap of 1 mm or less (our target; BMW asks only for the smallest gap possible). Expect hand-fitting at the seam to the rear panel; the side and front flanges match up (our reading of two builds).
  7. Mock it up with the M3 axle, or at least the diff, in place and the muffler on all three hangers. Check it against the donor's figures (Clearances at the mock-up below), and decide the canister.
  8. Plug-weld down-hand from the cargo side, through the 8 mm flange holes into the new floor underneath: the same number and positions as the factory spot welds, and at least 25 mm (1 in) apart (I-CAR CRN 1484, M346, 24:40). Skip around the four edges so no area gets hot, log the count on each edge (worksheet), and measure the body diagonals after every session.
  9. Dress and check. Grind each weld to no more than 3 mm (1/8 in) proud, without cutting into the panel. Check: every factory spot-weld position re-welded, no porosity or cracks, and melt-through visible underneath wherever you can see it.
  10. Seal and protect. 2K epoxy primer on bare metal; seam sealer on both faces of every lap and plug-weld row; then top coat (51:00). Fit a BMW body plug in every hole in the new floor, and light-test it (Massachusetts checks below). Underbody coating goes on outside, kept off the hanger rubbers and the shield standoffs, and cavity wax into the rails and box sections with a 360° wand (Tracks and Trails – Touring rear end (2025), 09:40). No structural foam while welding remains. Then refit the battery box parts.

Partial graft. Tracks and Trails kept more of the Touring floor and cut out only what the M3 panel replaces (Tracks and Trails – Touring rear end (2025), 01:20): trace the trimmed M3 panel on the Touring floor and cut about 5 mm inside the seams. Where a joint has no flange, lap it as for a flat panel. Calvin's team called the floor graft one of the hardest jobs on their car (Calvin's Car Diary – PT6 (2020), 10:40).

BMW's own floor change is heavier work than this guide's (TIS 41 12 535):

  • the car on a straightening bench, with the tail panel, tank and rear axle carrier out;
  • the spot welds drilled out along the side walls, the spare-wheel well and the floor assembly, and the rear side members cut at their 16 mm hole;
  • the new floor clamped with the bench's attachments, then plug-welded through drilled holes, with zinc-rich primer on every mating face;
  • the cavity foam parts bonded back in with window adhesive.

Keeping the rails whole, as this guide does, avoids BMW's rail cut.

Flat panel (option 3). No source gives the floor's gauge, so measure it at a cut edge and use steel no thinner. Stiffen the panel with transverse swaged or bead-rolled ribs, and with a hat-section across its front edge in place of BMW's reinforcement 51717894229 (our suggestion). Set it no lower than the rim of the old well, since the M3's own rear floor is flat, and hang the muffler under it in the mock-up before you close it. Plug-weld it to every original flange at the factory spot-weld positions, especially along both rails and the front seam, and leave no free edge near the mounts. Where a joint has no flange, joggle one edge and lap the panels by about 12–15 mm (0.5–0.6 in; our estimate); plug-weld through 8 mm holes in the top layer at 25–40 mm (1–1.6 in) pitch, add short stitches, and seal the lap on both faces, since laps trap water. In our view a lap is far more forgiving than a butt weld on thin steel; use an open butt joint over a copper backer only if your butt-weld coupons pass I-CAR's fold test. Hang the muffler from the outer underbody or the rails, as BMW does, never from the middle of the panel (BMW ST041). If the panel can hold water, give it one drain at its low point with a removable plug (our suggestion), never an open hole.

Hangers. BMW's catalog gives the M3 rear muffler, 18107831783, as 26.7 kg (58.9 lb); it's the same part on every 2001–06 M3 coupe and convertible (ETK). It hangs on three brackets at the outer ends of the underbody, two on the left and one on the right (Redish – Touring build part 1 (2022), 06:00), so, we infer, the new floor carries none of its weight. Your Touring's floor has two brackets, both on the left (ETK), for a 12.9 kg (28 lb) muffler (ETK); builders describe a single left-side hanger (Tracks and Trails – Touring rear end (2025), 03:20). Prices are BMWPartsDeal's, October 2026.

Bracket BMW number On your Touring What to do
H1: rear silencer bracket, front (left front) 41112497585 (ETK) Already fitted: the same part on every E46 Keep it if it's sound and sits at the donor's position; replace it if it's rusted ($27.20, BMWPartsDeal)
H2: rear silencer bracket, rear (left rear) 41122494844, M3 only (ETK) 41118204223, with short studs (ETK) Drill out the Touring's plate and plug-weld the M3 one at the donor's position ($27.19, BMWPartsDeal; one listing flags it, so confirm stock)
H3: bracket, rear muffler right (on the right rear side member) 41112493931, M3 only (ETK) None Buy it ($71.40, BMWPartsDeal), or cut the donor's off its rail with 20–30 mm (about 1 in) of metal round it (our estimate). Tack it at the donor's position, hang the muffler once, then weld it fully

Which catalog number is which physical plate hasn't been confirmed against the builds, so place each by the donor's measured positions. Check: every stud within ±3 mm of the donor's X and Y (our estimate, inside the rubber mounts' give), the studs square to the body, and no plate movement when you torque its M8 nuts to 22 Nm (16 ft-lb). Builders:

  • moved the existing hanger and cut the passenger-side hanger off the donor (Tracks and Trails, 03:40);
  • swapped the non-M stud plate, whose studs are too short, for BMW's plate with the longer M3 studs, welded the extra M3 bracket behind it after hanging the exhaust to find the holes, and welded a third bracket to the passenger-side rail (M346 Projects – pt 14 (2024), 09:20);
  • cut the M3's extra bracket off the donor and welded it on. The poster calls it the "drivers side", but on a UK right-hand-drive car that's the right-hand (US passenger-side) bracket, 41112493931 (our reading) (PistonHeads).

Each of the three hanger stacks, from the body down: the stud plate's two M8 studs; bracket 18207839657 on two M8 flanged nuts 18307620549 at 22 Nm (16 ft-lb); rubber mount 18201401797; then an M8×45 bolt 07119902955 with collar nut 07119927022 at 20 Nm (15 ft-lb) into the muffler's tab (ETK; torques from Flow p.87). Fit every nut and bolt.

The rest of the exhaust. The US M3's front section 18107832909, intermediate pipe 18107832313 and muffler bolt together (ETK). The front and middle pipes went into Touring tunnels with no tunnel work reported on at least five builds (Tracks and Trails – first drive (2026), 58:20, M346 Projects – pt 14 (2024), 48:49, LC's Garage – Stromung (2019), description, The BMW Wagon Guy – S54 slicktop Touring, 03:34, Project BMW – wagon pulls hard (2021), 04:00), and none reported trouble at the RACP plates, the V-brace or the center bearing. They hang from the center support 18211436309, the same part your Touring already has; fit the M3's rubber mounts 18207832991 (two) in place of the Touring's 18211745426. The center-bearing bracket and the RACP are shared too, so only parts that differ can get in the way: the Touring's fuel tank, kit welds left proud (grind them, as the kits say), V-brace boxes welded away from the M3 positions, and the Touring's canister (we infer). Joints:

  • Front section to intermediate pipe: gaskets 18307830674 with M8×30 bolts and nuts, at 22 ± 2 Nm (16 ± 1.5 ft-lb).
  • Intermediate pipe to muffler: new gasket rings 18111723379 and 18101405737, flange 18111719417, and four M8×50 bolts 07119904533 with square nuts 11621741172, at 15 Nm (11 ft-lb) (Flow p.87).

The M3's three sections (front section, intermediate pipe and muffler) weigh about 42.6 kg (94 lb) against about 26.9 kg (59 lb) for the Touring's three, and most of the extra 15.7 kg (35 lb) is the muffler, behind the rear axle (our sum of BMW's catalog weights). Allow for it in your springs and in Massachusetts' ±2 in ride-height rule (Suspension for Touring weight).

Heat shields. Fit the M3's: the rear-silencer shield 51482494848 (1.3 kg, M3 and CSL only; $259.12 at BMWPartsDeal, October 2026) and the tunnel shield 51487893366 (ETK). Your Touring's rear shield, 51487037885 (370 g), is sized for the small non-M muffler and won't cover the M3 box (ETK). One builder found the M3 and Touring tunnel shields (51488193807 on your car) interchangeable, "Same same, but you know, different", and fitted the cleaner one (Tracks and Trails – first drive (2026), 58:20); the M3's is the one shaped for the M3 pipes. The M3's rear shield hangs on body studs with 18 mm-flange nuts 07146949379 (ETK, drawing). Count and photograph its studs on the donor floor before you cut, because a new floor may not have them. With the exhaust in its final position, check its clearance to the floor, fuel tank, battery tray and tires at full bump, and add a shield wherever the pipes come close to the tank, the cargo floor or the battery. After 20 minutes' driving, the cargo floor over the muffler should feel warm but not hot to the hand (our check; there's no published limit). The M3's front shields are wider, to clear its larger control-arm brackets (Project BMW – engine installed (2021), 00:20).

Canister and leak-test pump. On your Touring the charcoal canister and the DM-TL leak-test pump sit under the right rear of the floor, fore and aft, "in between the battery tray and the spare tire well" (Tenza Motorsports – No more SULEV (2021), 01:30); BMW's wiring system puts the MS45.1 car's pump in the "RH rear wheelhouse" (WDS). BMW moved them on the M3: the canister lies across the car just behind the differential, in an M3-only holder 16132229735 under an M3-only cover 51717893604, with M3 vent and purge hoses (WDS, ETK). The canister, the pump and the canister brackets on the floor (41128204385, 41128227776) are the same parts on both cars. On the M3 the holder sits on four M6 studs with self-locking nuts 07147153450. The studs may sit on the M3 floor or on the rear axle carrier panel, perhaps on the shared floor brackets, so find them on the donor before the floor is welded in (ETK). BMW's move suggests the Touring position clashes with the M3 muffler's right end, though nobody has proved it (our inference). With the well kept (option 4), leave the canister where it is. Move it only with an M3 floor, and expect to; check the Touring canister's clearance to the muffler at the Phase 5 mock-up, at full bump and full rebound:

  • Within 25 mm (1 in) of the muffler or its right hanger, or touching (the likely result): fit the M3 arrangement at the donor's position: holder 16132229735 ($92.19 at BMWPartsDeal, October 2026) with its four M6 nuts, cover 51717893604 (ETK), the M3 vent pipes 16132283286 and 16132229415, and the M3 rear purge line 16132229417.
  • Clear by 25 mm or more: either arrangement works. Keep the Touring's mounting and its covers 51718233265 and 51718233266, or fit BMW's M3 layout anyway: on Renner's Touring, which has a new M3 floor, "The EVAP system is from the M3" (Larry Chen (2025), 22:39).

Keep the donor's holder, cover and hoses when you strip it, so you have them either way. With a flat panel, give the canister a fixed mount and cover equal to one of these; no tested design exists. The parts for each floor are listed in Filler and EVAP.

This moves an emissions part into BMW's own M3 arrangement and removes nothing: the canister and the leak-test pump must stay connected, sealed and working. Route the hoses without kinks (Tenza had to re-make one so it wouldn't kink in the tight space by the subframe, 04:35), use new clamps, and make sure the pump's plug reaches without strain; if it doesn't, extend the lead with proper terminals (repair leads). Prove it with the DM-TL leak test and a completed EVAP readiness monitor.

Clearances at the mock-up. Pass values for the muffler hung on all three hangers, against the figures you took off the donor:

Check Pass
Hanger studs Within ±3 mm of the donor's X and Y (our estimate)
The donor's gaps: muffler to shield, shield to floor, muffler to diff and subframe, pipes to tank, straps and V-brace Within ±5 mm of the donor's (our estimate)
Tips Centered in the bumper cut-outs, or at the donor's offsets within ±5 mm (our estimate)
Exhaust to any fuel, brake or EVAP line, or anything that burns At least 25 mm (1 in), or shielded
Any fuel part to the exhaust At least 38 mm (1.5 in), or shielded
Full bump (bump stop compressed) and full rebound No contact anywhere
Rubber hangers Hanging straight, with no side load (our estimate)

Massachusetts publishes no clearance figures. The 25 and 38 mm rules are British Columbia's inspection limits, which we use as targets (BC Vehicle Inspection Manual (2016, amended 2018), pp. 101–102).

Massachusetts checks. The floor and the exhaust are both inspection items (Massachusetts):

  • Seal every seam and hole. 540 CMR 4.04(12)(d) rejects "holes or cracks, due to rust or otherwise, in the floor pans or other body panels which would permit the passage of exhaust gases into the passenger or trunk compartments" (540 CMR 4.04). Plug every hole in the new floor, seal every lap and plug-weld row on both faces, and light-test it before the carpet goes back: a lamp under the car, the cargo area dark, no light at any seam. Then water-test the cargo area.
  • Fit every hanger fastener. 540 CMR 4.04(5) wants exhaust components "securely fastened with fasteners in place and undamaged", and the exhaust to discharge "beyond operator, passenger, and/or trunk compartment". The M3 tips at the rear bumper do; an exit under the cargo floor wouldn't.
  • Keep the muffler stock. M.G.L. c. 90 §16 bans a muffler "cut-out or by-pass", a muffler "from which the baffle plates, screens or other original internal parts have been removed and not replaced", and an exhaust "modified in a manner which will amplify or increase the noise" (c. 90 §16). Fit the M3 muffler intact, with no valved, gutted or "delete" rear section. A CSL rear section was never US-certified, so treat one like an aftermarket part (our reading). The inspector revs the engine to check for noise, so keep the receipts and part numbers that show an unaltered BMW M3 system, and ask your station how it judges an M3 system on a 325i.

Manifolds, catalysts and torques. Keep the M3 manifolds, catalysts and all four O2 sensors; the Sloan Motors Touring's catless headers wouldn't pass a US emissions inspection (BMWBlog). Manifold to front pipe: new nuts and gaskets, 24 Nm (18 ft-lb). O2 sensors: 50 Nm (37 ft-lb), with anti-seize on the threads only. M8 flanges: 22 ± 2 Nm (16 ± 1.5 ft-lb) (Flow p.86). Muffler clamp 15 Nm (11 ft-lb), hanger body nuts 22 Nm (16 ft-lb) and hanger bolts 20 Nm (15 ft-lb), as above (Flow p.87).

Rear bumper and towing. Mark the tip cut-outs with the exhaust in its final position; the bumper itself is covered in Rear bumper, skirts and trim. The M3's diffuser and muffler sit where a tow hitch would go, and its bumper carrier can't take a tow bar (Autoalex v2 – update (2024), 11:20).

Welding settings and safety

Most of this build's welding is 1.5–2.5 mm plate onto thinner floor skins, much of it overhead, plus the floor and arch seams, on a car that has held fuel. Set up and practise before you touch the car.

What you'll join:

Part Thickness Source
Properparts plates 1.5 mm (16 gauge) Properparts
Condor plates 14 gauge (about 1.9 mm) Condor – plate install, coupe (2019), description
CMP chassis rail plates 2.5 mm, zinc-coated CMP
LBL M3 rear arch repair sections 1.2 mm m3cutters, unverified
Your trunk floor Not published. BMW's catalog weights (13.3 kg Touring floor, 12 kg M3 floor) suggest about 1.0–1.4 mm (our estimate) ETK; measure with a vernier caliper at a cut edge or the first drilled spot weld, paint removed
Your RACP, rail and rear-panel flanges Not published Measure as above
Your arch skins Not published. I-CAR puts typical outer panels "in the range of 0.70 mm", so expect about 0.7–0.8 mm (estimate) I-CAR; measure as above

Buy steel for a flat panel or fill strips no thinner than the panel you measured.

Wire, gas and settings. Miller recommends 0.023–0.024 in (0.6 mm) wire for body panels up to 1/16 in (1.6 mm), and 0.030 in (0.8 mm) wire for 20 gauge to 1/8 in (about 0.9–3.2 mm), which likely suits the plate-to-floor welds better. Use argon/CO2: BMW's E46 rule is 82/18 with G3Si1 or G4Si1 wire (sold in the US as ER70S-6), and 75/25 is Miller's usual mix for body work (TIS 41 00). Voltage and wire speed depend on the machine, so start from the chart inside your welder's door, and spot and stitch on panels rather than running long beads (Miller). Never use pure argon: one Touring builder who ran 100% argon by mistake "could not get a good solid bead" and re-welded the floor with the right gas (M346 Projects – pt 14 (2024)).

BMW's rules for replacing spot welds. BMW's E46 body-repair rules in TIS 41 00 say the same as its current rules, which I-CAR quotes (TIS 41 00, I-CAR CRN 1484, I-CAR CRN 503):

  • "Take the number and position of welding spots and MAG weld seams from the separated part. Replace areas inaccessible to spot-welding tongs with MAG plug welds at the same distance." MAG is MIG welding with an active gas such as BMW's 82/18 or 75/25.
  • Plug-weld holes are 8 mm (5/16 in) across, with at least 25 mm (1 in) between welds.
  • Keep the gap between the layers "as small as possible": "The larger the weld gap, the lower will be the strength of the joint." BMW gives no figure; aim for 1 mm (0.04 in) or less (our target).
  • Clamp the welder's ground "directly to the component to be welded".
  • Remove the paint about 30 mm (1.2 in) around each weld and on its back, remove the zinc layer too where you MIG-weld, and coat every overlap with weld-through primer.
  • Reseal every seam that was sealed, and don't MIG-braze in a repair.

I-CAR adds that a plug weld should stand no more than 3 mm (1/8 in) high (I-CAR (2022)). The home-welder way to meet all of this on the floor is to drill the spot welds from the cargo side and plug-weld down through the same holes into the new floor (Exhaust and the spare-wheel well). That gives you BMW's hole size, count and spacing, with no overhead plug welds. The factory spot welds should already be at least 25 mm apart, but count and measure them to check (our inference).

Test coupons. Before each new combination of thicknesses, weld coupons of the same materials: a kit offcut, or plate of the same gauge, over sheet of your floor's measured gauge, cleaned the same way. Weld them in the position you'll use on the car, overhead included, with plug welds through holes of the size you'll use: BMW's 8 mm on the floor, the kit's on the plates. Break each apart in a vise. The weld should have fused into both pieces, not sat on top of the thin sheet or blown through it. Compare each coupon with I-CAR's pass values (I-CAR practice welding guide (2023)), adjust and repeat until it passes, and record it on the worksheet.

Coupon Pass on the face Pass when broken apart
Plug weld, 8 mm hole (BMW's size; I-CAR's thick-thick coupon) 10–13 mm (0.4–0.5 in) across, no more than 3 mm high A 5–10 mm hole torn out of the bottom coupon
Plug weld, 6 mm hole (I-CAR's thin-thin coupon, for skins) 8–10 mm across, no more than 3 mm high; melt-through on the back 3–6 mm across and up to 1.5 mm high A 3–8 mm hole torn out of the bottom coupon
Lap (fillet) stitch, thin-thin 25–38 mm (1–1.5 in) long, 3–8 mm wide, no more than 3 mm high The top coupon tears out along the whole weld
Open butt, thin-thin 25–38 mm long, 3–8 mm wide Folded face to face, no cracks in the back of the weld

Distortion.

  • Use plug welds and short stitches, never long beads. Move between mounts, or around a panel, so no area gets hot, and let each area cool between passes. The rear arches use the same method.
  • Close the gap before every weld: dolly the flange flat, put a cleco or clamp at each hole, and weld only where the layers touch.
  • Measure the body diagonals before the first weld. Mark the four rear subframe mounting points and the front subframe points, measure both diagonals across each set with a tape or tram gauge (a plumb bob down to the floor helps), and write them down. Measure again after each session; a change of more than about 2 mm (our estimate of what a tram gauge repeats to) means the floor is pulling. BMW's body control dimensions are in TIS 41 00 (Phase 5).

Fuel, brakes, battery and electrics.

  • The fuel tank, filler neck and lines come out before any welding, with the lines capped (Garagistic K0536). Drain and store the fuel safely (see Safety).
  • Remove every fuel and EVAP part near a weld. The charcoal canister and the DM-TL leak-test pump sit under the right rear of the floor, between the battery box and the spare-wheel well (Tenza Motorsports – No more SULEV (2021), 01:30), on canister brackets on the trunk floor (ETK: trunk floor). The liquid-vapour separator, which the catalog calls an expansion tank (16136752641), sits in the right rear wheel well behind the trim, on bracket 41148196386, inside the arch you'll graft (BMW ST041 Part 3, ETK: floor). Cap every hose.
  • The brake pipes along the floor stay full of fluid through the build: unclip and move each one clear of a weld, or shield it, and keep every opened end capped (Safety).
  • Disconnect the battery (Garagistic K0536) and take it out: its tray is on the trunk floor you'll be welding (ETK: trunk floor).
  • Clamp the welder's ground directly to the part you're welding, on clean metal close to the weld, as BMW asks; never through bushings or suspension parts.

Fire. BimmerWorld warns that BMW's chassis coating "can be extremely flammable" (BimmerWorld), and undercoating, seam sealer and sound deadening smoulder. Strip them back from the weld, protect glass and anything you're keeping from spatter, and keep two extinguishers and a fire blanket within reach. BMW also warns of "combustible foam in welding area" when it replaces an E46 side panel (TIS 41 35 101, coupe, p.12), so look into the cavity behind every arch seam and cut any foam back before you weld. Keep watching after you stop: OSHA's workplace rule asks for a fire watch of at least 30 minutes after hot work (29 CFR 1910.252, unverified).

Fumes. CMP's rail plates are zinc-coated, and weld-through primer is zinc-rich. OSHA's welding-fume fact sheet names zinc fume as a cause of metal fume fever and calls for local exhaust ventilation at the arc, with a respirator where that isn't enough (OSHA FS-3647). Grind zinc coating off where you'll weld (M346 Projects – pt 14 (2024), 11:00), pull the fume away from you with an extractor, and wear a respirator rated for metal fume.

S54 refresh on the stand

The engine will never be easier to work on than now. Do these before it goes in.

Rod bearings. They're the S54's best-known weak point; BMW's service action replaced them on E46 M3s built from 02/2001 to 05/2003 (BMW SI B11 04 04). On the stand you can take the oil pump off for room; FCP Euro calls rod 1 the hardest part with the pump in place (FCP Euro – S54 rod bearings (2022), 51:17).

  1. Identify the bolts by their heads, not the build date. A 12-point head (12 mm 12-point socket) is the M11×1.25 bolt; an E-Torx head (E12) is the M10×1.25 bolt (SI B11 04 04). BMW changed over at 12/12–13/2002 production; the parts catalog and vendors say 02/2003, and a replacement rod can bring M10 bolts to an earlier engine (ETK).
  2. Buy the parts. BMW's current shells are blue on the rod side (11247835440) and red on the cap side (11247835439), with 0.25 mm undersizes for a reground crank (ETK, SI). BMW's 2001 TIS sheet, linked in step 4, mentions yellow-coded shells; the 2004 SI and today's catalog give blue and red. Late engines need 12 new M10 bolts (11247834310). BMW doesn't sell the M11 bolt, which is reused (BimmerWorld).
  3. Mark everything. Each cap goes back on its own rod, and each M11 bolt in its own hole: the "bolt from the exhaust side must be reinstalled again on the exhaust side" (SI). The rods are fracture-split, so a cap fits one way only (FCP Euro, 17:28).
  4. Measure the clearance with Plastigauge (BMW specifies Plastigage PG-1). Put the piston at bottom dead center and lay the strip on the clean, oil-free crank pin. Fit the cap with matching pair numbers, tighten the bolts as in step 5, then remove the cap and read the strip's width against the scale. BMW's range is 0.040–0.070 mm. Below 0.040 mm, fit new shells; if new shells still read below 0.040 mm, replace the rod (BMW TIS 11 24 571). FCP Euro and The Bimmer Barn quote 0.03–0.07 mm on camera (FCP Euro, 21:43, The Bimmer Barn – rod bearings (2022), 10:50); use BMW's figure. On M10 engines, measure with the old bolts and keep the new ones for final assembly, because BMW's procedure uses all three of their tightenings.
  5. Assemble. Remove the plastic, oil the crank pins and shells, fit the caps by their pair numbers and tighten with an angle gauge:
    • M11 (12-point): 5 Nm, then 30 Nm (22 ft-lb), then 70° in one continuous pull (TIS 11 24 571, SI).
    • M10 (E-Torx): new bolts, tightened three times. Each cycle is 5 Nm, 30 Nm, then 105° in one pull; back each bolt off about one turn between cycles, and leave the third cycle as final. BMW warns that not following it "will result in serious engine damage" (SI). FCP Euro cleans the new bolts with alcohol and then oils them; the SI doesn't say (FCP Euro, 20:27).
  6. Oil pump and pan. Oil-pump sprocket nut: 25 Nm, left-hand thread (SI). Check the pump housing for chain rub (FCP Euro). Oil-pan M6 screws: 10 Nm, with Hylomar at the timing-cover, block and bell-housing joints (SI); FCP Euro used RTV there, and Flow names Drei Bond 1209 (FCP Euro, 33:19, Flow p.53). Drain plug: 25 Nm with a new sealing ring (Flow p.53).
  7. Oil and break-in. After this job BMW's fill is 6.5 L of 10W-60, against 5.5 L for an ordinary oil change; check the dipstick. Break the bearings in for 1,200 miles below 5,500 rpm (SI). FCP Euro's video fills 6 L and suggests about 1,000 miles (FCP Euro, 47:21, 49:07); follow BMW. An oil change at the end of break-in is cheap insurance.
Warning

The Bimmer Barn's video says "5, 30 and 105 newton meters" for late engines and never mentions the three cycles (The Bimmer Barn – rod bearings (2022), 03:36). The 105 is degrees, and the M10 bolts need all three cycles.

ARP bolts. ARP's sheets give a stretch value first, and a torque only as a fallback with ARP's lube: for 201-6103 (M11), 0.0075–0.0080 in (0.19–0.20 mm) or 70 ft-lb (95 Nm); for 201-6102, sold for M10 engines, 0.0065–0.0070 in (0.165–0.178 mm) or 50 ft-lb (68 Nm) (ARP 201-6103, ARP 201-6102, BimmerWorld). The 201-6102 sheet names the BMW S50 Euro engine, so check thread and length against your rods. Both sheets say the rods "should always be re-sized after new rod bolts are installed", a machine-shop job that's practical with the engine on a stand. Never use BMW's angle procedure on ARP bolts. Log each bolt's free length; ARP says to replace any that grows more than 0.001 in.

Crankshaft end play. While the crank is exposed, check it with a dial gauge: 0.141–0.253 mm (Flow p.43).

Watch: FCP Euro – S54 rod bearings (2022), 20:51, Paul Vo – rod bearing torque (2017), 11:35, The Bimmer Barn – rod bearings (2022), 10:50 (Plastigauge; mind the warning above).

VANOS. Beisan Systems' procedure is the reference (Beisan); it quotes about 5 hours for a mechanic and 7 or more for a DIYer.

  • Tools. BMW crank-turning socket 83300491056, or a 36 mm 12-point socket on early engines, which have four Torx bolts at the crank hub (later engines have an adapter with a 27 mm hex); a 32 mm fan wrench; and water-pump pulley holder 83300491046 (Beisan). Add the S54 timing set, a cam bridge and crank locking pin (ECS Tuning – S54 valves and VANOS (2025), 01:30). Turn the engine on the four balancer bolts, never on the stamped cover's 32 mm hex (FCP Euro – S54 rod bearings (2022), 09:39), and inspect the balancer while it's exposed (FCP Euro – S54 valves (2022), 09:42).
  • Oil-pump disc and exhaust hub. Replace the oil-pump drive disc (Beisan BS025) and the seals, and inspect the exhaust hub. Its driver tabs can crack and drop fragments into the pump or pan. If the hub only has play, the new disc's tighter holes take it out; if a tab is cracked, replace the hub (Beisan).
  • Upper chain guide. BimmerWorld says that by about 85,000 miles it "is likely to be worn thin and may even be a bit broken at the tail end", causing rattle or VANOS faults; its kit replaces it with the exhaust hub (BimmerWorld). ECS found it broken on its car (ECS Tuning, 50:31).
  • Other updates in ECS's rebuild: S62 diaphragm springs and pressure plates, BMW's later Torx exhaust-sprocket bolts in place of hex bolts that can shear, and transfer-gear bearing parts lapped to a slight preload to stop "VANOS knock" (ECS Tuning, 42:13, 47:02, 48:51). ECS's on-camera torques aren't BMW-sourced; check TIS group 11 36.

Watch: ECS Tuning – S54 valves and VANOS (2025), 17:30, done in the car, with E39 M5 (S62) diaphragm springs and plates fitted in place of the S54's; its "magic tooth" and quarter-turn preload steps start at 56:13. Engine-out sequences, chapters only checked: OnlyyDans – S54 build pt 4 (2024), 29:19, CRANK – S54 timing (2023), 26:59.

Valve clearances. BMW's S54 training module gives intake 0.18–0.23 mm and exhaust 0.28–0.33 mm, measured with the coolant below 35 °C (BMW S54 module, ECS guide). Each valve has a 9 mm shim sitting loose in a pocket on its spring retainer, under a finger follower; a spring clip holds each finger on its shaft. To change a shim, release the clip, slide the finger aside and lift the shim out with a magnet (BMW S54 module, FCP Euro – S54 valves (2022), 20:22).

  1. Take the plugs out and turn the engine clockwise. Measure each valve with its cam lobe pointing straight up (FCP Euro, 17:49).
  2. Aim for the middle of the range: 0.20 mm intake, 0.30 mm exhaust (18:06, 25:31).
  3. Measure the old shim with a micrometer and choose the new one as old shim + (measured clearance − target). FCP Euro and ECS each moved one size, 0.04 mm, to correct a valve.
  4. Early heads have no screen in the oil-drain gallery to catch a dropped shim (16:34), so pack the valley with rags before you lift any shim.
  5. The videos disagree on reassembly torques: spark plugs 23 Nm against 25 Nm, valve-cover nuts 10 Nm against 8 Nm (FCP Euro, 31:23, 34:58; ECS Tuning, 1:11:04, 1:13:45). Use the TIS values.

Watch: FCP Euro – S54 valves (2022), 18:06, filmed on an S54-swapped E46 sedan; ECS Tuning – S54 valves and VANOS (2025), 12:50.

Throttle actuator and idle valve. One actuator drives all six throttles through plastic gears that wear; sudden limp mode with EML and DSC lights is the classic symptom (Pelican, Z4 M article on the same S54 actuator, unverified). Owners describe rebuild services for the E46 M3 and Z4 M actuators, and new units being no longer available (z4-forum). Test it, budget for a rebuilt unit, and clean the idle control valve.

Oil-pump nut. The nut that E36 (M52/S52) and M54 owners safety-wire is mostly a non-issue on the S54, though one forum member knows of an S54 that lost it at a track event. Owners use red Loctite, and some safety-wire it (NAM3).

Also while it's out: rear main seal, oil-pan gasket, valve-cover gasket, the CPV O-ring (the seal on the crankcase-vent constant-pressure valve, a known oil leak; BimmerWorld), water pump and thermostat, engine mounts and oil-cooler lines. Autoalex's donor had a "completely shot" water pump (Autoalex – build part 2 (2023), 08:40). Fit the secondary-air valve before the engine goes in (M3projekts – S54 install (2023), 14:00). Forum advice for a donor engine is to do the rod bearings, CPV O-ring, gaskets and VANOS before it goes in (e46fanatics).

Front axle and steering

Your front subframe can stay: BMW's catalog lists the same front axle support (31111096902) for every rear-drive E46, M3 included; only the xi differs (ETK, e46fanatics). The fasteners that meet the body or the subframe are shared too: the four subframe bolts, the control-arm bracket bolts, the strut-top nuts and the anti-roll-bar supports have the same part numbers, in the same quantities, on both cars (ETK: M3, ETK: Touring, ETK: top mounts). BMW slots every E46's strut towers for camber (BMW ST056), and the M3's top mount gets its extra caster from an offset center (BMW ST041), so the towers need no change (our inference). Tenza's 2004 Touring took "an entire M3 front and rear subframe" and the M3's aluminium plate, and found that "everything should be a direct bolt-on" (Tenza Motorsports – 5 things they don't tell you, part 2 (2021), 03:20, Tenza Motorsports – Front end with M3 parts (2021), 00:40, 06:00).

Almost everything bolted to the subframe changes. The M3 has its own control arms and brackets, struts, knuckles, hubs, top mounts, tie rods, rack, anti-roll bar, reinforcement plate and brakes. Its control arms also move the wheel slightly forward, so single parts don't simply swap across (e46fanatics), and the M3 knuckle takes a bigger lower ball-joint taper (e46fanatics). A UK 330i Touring that took M3 hubs for a big-brake kit also got new M3 lower arms, "slightly longer, which gives you a slightly different caster and potentially camber angle" (Autoalex v2 – We fitted expensive mods to our fast Tourings (2026), 15:40, 21:40). Move whole M3 corners rather than mixing parts.

The one thing to prove at mock-up: the reinforcement plate. BMW fixes the M3's aluminium plate with 12 M10×35 10.9 screws, six across the front and six across the rear, plus six small edge screws; your Touring's steel plate uses four across the front, four across the rear, whose threads are in the body, and three small screws (TIS 51 71 374, M3, Touring, ETK: M3, ETK: Touring). BMW says the M3 plate bolts to "the control arm joints, front axle carrier and the rear control arm mounts" (BMW ST041), and Tenza fitted one. But the M3 plate has one extra screw on each side of each row, and TIS doesn't say whether those threads are in the shared front axle support or in the body; the rear row's are the doubtful ones (our inference). Before you take the plate off the donor, note which part each hole threads into. At the mock-up, offer the plate up and run every screw in by hand before you order new ones; if a thread is missing, fit your own plate on its 8 screws.

Steering ratio. The M3's steering is slower than your Touring's. BMW USA's 2003 figures:

2003 US 325i Touring US M3
Overall steering ratio 13.7:1 15.4:1
Turns lock to lock 3.0 3.0
Turning circle 10.5 m (34.4 ft) 11.0 m (36.1 ft)

Sources: BMW USA spec sheets for the 325i Sport Wagon and the M3; BMW ST041 also gives 15.4:1 and 11.0 m. So with the M3 rack and knuckles you turn the wheel about 12% further for the same corner, through the same 3.0 turns, and the car needs about 0.5 m (1.7 ft) more to turn round (our arithmetic). Your DSC unit is coded for your own rack; what that means is in DSC, brakes and steering angle.

The ratio depends on the rack and on the knuckle's steering arm. The NAM3 steering thread measures rack travel per turn of the wheel (NAM3 steering thread):

Rack Travel per turn Ratio with M3 knuckles ETK number
Standard M3 47 mm 15.4:1 32132229397
M3 Competition (from 12/2004) and CSL 50 mm About 14.5:1 32132282642
330i and 330Ci M Sport II, 11/2000–04/2001 (for reference) 50 mm About 14.5:1 (13.7:1 in a 330i) 32132282296

The 14.5:1 figures are worked out from the travel numbers. The 32132282296 rack, often sold as the "ZHP rack", is listed in ETK only for those early M Sport II cars. If you buy a replacement rack, check that its hard lines clear the subframe; an aftermarket rack's lines hit it on 50sKid's car (50sKid – steering rack, non-M (2018), 23:35).

Power steering. The pump, pressure hose, suction hose, return pipe, cooling coil and the coil's return line are all M3 parts. The reservoir, its lid and bracket, the lower steering joint, the flexible coupling, the column and the steering-angle sensor are the same parts on both cars (ETK: M3 lines, ETK: Touring lines, ETK: column). The lower joint changed from 32301094700 to 32306764006 on both cars at 11/2003; keep whichever yours has. The M3's ZF pump makes up to 120 bar and delivers 11 L/min, and the M3 rack has no hydraulic end stops (BMW ST041), so at full lock the pump runs at its limit: don't hold the wheel there (our inference). The circuit runs reservoir → suction hose → pump → pressure hose → rack → return pipe → cooling coil in front of the radiator → return line → reservoir. Fit new sealing rings at every hollow bolt and banjo (50sKid, 10:58): Autoalex's 330i Touring had a weeping rack banjo (Autoalex v2 (2026), 20:40). Keep the lines clear of the anti-roll bar and oil pan; one owner's lines wore a mark in his pan (Paul Vo – rod bearing torque (2017), description). The fluid is ATF; filling and bleeding are in Brakes and bleeding.

When to torque what. Torque the whole front axle on stands except the anti-roll-bar clamp nuts. The compilation's cover note asks for the "loaded" position for suspension bushings (Flow p.1), but at the front its BMW annotations put that condition only on the anti-roll-bar clamps, "tighten in normal position to avoid preload" (Flow p.6). The control-arm bracket bolts carry "always replace" and no position, both there and in Department 69's TIS list (Flow p.2, Department 69). The arm's rear bushing is pressed into its bracket, not clamped by those bolts, so tightening them on stands doesn't twist it (our inference).

Fitting order and torques (Phase 8). Values are from Flow pp.2–14 and 28 and Department 69, which cites TIS, unless another source is named.

  1. Brake pipes first. When the old front axle comes out (Phase 4), cap every brake pipe end you open and keep the reservoir full, so no air reaches the DSC unit (Brakes and bleeding).
  2. Subframe. If it has to come down for the engine, unplug the headlight-level sensor lead first; the sensor drops with the subframe but its lead doesn't (FCP Euro – S54 rod bearings (2022), 11:19). Subframe to body, M12 10.9: new bolts (31116781023; TIS says replace), 110 Nm (81 ft-lb). Tighten the rear bolts first; their dowels center the subframe (40:37).
  3. Bench-build each corner: knuckle, hub, strut and top mount. Strut to knuckle: new M12 clamp bolt, 81 Nm (60 ft-lb). Damper rod nut: new, 64 Nm (47 ft-lb). The top mounts are handed, left and right. Only if you replace a hub (31222229501): a new collar nut (31211128336) at 290 Nm (214 ft-lb) (Flow p.14).
  4. Control arms. Arm to subframe: new M14 self-locking nut, 90 Nm (66 ft-lb). Arm bracket to body: new M10 bolts (33306760652), 59 Nm (44 ft-lb), on stands. Ball joint to knuckle: new self-locking nut, 65 Nm (48 ft-lb), no impact wrench.
  5. Strut tops. Three new nuts per side (31316769731) at 34 Nm (25 ft-lb). The M3's own TIS page gives 34 Nm for the E46's 21 mm-flange nuts; the 24 Nm (18 ft-lb) in the M3 compilation is TIS's figure for older models' 18 mm-flange nuts (TIS 31 31 1AZ, Flow p.3). Leave the camber pin in for a standard alignment: driving it out lets the mount move for up to about 0.5° of camber (BMW ST056).
  6. Reinforcement plate (51717893609): every screw run in by hand first (above). Then new M10×35 10.9 screws, rear row first, at 59 Nm (44 ft-lb) + 90° (BMW allows +30° on the angle), then the six small edge screws (TIS 31 10 8AZ, TIS 51 71 3AZ, SI B11 04 04). BMW: "Vehicles must not be driven without reinforcement plates."
  7. Anti-roll bar. End-link nuts: new, 65 Nm (48 ft-lb). Clamp nuts: snug now, then 21 Nm (15 ft-lb) with the car on its wheels in normal position, at the M3 load (Phase 12).
  8. Rack and tie rods. Rack to subframe: 42 Nm (31 ft-lb). Inner tie rod to rack: 110 Nm (81 ft-lb). TIS prints "100 + 10 Nm" for every E46, the M3 included, as the M3 compilation does, and 110 Nm meets it whether the "+ 10" is a tolerance or a final step (our reading). TIS's separate 110 Nm row is for the Z4 M (E85/E86 with the S54); that's the figure Department 69 gives for the M3 (TIS 32 21 2AZ, Flow p.9, Department 69). Outer tie-rod lock nut: 45 Nm (33 ft-lb). Tie-rod end to knuckle: new nut, 65 Nm (48 ft-lb), no impact wrench. Count the turns as you unscrew a tie-rod end, so the toe starts close (50sKid – steering rack, non-M (2018), 06:22).
  9. Center the rack before you join the steering shaft. Lock the column, set the wheel straight ahead, and line up the notch in the shaft with the coupler's pinch-bolt hole (FCP Euro, 39:54, 50sKid, 21:43). Fit new M8×33 Torx bolts at 22 Nm (16 ft-lb) (SI B11 04 04).
  10. Power-steering lines at the rack: M16 hollow bolt 40 Nm (30 ft-lb) and M14 banjo with its check valve 35 Nm (26 ft-lb), each with new rings (Flow p.8). At the pump, with the engine: the other M16 hollow bolt, 40 Nm. If the pump comes off: mounting bolts M8×80 21 Nm (15 ft-lb), pulley bolts 27 Nm (20 ft-lb) (Flow p.11).
  11. Wheel-speed sensors: your own, seated flush in the M3 knuckles, screw at 8 Nm (71 in-lb) (Flow p.4). The strut's sensor and hose bracket (34526780591/592) is the same part on both cars.
  12. Wheels: 120 ± 10 Nm (89 ± 7 ft-lb). Brakes, and filling and bleeding the power steering, are in Brakes and bleeding.
  13. Check before the wheels go on: every fastener torqued and paint-marked except the clamp nuts; each wheel spins freely; no sensor lead or brake hose under tension at full droop.
  14. Align, then calibrate. Have the car aligned in BMW's design position, at the M3 load with the ride height checked (Wheel alignment, After the build), before you calibrate the steering-angle sensor (DSC, brakes and steering angle). After rack or tie-rod work, "you absolutely need to get an alignment" (50sKid, 06:39). Caster can't be adjusted on an E46 (BMW ST056), so a caster reading inside the M3's window (7°25' ± 30' at ±10° lock) tells you the M3 top mounts and arms are in and the body is straight (our inference).

Watch: FCP Euro – E46 M3 control arms (2020), 15:58 (M3-specific; no captions, chapters only checked), 50sKid – steering rack, non-M (2018), 12:35 (same rack mounting; no torques).

Driveline and rear axle

Gearbox (420G) on the bench.

  • Seals: input shaft 35×52×7 (23121228493), selector shaft 15×21×6.5 (23127501582) and output 52×68×8 (23121222769) (Flow p.74).
  • Oil: BMW MTF-LT-2 (75W-80 GL-4) (BimmerWorld). BMW's US M3 owner's manuals give about 1.8 L (1.9 US qt), and ST041's "1.9 L" matches the quart figure (our inference), so buy 2 L and fill to the fill plug with the car level (2003 M3 coupe manual, p.147, BMW ST041); check the label on the gearbox. Drain and fill plugs (M24×1.5): 52 Nm; reverse-light switch: 20 Nm (Flow p.74). Undo the fill plug before the drain plug, so you know you can refill it.
  • Gear-identification switch (23142229113), an M3, M5 and Z8 part (ETK). The MSS54 reads the clutch through it for cruise control; the car starts and runs without it (NAM3). Check or replace it now; its wiring is in Harness and re-pinning.
  • Shifter and mounts: take the donor's complete shift carrier, lever and selector rod with new bushings, and its gearbox support (22312229198) and mounts (22322282340); your Touring's support (22316769911) is a different part (ETK). Gearbox mounts and crossmember (M8): 21 Nm (Flow p.78).

Clutch and flywheel.

  • Flywheel: BMW's TIS gives 105 Nm (77 ft-lb) for the S54, the same as the M54, with the threads oiled and no thread locker. Fit eight new M12×1.5×50 bolts (11222243051), which the parts catalog marks "required for repair" (TIS screenshot on NAM3, ETK), and tighten them in a cross pattern (Flow p.68). Ignore the 100 Nm in FCP Euro's non-M DIY (FCP Euro). An aftermarket single-mass flywheel follows its maker's sheet.
  • Pilot bearing (11211720310) and rear main seal: replace both (ETK, FCP Euro – E46 M3 clutch (2022), 11:54).
  • Pressure plate: the M3 uses six M8 10.9 micro-encapsulated screws (21207548052) at 34 Nm (25 ft-lb); fit new ones (ETK, Flow p.69). The 25 Nm in non-M guides is for 8.8 screws (Department 69). Center the disc with a clutch alignment tool.
  • Release parts: FCP Euro's M3 clutch job also renews the steel fork pivot pin (21511223281), the fork (21511223302) and the release-bearing guide tube (23117512866) (FCP Euro – E46 M3 clutch (2022), description).
  • Which flywheel: for a road wagon, a dual-mass flywheel with an OEM-type clutch is the quietest choice; single-mass flywheels bring chatter and gear rattle (NAM3).

Watch: FCP Euro – E46 M3 clutch (2022), 17:19 (no captions; chapters only checked).

Fitting the engine and gearbox (Phase 9).

  • Use the M3's engine arms and mounts, and check the gap between the oil pan and the steering rack and subframe brace before you tighten the mounts. Engine mount nuts (M10): 45 Nm; engine support arm to block (M8): 21 Nm (Flow p.54, FCP Euro – S54 rod bearings (2022), 41:26).
  • Two Touring builders had to make room. Project BMW lowered the engine and gearbox in together with the rack out (Project BMW – engine installed (2021), 05:20); Tracks and Trails dropped the front subframe: "I don't know how you guys get it in without dropping this subframe" (Tracks and Trails – first drive (2026), 55:40). Disconnect the oil-cooler lines so the cooler clears the crossmember (Project BMW – swap on jack stands (2021), 01:20).
  • Bell-housing Torx bolts: M8 28 Nm, M10 52 Nm, M12 98 Nm; confirm the M12 value in TIS, because Flow's own general table gives 82 Nm. Starter (M10): 45 Nm. Clutch slave cylinder nuts: 22 Nm (Flow pp.70–77).

Driveshaft. Use the complete M3 driveshaft (26112229240, 1,404 mm) with a new flex disc (26112226527), its bolts (26117635643) and self-locking nuts (26127536563), and a new center mount (26122282495) (ETK). Your 325i's 5-speed shaft (26111229557, 1,585 mm) is the same part in the sedan, coupe and Touring, so the M3 coupe's shaft should fit your car as it does an M3; measure before final assembly anyway (ETK). Don't try to combine halves. A shop told one swapper it's "NOT possible to make a driveshaft out of 2 different ones" (e46fanatics), and a 325Ci owner who kept his 5-speed with an M3 rear axle needed a custom hybrid shaft (e46fanatics).

  • Flex disc, M3 M12 10.9 bolts: 115 Nm, bolted to the shaft on the bench in Phase 3 and to the gearbox's output flange in the car in Phase 9. The value is the "M3 / M5, M12 10.9" row of BMW's all-model TIS table (BMW TIS 26 11); Department 69 and Flow give 115 Nm for the E46 M3. Turn the bolt, not the nut (Flow p.79).
  • Center mount: 21 Nm, preloaded 4–6 mm forward (Flow p.79).
  • Driveshaft to diff (M10 Torx): 70 Nm. The shaft is balanced, so mark its position before you take it off (Flow p.79; FCP Euro, part 3).

Clutch hydraulics. Your pedal, master cylinder and flex hose, and the slave on the donor's gearbox, carry the same part numbers on both cars (ETK). Only the hard line and its hose bracket differ, so fit the M3's (21522229675, 21522229699); the M3 line is insulated (Project BMW – engine installed (2021), 01:40). BMW's catalog lists the clutch delay valve (21526755892) for your 325i but not for the M3 (ETK), so the M3 line leaves it out; a few early-M3 owners report finding a differently designed valve (e30sport). Bleeding is in Brakes and bleeding.

Rear axle. The M3 rear subframe (33312282490) is a different part from yours (33316770865) but bolts to the same body points. Owners have fitted complete M3 rear subframes to non-M E46s (e46zone), and a Touring builder found "the bolts are the same" (Tenza – M3 rear end (2021), 15:00). What differs is everything bolted to the subframe: BMW lists M3-only trailing arms (33322229685/686), diff (33102282480) and parking-brake shoes (34416761293) (ETK), and swappers move the M3 half-shafts and sway bar with them (e46fanatics). Move these over together:

  • Trailing arms with hubs, brakes and parking-brake shoes. Your parking-brake cables fit them (ETK).
  • Half-shafts. They're a tight fit but go in (e46fanatics).
  • Wheel-speed sensors. Use your own, or those of a donor built from 09/2002. An M3 built before 09/2002 has inductive sensors for its MK20, with plugs that don't fit your harness and a signal your MK60 isn't made to read (manual). BMW lists the same current rear sensor for both cars (ETK), and on a 2003 xi Touring the M3 sensors "plugged right in", though only into the xi's Bosch harness, whose sensors use the same blue housings (e46fanatics). One S54 Touring, a 2004 car with a 2002 donor, showed an ABS light at its first start with its own sensors in the M3 hubs, but the car was standing and its brakes not yet bled, and three months later the builder reported no problems; it isn't evidence that the sensors don't suit (DSC, brakes and steering angle). His fallback of splicing in the donor's sensor leads would have put MK20 sensors on an MK60, so don't (Tenza – 5 things, part 2 (2021), 03:15, 04:00). Read the wheel speeds in INPA before you drive (DSC, brakes and steering angle).
  • Sway bar. The non-M bar hits the M3 diff (e46fanatics); use the M3's 21.5 mm bar (33552282181) and links (33552283743) (ETK).
  • Diff. Every E46 M3 has the same large-case diff (Redish: "Type 210/215") with the M variable lock (ETK, Redish). BMW USA's 2002 and 2003 spec sheets give its ratio as 3.62:1; BMW's 2006 sheet and ST041 print 3.64:1 (BMW USA, 2002, BMW USA, 2006, BMW ST041). Redish sells BMW Motorsport's 4.10 gear set (now 23008437087, £1,054 in October 2026) and recommends a Quaife unit to cure the "M clunk" (Redish). Fill it with BMW's friction-modified SAF-XJ+FM, not ordinary gear oil (Fluids and capacities). Drain and fill plugs: 60 Nm with an O-ring, 65 Nm with a sealing washer. If the output flanges come out, mark each flange bolt first and reassemble to the mark (Flow pp.80–81).
  • Subframe and diff mounts: new M3 parts (front 33312283573/574, rear 33312283419, diff front 33172282484) (ETK: M3 carrier). The push rod and V-brace are in Rear subframe mount reinforcement.

Assembly and torques (Phases 3 and 7). Values are from Flow pp.15–19 and 81–83 unless another source is named.

  1. Build the axle on the bench (Phase 3). Fit the rear control arms to the subframe before the diff: with the diff in place, one arm bolt can't go in (Tracks and Trails – Touring rear end (2025), 33:20). Then fit the diff and torque its mounts while you can reach them: front M14 bolt 200 Nm; rear M12 Torx bolts 20 Nm + 90° (Department 69, NAM3). Condor's diff-bushing video gives 128 ft-lb and 70 ft-lb, which look like Department 69's non-M figures swapped between the mounts (our inference); don't use them on the M3 diff (Condor – M3 diff bushings (2019), 01:32). Leave the rubber-bushed joints snug.
  2. Studs first (Phase 7). The subframe hangs on four mounts. At each front mount an M12×1.5 stud screws into the body: torque both to 90 Nm before the axle goes up (Department 69, FCP Euro, part 3).
  3. Raise it level on a table or transmission jack, because the subframe goes up over the studs (Tenza – M3 rear end (2021), 04:40). Line up the front studs first, then the rear bolt holes.
  4. Subframe to body: set the push rod with your kit's spacer plates over the front studs, then fit the self-locking collar nuts on the studs and one M12×1.5×116 bolt at each rear mount. Torque the collar nuts and rear bolts to 77 Nm, then the push rod's bolts to 21 Nm, BMW's figure (Rear subframe mount reinforcement).
  5. Joints that don't need ride height, as they go in: trailing-arm bracket to body 77 Nm, and the two M12 10.9 ball-joint bolts at each trailing arm (one of them the eccentric bolt) 110 Nm, with new nuts (Flow p.16, TIS 33 32 11AZ).
  6. Half-shafts to diff: the M3's black ribbed M10 Torx bolts (33211227664, 12 of them, new) at 100 Nm. The 80 Nm the compilation also prints is for silver bolts, not the M3's (FCP Euro, part 3, Flow p.83). Rear drive-flange collar nut: new, 300 Nm.
  7. At ride height (see Targets for the mock-up and the bushed joints): trailing arm to bracket (the through-bolt) 110 Nm (FCP Euro, part 2); control arms at the subframe 77 Nm; damper lower bolt 100 Nm. BMW's diagrams mark these three "loaded" (Flow pp.16–17). Do the anti-roll bar's brackets and links (22 Nm) at the same time: their mounts are rubber too, though the diagram doesn't say (our recommendation). Tracks and Trails approximated ride height by jacking under the axle until the car began to lift off its rear jack point (Tracks and Trails – Touring rear end (2025), 35:00). Without the engine and gearbox that leaves the suspension a little extended, so set each hub to its target hub-to-lip instead, or torque these joints once the car is complete on its wheels and loaded to BMW's normal position for an M3 (a full tank, 68 kg on each front seat, 14 kg in the cargo area).

Read: FCP Euro's written M3 rear subframe overhaul, part 1, part 2 and part 3.

325xi: rear drive or all-wheel drive

Read this if your Touring turns out to be a 325xi, the all-wheel-drive version BMW sold in the US for 2001–05. The rest of the guide assumes a rear-drive 325i. Behind the front seats an xi is the same car, so the floor, arches, rear-axle mounts and fuel system follow the guide. In front almost everything differs: the body, front axle, gearbox mounting, oil pan and DSC are all xi parts (BMW ST040). You can convert the car to rear drive, which is hard but feasible and what we recommend, or keep all-wheel drive, which is harder still and has already wrecked one S54's bottom end.

How to tell an xi

  1. Decode the VIN at bmwfans: it names an xi "325xi". Don't rely on NHTSA's decoder for this. It reads a 2001 325xi Touring's VIN as a "325i" wagon and gives no drive type (NHTSA vPIC).
  2. Read the vehicle order from the light module (ALSZ), as Phase 0 and the manual's Session 1 do. All-wheel drive is option $203 (BMW ST040). Note the type key in the order's * field as well, because Route 1 replaces it for one coding session. On cars built from 09/2001 it's also the VIN's characters 4–7: EN33 on a US 325i Touring (BMW SP-Daten V32), EP33 on the 2004 325xi Touring in Documented xi builds, whose VIN bmwfans decodes as a 325xi built in 11/2003. On an earlier car the type key doesn't settle it: BMW's coding data lists AW33 for the US 325i Touring of 09/2000–08/2001 (BMW SP-Daten V32), yet bmwfans decodes a May 2001 AW33 VIN as a 325xi, so go by the decode and $203 (our reading).
  3. Look underneath. An xi has a transfer case on the back of the gearbox, a prop shaft running forward along the left of the engine, a front differential bolted to the oil pan and two front drive shafts. Its DSC unit sits on the right of the engine bay with a blue 42-pin plug; a 325i's MK60 sits on the left, under the master cylinder (BMW ST056, WDS: xi, WDS: MK60).
  4. Note the build month. An xi built before 09/2001 stores a key code (ZCS) instead of a vehicle order, and BMW wants a changed ZCS to come from its technical hotline (BMW ST406). That makes the MK60 swap harder. A 2003 car has an order.

Rear drive or all-wheel drive: the verdict

Convert to rear drive: our recommendation. You fit the donor's complete M3 front axle, the M3 lower steering joint with its flexible coupling, the M3 gearbox crossmember on a fabricated adapter and the whole MK60 DSC system, then sell the xi's drivetrain. Three xi Tourings have been made rear-drive on M3 running gear, though none has documented its DSC swap. Our estimate is $0–$1,500 more in parts than the guide's plan with a donor built from 09/2002, or $1,000–$3,000 with an earlier one, plus 4–8 weekends.

Keep all-wheel drive only if all-wheel drive is the point. It keeps the xi's front axle and DSC, but it needs an oil system BMW never made, the 330xi six-speed and a matched pair of differentials. Two US cars have done it, and one wrecked its S54's bottom end through the oil system.

Route 1: convert to rear drive (recommended) Route 2: keep all-wheel drive
Extra cost About $0–$1,500 in parts with a donor built from 09/2002, $1,000–$3,000 with an earlier one, after selling the xi's drivetrain (our estimate; breakdown in Route 1) Not costed: no source splits it out. You buy a 330xi six-speed set, a matched pair of diffs, a second oil pan to rework, oil-pump parts, a Z4 M clutch, new front shafts and a custom steering line, and the donor's 420G, front axle, MK60 and diff go unused
Extra time 4–8 weekends (our estimate) More, and open-ended. The documented AWD car took 280 hours of mechanical work in all, and FCP Euro's went "over budget and over time" (BimmerLife, FCP Euro, part 2)
Difficulty Hard. In How hard each job is, "DSC and brakes" rises from Moderate to Hard, and "Front and rear axle transplant" from Moderate to "Moderate to hard" (our rating) Very hard: fabrication plus one-off integration
Risk Two undocumented jobs, the DSC loom with its coding and the gearbox-crossmember adapter, plus the front-subframe trial fit. Each one shows up on the bench or at mock-up An oil system BMW never made, which wrecked the bottom end of one of the two documented engines. Drivetrain torque above BMW's figures for the transfer case and diffs (our arithmetic). The MSS54-to-DSC 5.7 link is untested
What you keep Everything behind the front seats, the steering column and its angle sensor, the brake booster The xi's front axle, rack, DSC 5.7, rear axle, gearbox crossmember and rear prop shaft; on a car built from 03/2003, its transfer case and front prop shaft too
What you add The donor's front axle and MK60 system; the M3 lower steering joint with its flexible coupling; the M3 gearbox crossmember on an adapter; a DSC adapter loom The parts listed under Extra cost
What you get M3 handling and parts, and about 100 kg (220 lb) less weight, BMW's figure for the xi system (BMW ST040) Traction on snow and gravel, 17 mm (0.7 in) more ground clearance, and the xi's four-wheel brake traction control
Legal standing LEV in every model year, the S54's category (Emissions and Massachusetts for an xi). Once it can't drive all four wheels, Massachusetts' four-wheel-drive rules (540 CMR 6.00) stop applying (our reading) LEV in every model year too. Still a four-wheel-drive vehicle under 540 CMR 6.00: no wheel spacers, a track widened by at most 4 in (102 mm) through tires and rims, and the body level to within 2 in (51 mm) front to rear
Documented The Bring a Trailer car, JMCCRNA's and a 2004 car from Buffalo Baca's, and the Colorado car that became FCP Euro's "M3xi"

What differs on an xi body

BMW built the xi on "a specially designed body pan with a widened transmission tunnel and modifications on the driver's side to accept the transfer case", with "a completely new front engine carrier", reinforced front strut mounts and a new gearbox crossmember (BMW ST040). The parts catalog shows where (ETK: xi, ETK: 325i):

Area 325xi Touring 325i Touring and M3 What it means for you
Front frame rails, inner 41007037635/636: 325xi, 330xi and 330xd only (ETK) 41118234033/034, on every rear-drive E46 (ETK) The rear-drive front subframe probably bolts up, but prove it with the trial fit
Front frame rails, outer 41117029237/238 41117029239/240 As above
Strut towers 41007037637/638 41148234035/036 The top mounts, collar nuts and reinforcement plate (51717036781) are common. Check ride height at mock-up
Front anti-roll-bar body brackets 41117161089/032 41118239195/196 Check that the M3 bar's brackets seat; weld on the rear-drive pair if they don't

Front subframe fixings Two M12×1.5×140 collar screws at the front; at the rear, adaptors on four M10×50 bolts and two M12×1.5×50 bolts Four M12×1.5×100 collar screws (31116781023) The same M12×1.5 thread at the front, used differently at the rear
Left front seat console 41117037741 41118239493 BMW puts the xi's yaw sensor and the MK60's sensor cluster both under the driver's seat (BMW ST056); check the bracket holes
DSC unit mounting Right side, bracket 34516750966 Left side, bracket 34516752664 on body bracket 41148201492 The xi body has the left body bracket too (ETK)
Behind the front seats: rear-axle body insert (41117000246), rear wheelhouses, trunk floor and partition, tank, pump, senders, fuel and vent lines, parking-brake cables, exhaust hangers Same parts as the 325i Touring As in the guide The guide's plan applies. The xi adds a tank protective plate (16111183924): keep it. One gearbox-mounted exhaust bracket differs (18207502523 against 18311728547) (ETK, ETK: fuel, ETK: exhaust)

Route 1: convert to rear drive

You fit the donor's complete front axle with the M3 lower steering joint and its flexible coupling, mount the M3 gearbox crossmember on an adapter, and replace the Bosch DSC with the whole MK60 system (next section). The xi's transfer case, front differential and shafts, front subframe and rack come out. The M3 rear axle, floor, arches and fuel system go in as the guide describes.

Item 325xi Touring (yours) 325i Touring US M3 (donor) For an xi
Front axle support (subframe) 31101096954, with collar screws 31101095617, adaptors 31106768293/294 and bolts 07119902899 and 07149112451 31111096902, four collar screws 31116781023 Same as the 325i's, plus reinforcement plate 51717893609 The donor's, after the trial fit
Lower arms and their rear mounts 31126758533/534; ball joints 31126756695/696; brackets 31121139791/792 on the subframe 31122282121/122; brackets 31126783376 on the body 31122229453/454; brackets 31122229623/624 on the body The donor's

Part numbers are from ETK (xi front axle, M3 front axle, xi gearbox mount, M3 gearbox mount, xi DSC sensors, M3 DSC, xi rear brake pipes, M3 rear brake pipes from 09/2002, fuel filter). Check every number against your VIN.

The gate: trial-fit the front subframe before you commit. The xi's front frame rails are their own parts and its subframe fastens differently, so nobody can promise that the rear-drive subframe bolts up. Three xi Tourings run M3 or rear-drive front subframes, and none of their builders reported making mounts (Built for Backroads, vmax.si, e46fanatics). BMW bolts the xi subframe to "the vehicle frame at both the front and rear attachment points", and its front screws use the rear-drive thread, only longer, so we expect it to fit (our inference). Prove it at the start of Phase 5, before any cutting, with the xi's front axle out:

  1. Offer up the donor's subframe, arm brackets and reinforcement plate on loose screws. All four M12×1.5 collar screws (31116781023) must start by hand and run to full depth, the rear dowels must engage, and no mount face may show a gap before torque.
  2. Every M10 screw must start by hand at each arm-bracket and reinforcement-plate hole.
  3. Fit the anti-roll bar on its brackets. Both bushing brackets must seat on their studs, and the bar must clear the oil pan, rack and lines at full lock and full bump.
  4. With the subframe off again, measure the diagonals across its four body mounting points and write them down, as the guide does at the rear (Phase 5): they're your reference for the welding that follows.

If a screw won't start, stop. Measure against BMW's body dimensions and get a body shop's view. Fit thread inserts only where those dimensions confirm the position.

Note

Keep the xi's front axle, transfer case, gearbox and DSC until the trial fit passes. They're your way back to Route 2 or to a stock car.

Gearbox crossmember. The xi's cast crossmember (22316750856) bolts to the xi tunnel with two M8×22 and two M8×60 bolts. The M3's (22312229198) needs four M8 threads at the rear-drive positions, which the xi tunnel may not have (ETK: xi, ETK: M3). JMCCRNA's converted xi needed a custom bracket, which then clashed with its Euro exhaust (e46fanatics), and the Bring a Trailer car's seller lists a custom brace across the xi tunnel (Bring a Trailer).

  1. Phase 1: on the donor, measure where its crossmember bolts sit against its driveshaft center-mount studs and its front subframe's rear screws. That's your template.
  2. Phase 5: make an adapter, or weld in nuts at the rear-drive positions (Welding settings and safety).
  3. Phase 9: fit the M3 crossmember as the guide does, M8 bolts at 21 Nm (15 ft-lb) (Driveline and rear axle). Pass: the 420G's mounts sit square without force, and the exhaust clears the adapter.

Steering. The xi's lower steering joint is a double-cardan part made for the xi rack (32306750815 to 11/2003 or 32306764009, with double joint 32306754165). Fit the M3's (32301094700 to 11/2003 or 32306764006) with its flexible coupling (32301094703) (ETK). The column (32303450159) and steering-angle sensor (32306793632) are common to all three cars, so they stay (ETK).

Anti-roll bar. The M3 bar's bushing brackets (31351094552) clamp onto studs on the body brackets, and the xi's body brackets are made for a bar that runs round the front diff and shafts. If the M3 brackets don't seat, weld on the rear-drive body brackets (41118239195/196, €7.85 and €7.81 list at bmwfans, October 2026) at the positions you measured on the donor (ETK). In Phase 2, cut the donor's brackets out with margin to use as templates.

Driveshaft, fuel, heat shields and clutch line.

  • Driveshaft: the M3's (26112229240, 1,404 mm (55.3 in)) with its center mount (26122282495). The xi's shaft is only 1,244 mm (49.0 in) because its gearbox and transfer case are longer. The M3 shaft should fit if the center-mount studs sit where rear-drive cars have them (our inference). Pass, as in Driveline and rear axle: the center-mount bolts start by hand with the shaft fully home, and take 21 Nm (15 ft-lb) with 4–6 mm (0.16–0.24 in) forward preload.
  • Fuel: the guide's plan applies. Use the donor's filter cover if the xi's (13327500083) doesn't clear the M3 filter-regulator (ETK).
  • Heat shields: fit the donor's tunnel shields, or trim the xi's, in Phase 10.
  • Clutch line: fit the M3 hard line as the guide does, and check its route along the xi tunnel.

Extra cost (our estimates; the euro figures are BMW list prices at bmwfans, October 2026):

Anti-roll-bar body brackets, if needed €7.85 and €7.81, plus welding Same

MK60, sensor cluster, four sensors, master cylinder with pressure sensors, reservoir, pipes The donor's $800–$2,500, used or new (new: sensor cluster €360.48, master cylinder €328.81, pressure sensors €93.64 each)

Tunnel heat shields $0–$150 Same
Selling the xi's drivetrain and DSC Recovers perhaps $300–$1,500 Same

Extra time: 4–8 weekends: the front-end trial fit and transplant, with any anti-roll-bar brackets, 1–2; the crossmember adapter 1–2; DSC hardware and pipes 1–2; the loom and coding 1–2 (our estimate).

Route 1: swap the Bosch DSC 5.7 for an MK60

The xi's DSC can't stay. BMW: "The front sensors of the 2wd and 4wd versions of E46 are physically different and will not fit in the wheel hub", and the MK60's rear sensors "will fit in the rear axle of the 4wd car however they are not compatible with the Bosch system" (BMW ST056, pp.17–18). M3 hubs need MK60 sensors, so you need the MK60 and everything around it. On a converted xi the guide's Option A, keeping your own unit, doesn't exist, and its Option B (DSC, brakes and steering angle) needs more than the unit. The 2004 Buffalo xi kept its Bosch unit, and its seller listed that as a known flaw (Built for Backroads).

Sources: BMW ST056, ETK: xi, ETK: M3, WDS: CAN.

Use a donor built from 09/2002. It brings every left-side part: the MK60 with its bracket and mounts, the sensor cluster with its bracket, all four sensors, the master cylinder with both pressure sensors, the reservoir and cap, every brake pipe and clip, and above all its DSC harness branch. A 325i built from 09/2001 is the second source; with its unit, use the 325i master cylinder and the M3 front hoses. An earlier M3's MK20 sits on the right like the xi's unit, but it has other sensors, another plug and its own charge pump, and nobody has documented it in an xi: don't use it (our inference).

Build the adapter loom by signal, never by pin number. The two plugs number their pins differently. On the MK60, pin 24 is the sensor cluster's ground and pin 6 its supply, so moving the xi's wires across pin for pin would put PT-CAN high on a ground and a battery feed on the sensor supply (our inference from the WDS drawings). Cut the donor's DSC branch out long before you strip the donor: the 47-pin plug with every lead back to its next joint, labelled at both ends. Then join it to the xi harness signal by signal. "Move" means re-terminate the xi's own lead at the MK60 pin:
