Sources: WDS MK60 supply, front sensors, rear sensors, sensor cluster, pressure sensor 1, pressure sensor 2, parking brake, DSC button, fluid level, CAN; the DSC 5.7's supply and overview. One WDS steering-angle page also draws the MK60's CAN on pins 24 and 40 (SP0000017308); the CAN-bus page contradicts it, so trace the twisted pair on the donor's plug before you cut.

Safety

Disconnect the battery before you work on the loom. Fuse each MK60 battery feed at 30 A, as on the 325i (F56 and F61): the xi's 50 A feed (F35) was sized for the Bosch unit (our inference). DSC is a safety system, so if a check below fails, find the cause before you drive.

Make the dead circuits safe. The xi's pre-charge pump, hill-descent and analogue-sensor circuits go dead. So does a separate flat-tire warning unit (36236753289), if your car has one, because the MK60 from 2002 does that job itself (BMW ST056). Insulate each lead end and tie it back. The steering-angle sensor stays: it's the same part, on the same pins, on both systems.

Checks before the first key-on (Phase 11):

Check Pass If it fails
Battery disconnected, MK60 plugged in: resistance across the CAN at the DME or cluster (CAN bus resistance) About 60 Ω About 120 Ω: the MK60 isn't on the bus, so recheck pins 11 and 15
MK60 unplugged, battery connected: voltage at the harness plug Battery voltage at pins 1 and 32 only; pin 4 live only with the ignition on; pins 16 and 47 grounded; nothing at pin 6 (our check) A feed on the wrong pin: stop and re-pin

Checks after coding (Phases 11 and 12, after Session 5's compensation routines):

Check Pass If it fails
Identification and fault memory INPA identifies the MK60; the fault memory is clear after the routines Recheck CAN pins 11 and 15 and the ignition feed
Pressure sensors About 0 bar with the pedal released; the brake-light switch changes state before either sensor reads 5 bar (73 psi) (BMW ST056) Swap the two sensors' leads; check their supply
Steering angle About 0° with the wheel straight, after the post-alignment calibration Recalibrate (Session 7)
Wheel speeds All four within about 1 km/h (0.6 mph) rolling straight at a steady 20 km/h (12 mph) (our check) Swapped sensor leads, or an xi sensor left in
Lamps ABS, DSC and yellow BRAKE lamps out after the self-test; red BRAKE lamp out with the parking brake off and the reservoir full Read the faults; check the BRFN and FSB leads

Route 1: code the MK60 from an xi order

The rule BMW applies. Your xi's order carries $203 and the xi's type key. BMW's coding data allows every non-M MK60 coding index only when the order doesn't say ALLRAD (all-wheel drive), and the M3's index only when it says S54B32, as an M3 type key does (BMW SP-Daten V32, E46SGVT.000). So NCS should refuse to code an MK60 from your stored order (our reading of the rule).

  1. Write your VIN into the MK60, as Session 5, Option B, describes.
  2. Set up the session order as Option B does, read from ALSZ, with one more change: delete $203. For the M3's MK60, Option B already gives the session order the donor's type key, which says S54B32 and also removes the xi's. For a 325i's MK60 coded with 325i values, put in the US 325i Touring's type key, EN33, instead (BMW SP-Daten V32). Don't run FA_WRITE: the change lasts for this session only.
  3. Code, check and keep the coding as Option B does, then run all three compensation routines, because the unit is new to the car.

Expect: "coding ended", with no "Codierindex … nicht zulässig". If NCS refuses, check that the session order has no $203, an allowed type key and a late enough date.

Leave the stored order alone. The light module keeps your xi's order, $203 and type key included, and the M3 cluster keeps the donor's, exactly as on a 325i (Session 4). The MSS54 isn't coded from the order, so $203 doesn't reach it, and your xi VIN goes into the MSS54, the cluster and the MK60 as a 325i's would (our inference). One light-module difference: BMW codes the xenon headlight-levelling sensor curves differently for ALLRAD cars, so with xenons, check those values in Session 9 (BMW SP-Daten V32, E46CVT.000).

Steering angle. Calibrate with the MK60's job, lenkwinkel_dsc_abgleichen in DSC_MK60.PRG, not the xi's test_lenkwinkel (Session 7).

For Route 1, buy a donor built from 09/2002, of your xi's model year or newer

Route 2: keep all-wheel drive

Keep all-wheel drive only if it's the reason you want the car. You keep the xi's front axle, rack, DSC and rear axle, and put the S54 into the xi's driveline. That needs three things BMW never built: an S54 oil system that clears the xi's front axle, an S54-rated gearbox with a transfer case, and a matched pair of differentials with the gearing you want. Two US cars have done it; one wrecked its S54's bottom end through the oil system (BimmerLife, FCP Euro, part 1).

How the driveline is laid out. The gearbox drives the NV 124 transfer case on its tail. The NV 124 sends 62% of the torque back down the tunnel to the rear diff on a 1,244 mm (49.0 in) prop shaft, and 38% forward on a 723 mm (28.5 in) shaft that runs along the left of the gearbox and engine to the front diff. The front diff is bolted to the left side of the oil pan. The left front shaft runs straight from it; the right one runs through a tube welded across the front of the pan to a support bracket with a bearing on the pan's right side, then out to the hub. Both prop shafts turn at the same speed (BMW ST040, ETK). The S54's headers sit on the right, next to that shaft.

What changes against the guide's plan:

  • Oil pan and pump: your xi pan, reworked around a single-stage pump (below).
  • Gearbox, transfer case and diffs: the 330xi six-speed and a matched pair of diffs (below).
  • Front axle, steering and DSC: keep the xi's (below).
  • Rear axle: keep the xi's, with the rear half of your matched diff pair. The guide's M3 rear axle doesn't apply: its 3.62 limited-slip diff has no front partner.
  • Body, floor, arches, fuel, cooling, wiring and coding: as the guide describes. Keep the xi's tunnel insulator, center underbody screen, right engine-mount heat shield and gearbox exhaust bracket, which are shaped for the xi (ETK).
  • Left over: the donor's 420G, front axle, MK60 and diff.

Route 2: the oil pan, and why a shared gasket proves nothing

Same gasket, same pan? No. BMW uses one oil-pan gasket, 11131437237, on essentially every M50, M52, M54, S50, S52 and S54 six since 1997: the rear-drive 325i, the 325xi and 330xi, the M3, the Z4 M and the E36 M3 (ETK). It fixes the flange where the pan meets the block, and nothing more: the rear-drive 325i's pan (11131432703) takes the same gasket and is a third, different pan (ETK). What matters sits inside the pan, and there the xi and the S54 clash:

  • The xi pan carries the front axle. BMW: "The differential for the front axle is bolted to left side of the engine oil pan. … A connecting tube is welded into the oil pan. A shaft runs inside of the connecting tube between the front differential and the axle shaft on the right side" (BMW ST040). The tube crosses the front of the pan, on the front axle line.
  • The S54's pump draws from the front of the pan. "The S54 oil pump is two stage, supply and scavenge … the scavenge chamber (1) draws oil from the pickup at the front of the oil pan" (BMW ST041). Its pump (11417838123) and pickup (11417834887) are shared only with the Z3 M and Z4 M, and the pickup and its return pipe (11417834889) are made for the M3's pan (ETK, ETK).
  • The "330xi pan" is your own pan. Both documented builds bought a "330xi oil pan". ETK lists one pan, 11137519432, for the 325xi, the 330xi and the M54 X3 (ETK). Even the M54's pickup differs between the xi and the rear-drive pan (11417502667 against 11417503258), so the sumps differ too (ETK). Buy a second xi pan to rework and keep yours as a spare.
  • Both builds changed the pump. Each fitted a single-stage M50-family pump, which has no front scavenge pickup, and machined or re-made the pan. Baca's car also has an S52 windage tray (BimmerLife, German Cars For Sale). The US M50, M52 and S52 pump is 11411740154 and the tray (oil deflector) 11131433060 (ETK, ETK). The pump's sprocket nut is a left-hand thread: the Colorado car's builder welded it, and a vendor sells a shaft kit for this conversion (Turner, unverified). Neither build says which pickup it ran.

What went wrong on the Colorado car. After FCP Euro bought it, "the oil pump chain was digging into the pan, and the pickup tube didn't have enough clearance to supply oil properly". The result was "spun bearings, cracked rods, and a damaged crankshaft" (FCP Euro, part 1). The mechanic found the engine full of "really fine aluminum dust", yet the oil filter "looked clean". The fix was a rebuilt bottom end and a new pan cut from the old one "with correct clearances", with baffles. The car then covered 1,600 "trouble-free miles" (FCP Euro, part 2).

Safety

No BMW part fits this combination, and nobody has published the xi pan's inside dimensions. Treat the pan, pump and pickup as a fabrication job that you prove by measurement, not a parts swap. Prove it before the engine goes into the car.

The checks that would have caught it. BMW publishes no values for this combination, so the pass values come from your own two engines. That approach, and every pass value below except the guide's 0.7 bar, is our inference.

When Check Pass
Phase 1, donor running A mechanical gauge at the oil-pressure switch's port, as in Phase 12. Record the pressure and oil temperature at hot idle, 3,000 rpm and 5,000 rpm Readings recorded: they're your pass values. 5,000 rpm keeps the later test inside the S54's break-in limit
Phase 4, the M54 out of the car but still in its xi pan Modelling clay on the pan's front wall facing the pump sprocket and chain, and under the pickup mouth; pan on with its gasket, crank turned two full turns, pan off; measure the clay Both gaps recorded: they're your minimums
After that, the S54 on the stand (bench work) The M50-family pump, pickup and deflector fitted; the reworked pan trial-fitted on clay with its gasket; the crank turned two full turns by hand No contact anywhere, and no clay thinner than the M54's gaps. If it fails, rework the pan and repeat
Same, after the baffles The clay check again; the xi dipstick tube against the S54's intake side The same pass; the tube fits without force
First fill A measured fill against the dipstick You know the volume that reaches each mark. The level sensor is common to both pans, but its warning point follows the xi pan's shape
First start The gauge at hot idle, 3,000 and 5,000 rpm At least 0.7 bar (10 psi) at hot idle (the guide's figure) and at least the donor's reading at each speed and oil temperature. Any shortfall: stop
About 800 km (500 miles), then 1,600–2,400 km (1,000–1,500 miles) Oil analysis for aluminium Aluminium not rising between samples. Don't rely on the filter: the FCP car's looked clean

Route 2: gearbox, transfer case and differentials

Not your five-speed. The 325xi's five-speed is "S5D 320Z" in ETK and "S5D-280Z" in BMW's training text (ETK, BMW ST034). In BMW's naming that number is the torque rating in Nm (BMW ST045), so either way it's below the US S54's 355 Nm (262 ft-lb) (BMW ST041) (our reading). No build used it.

Fit the 330xi six-speed, as both builds did. It's the ZF GS6X37BZ (23007563053), built from 03/2003 (ETK). BMW ran the S54 through the same gearbox family in the Z4 M (GS6-37BZ, 23007837983), where it makes "262 lb-ft at 4900 rpm" (ETK, BMW ST601). The 330xi box's input guide tube and seal are the Z4 M's parts, and the Z4 M pairs the M3's dual-mass flywheel (21212229900) with its own clutch set (21217837984, disc 21217837095) and the M3's release bearing (21511223582) (ETK: clutch, ETK: seals). So the M3 flywheel with the Z4 M clutch is BMW's own way of joining an S54 to this gearbox (our inference). Fit the flywheel as the guide does (Driveline and rear axle). The Colorado car ran a 330 clutch kit, which fits the spline but is built for M54 torque.

Buy it as a set. Take the box with its NV 124 transfer case (27107530812), both adapter shafts, the 723 mm (28.5 in) front prop shaft (26207525970) and the six-speed shift parts (ETK: prop shafts, ETK: shift parts). A 325xi built from 03/2003 already has that transfer case and front shaft. An earlier one has the older pair (27107509763, and a 718 mm shaft), so use the 330xi's (ETK). The crossmember (22316750856) and the 1,244 mm rear prop shaft are the same on both cars: keep yours.

There is no all-wheel-drive 420G. ETK lists the M3's gearbox (23002229721) for the E46 M3 only, with no transfer-case version (ETK). The Baca car's sale listing says "420G", but BimmerLife's "330xi six-speed" is the account that fits.

No gear switch. The 330xi box carries only a reversing-light switch (23147524811). The 420G's gear-recognition switch, which the MSS54's clutch chain expects, isn't there (ETK, Clutch switch, gear switch and cruise). Without it the car starts and runs, but cruise doesn't work (Driveline and rear axle). Bridging the switch's plug would make the DME read "in gear" whenever the pedal is up, even in neutral; nobody has tested that (our inference).

Transfer case. The NV 124 is a single-speed gear unit with an open planetary center: "Torque Distribution: 38%: 62%. Maximum Torque: 300Nm", with both outputs at the same speed (BMW ST040). That 300 Nm (221 ft-lb) is below the US S54's 355 Nm (262 ft-lb) and equal to the US 330xi's own engine torque. Yet BMW fitted the same NV 124 part numbers to the European 330xd (ETK), a diesel of 390–410 Nm (288–302 ft-lb) (BMW Group Classic, unverified). So 300 Nm isn't the case's hard limit, but BMW never rated it behind an S54 (our inference). It takes 0.24 L (0.25 US qt) of MTF-LT-1 (83229408942), with drain and fill plugs at 33 Nm (24 ft-lb); BMW lists only its three oil seals and its mount as repairable (BMW ST040).

Matched differentials. The NV 124 turns both prop shafts at the same speed, so the front and rear diffs must have the same ratio. BMW never sold a mismatched pair and publishes no tolerance, and both builds changed both diffs together. With an open planetary center a small mismatch wouldn't bind the driveline, but it would keep the planetary turning all the time; nobody has tested that, so don't (our inference). Both builds fitted X3 3.91 pairs (the X3 2.5i's ratio), which shorten the gearing about 11% against an M3's. The xi automatic's 3.46 pair comes within 2% of the M3 and is E46 xi hardware at both ends (ETK: xi front, ETK: xi rear, ETK: X3 front, ETK: X3 rear):

Pair, front and rear Part numbers First gear, overall Against the M3's 15.30 Notes
3.23, 325xi manual (yours) 31507526216 (31507500797 before 03/2003); 33107500783 14.05 8% taller Stock
3.46, 325xi and 330xi automatic 31507500799; 33107531623 (or 33107531622) 15.05 2% taller Our pick: the xi's mountings, 94 mm rear flanges and support bracket
3.64, X3 3.0i (M54) 31507523653; 33107523667 15.83 3.5% shorter X3 diffs need the changes below
3.91, X3 2.5i (the builds' ratio) 31507523651; 33107537722 17.01 11% shorter As above

The overall ratios are our arithmetic: first gear 4.350 times the diff, assuming the 330xi box has the GS6-37BZ's petrol ratios, which ETK doesn't print, against the M3's 4.227 × 3.62 (BMW ST045, BMW ST041). Bench-check each diff before it goes in: hold both output flanges so they turn together and count the input turns for one output turn. Pass: the stated ratio within a tenth of a turn (our check).

  • X3 diffs need adapting. The X3's rear output flanges have an 86 mm bolt circle against the xi's 94 mm. Moving your E46 flanges into it should work, since the seal (33107505604) and lock ring (33131214961) are common, but neither build says so (our inference). The X3 front diff shares the xi's seals, gaskets and bolt size, but its support bracket differs (31507516064): keep the xi's (31537500850, $166.73 at BimmerWorld, October 2026) and its right-hand shaft.
  • Not the M3's limited-slip diff. Its 3.62 has no front partner, and it's a larger unit with other mountings. FCP Euro fitted a Wavetrac limited-slip unit in a matched-ratio diff instead (FCP Euro, part 1).
  • Tires. BMW asks for tires "of the same manufacture and tread configuration" on an xi (2004 Sports Wagon owner's manual, p.127). The M3's 225/45R18 front and 255/40R18 rear tires are within 0.2% of each other in diameter (our arithmetic).

Torque margins (our arithmetic). In first gear a US S54 puts about 1,544 Nm (1,139 ft-lb) into the NV 124: 587 Nm forward and 957 Nm back. With 3.91 diffs that's about 2,294 Nm (1,692 ft-lb) at the front axle and 3,744 Nm (2,761 ft-lb) at the rear, 15% and 25% above BMW's figures of 2,000 Nm (1,475 ft-lb) and 3,000 Nm (2,213 ft-lb) for the two diffs; with 3.46 diffs it's 2% and 10% above (BMW ST040). BMW doesn't say where its figures apply. Neither documented car has reported a diff, transfer-case or shaft failure, over roughly 16,000 km (10,000 miles) and 8,000 km (5,000 miles) (our estimate).

Route 2: front axle, DSC 5.7 and what is still open

Keep the xi's front axle and rack. The M3's front axle can't carry drive shafts. Keep the xi's subframe (31101096954), steel arms, struts, knuckles, hubs and front shafts (605 mm and 926 mm, 31607505199/200), and its rack (32136759815) with its lower joint (BMW ST040, ETK). Fit new front shafts and keep a spare, as both builds did; Baca's are new GKN units (BimmerLife, German Cars For Sale). FCP's driver found the xi rack less quick and communicative than an M3's (FCP Euro, part 2).

  • Brakes. The 330xi's 325 × 25 mm front brake (discs 34116864047, calipers 34116765881/882, carriers 34106765880) bolts to the xi knuckle used from 03/2002 (31216759311/312) and its dust shields (ETK). The M3's 325 × 28 mm brake needs longer carrier bolts (M12×1.5×41, 34116767217), M3 dust shields and possibly machining.
  • Engine brackets. Use the xi's brackets (left 22116750853, right 22116750852) and mounts; its left mount is already the M3's part (11812283798). The right bracket should bolt to the S54, because the 325i and M3 share theirs. The left differs between the 325i and M3, so offer the xi's up and check. Use bolt lengths that suit the S54's iron block: the M3 uses M8×26 and M8×35 where the M54 uses M8×34 (ETK: xi, ETK: M3) (our inference).
  • Power steering. The S54's pump and the xi rack share no hose, so plan a custom pressure line; both builds appear to have made one (our inference).
  • Ride height and wheels. Keep the car at the xi's stock height or higher. BMW cut its front spring travel by about 20 mm (0.8 in) for the shaft angles, and the Colorado car wore out its front CV boots when lowered (BMW ST040, German Cars For Sale). BMW also gave the xi 17 × 7.0 wheels "to ensure there is enough room for the front axles and brakes", so check M3 wheels and brakes at full lock and full bump.

Keep the DSC 5.7. It's the only unit that reads the xi's Bosch sensors and runs four-wheel ADB-X, its brake-based traction control, and an MK60's front sensors won't fit the xi's hubs (BMW ST040: DSC 5.7). Keep its sensors, yaw sensor and steering-angle sensor too. Its coding comes from your car's order, so the engine change gives no reason to recode it (our inference). Whether it talks cleanly to the MSS54 is undocumented. The DSC 5.7 reads engine speed and fill from the DME and sends road speed back, and the MSS54 logs a fault if the DSC's or the steering-angle sensor's message goes missing (SGBD: DSC57, SGBD: MSS54). The M3 cluster takes the DSC and yellow brake lamps over CAN, while the DSC 5.7 drives the ABS lamp directly. Run these checks:

Check Pass If it fails
Phase 0, before anything changes: Tool32 DSC57.PRG → FS_LESEN, then STATUS_IO_LESEN_ANALOG with the wheel straight No stored faults; STAT_LENKWINKEL_WERT near 0°. This is your baseline Fix the xi's DSC first
Key on, engine started, car rolled a few metres The DSC, yellow BRAKE and ABS lamps light, then go out Read both fault memories
MSS54 fault memory None of 131 (0x83) DSC intervention implausible, 132 (0x84) DSC message timeout, 133 (0x85) steering-angle message timeout or 134 (0x86) cluster message timeout; no fault of type "DSC meldet V-Fehler" 132: no road speed from the DSC, which also stops cruise. 133: the steering-angle sensor's message isn't what the MSS54 expects
DSC57.PRG → STATUS_IO_LESEN_CAN at idle and at 3,000 rpm STAT_MOTORDREHZAHL_WERT matches the tachometer, and STAT_NORM_FUELLUNG_FAHRER_WERT rises with throttle The DSC 5.7 isn't reading the MSS54: check the CAN at the DME
MSS54 STATUS_V_CAN on a drive Matches the speedometer As for fault 132
After the alignment: DSC57.PRG → TEST_LENKWINKEL Job OK and ABGL_LWS_ID returned; about 0° straight ahead; DSC lamp off Repeat with the wheel dead straight
Low-speed traction test on a loose surface The DSC lamp flashes and power drops during wheelspin; with DSC switched off, ADB still brakes a spinning wheel (BMW ST040: DSC 5.7) Read the faults

Mechanical checks (our checks; BMW gives no figures):

When Check Pass
Phase 9 xi engine brackets on the S54 Every hole lines up without force; full thread engagement in the iron block
Phase 9, at full droop and full bump with the steering at both locks The headers against the right front shaft and its support bracket; the front prop shaft against the starter and oil-cooler lines; the exhaust against the NV 124 and tunnel insulator No contact, with every heat shield refitted. A rub mark found later is a fail
Phase 8, at full droop The front CV boots Not stretched or kinked
About 800 km (500 miles) The NV 124, diff and gearbox seals; the boots; any rub marks Seals dry, boots intact, no marks

Still open. Nobody has published:

  • the clearance between the S54's headers and the right front shaft and its support bracket, or between the M3's front pipes and the NV 124;
  • whether the xi's left engine bracket bolts to the S54 block;
  • whether the MSS54 and the DSC 5.7 talk cleanly (the checks above settle it for your car);
  • the xi pan's inside dimensions, how either builder reworked it, and which pickup each ran;
  • an S54 oil-pressure figure on an M50-family pump, and torque ratings for the GS6X37BZ, NV 124 and diffs behind an S54;
  • how the MSS54's clutch chain should be wired without the gear switch.

Emissions and Massachusetts for an xi

An xi is the best case for the engine-switch rule. EPA certified every 2001–05 325xi Sport Wagon in a LEV test group, the S54's category. For 2004–05 that meant California LEV and federal Bin 9, exactly as for the S54 (EPA certification data):

Model year 325xi Sport Wagon test group Level The S54 (M3), same year
2001 1BMXV02.5M54 or 1BMXV03.0LER LEV 1BMXV03.2S54, LEV
2002 2BMXV03.0LER LEV 2BMXV03.2S54, LEV
2003 3BMXV03.0LER LEV 3BMXV03.2S54, LEV
2004 4BMXV03.0LER LEV (California), Bin 9 (federal) 4BMXV03.2S54, LEV and Bin 9
2005 5BMXV03.0LER LEV (California), Bin 9 (federal) 5BMXV03.2S54, LEV and Bin 9

So under the "same emissions certification category" test in Massachusetts, an xi matches in every year, where a 2003–05 325i Touring may be ULEV or SULEV (our reading). Your VECI label should name an LER group; if it names another, go by the label. EPA's policy also expects a donor of the same model year or newer.

Ride height. Your Massachusetts baseline is your xi's own height, which BMW lists 20 mm (0.8 in) above a 325i Touring's: 1,429 mm (56.3 in) against 1,409 mm (55.5 in) (2004 Sports Wagon owner's manual). Record it in Phase 0 as the guide describes (Massachusetts ride-height baseline). A rear-drive conversion on M3 axles will probably sit lower than that, so check your spring choice against the 2-inch rule at mock-up (our inference).

The four-wheel-drive rule. 540 CMR 6.00 covers "Any vehicle that is capable of providing torque to all four wheels". In place of the general 2-inch rule it sets such a vehicle's own limits for raising or lowering it more than two inches from the maker's height; it also keeps the body level to within two inches front to rear, bans wheel spacers and limits a track increase through tires and rims to four inches (540 CMR 4.04(13), 6.01, 6.03, 6.04). A Route 2 car stays under it, so check the M3 wheels' widths and offsets against it, and in Phase 0 also record the height the way 6.00 measures it: unladen, from the floor to the lower edge of the driver's door at its center line (6.03). A Route 1 car can't drive all four wheels, so 6.00 no longer applies and the general 2-inch rule does (our reading; say so in your letter to the RMV).

Title and insurance. Massachusetts titles don't record the drive layout, and no rule we found ties certification or title to it. The VIN will still decode as a 325xi. Tell your insurer the car is now rear-drive, and keep the receipts. Ask MassDEP whether it treats the change of drive as part of the engine switch (Questions for your state program).

The Colorado car and the "rivet-flare" S54 Touring that BMWBlog showed in 2018 are the same car: listed in Denver in November 2018 and sold through Glen Shelly in March 2019 to FCP Euro's Daniel Sloan. BimmerLife names one more all-wheel-drive S54 builder, Austin Sera, whose car isn't documented.

Suspension for Touring weight

Your finished car rides on M3 axles but keeps the Touring's body, its heavier rear and its door-label load ratings. At the front, M3 coupe parts suit it as they are. At the rear it needs more spring than an M3 coupe. BMW's own ride-height method and its figures for both cars give you targets and checks from the donor to the alignment.

  • Decide by Phase 3. The arches are cut and welded around the mock-up in Phase 6, so buy the final springs, dampers, wheels and tires first.

Weights and axle loads

Compare like with like. BMW USA's spec sheets give US curb weights, which include a full tank. The 1,495 kg (3,296 lb) DIN weight that BMW ST041 gives the M3 coupe leaves out the driver and assumes 90% fuel, so don't set it against a US figure.

Car, manual gearbox US curb weight Front axle Rear axle Door-label ratings: front / rear / GVWR
2003 325i Touring 1,525 kg (3,362 lb) 727 kg (1,604 lb) 798 kg (1,758 lb) 900 / 1,210 / 2,045 kg (1,984 / 2,668 / 4,509 lb)
E46 M3 coupe 1,549 kg (3,415 lb) 779 kg (1,718 lb) 770 kg (1,697 lb) 970 / 1,150 / 2,020 kg (2,138 / 2,535 / 4,453 lb)
E46 M3 convertible 1,715 kg (3,781 lb) 856 kg (1,887 lb) 859 kg (1,894 lb) 990 / 1,170 / 2,100 kg (2,183 / 2,579 / 4,630 lb)
Your S54 Touring (our estimate) 1,584–1,614 kg (3,490–3,560 lb) 760–772 kg (1,676–1,702 lb) 824–842 kg (1,817–1,856 lb) Your Touring's: 900 / 1,210 / 2,045 kg

The axle loads are BMW USA's curb weights times its weight distribution: 47.7/52.3 for the Touring, 50.3/49.7 for the M3 coupe and 49.9/50.1 for the convertible (BMW USA: Touring, BMW USA: M3, 2003). The 2002 and 2006 M3 sheets print the same weights. The ratings come from BMW's US owner's manuals (2004 Sports Wagon, p.162, 2003 M3 coupe, p.146, 2003 M3 convertible, p.152).

  • The stock Touring is lighter than an M3 coupe, but heavier at the back. In like-for-like US terms it weighs 24 kg less, yet carries about 28 kg more on its rear axle.
  • How we estimate your car. We add to the 325i Touring what the M3 package adds over a 330Ci coupe in BMW USA's figures: +33 kg front and +26 kg rear for the S54 and 420G, the M3 axles, brakes, 18-inch wheels, exhaust and panels (BMW USA: 330Ci). The upper end also adds what a 330 weighs over a 325i. Allow ±20–30 kg for equipment, fuel and aftermarket parts, and weigh the finished car on corner scales if you can. Tracks and Trails calls his "a 3600lb wagon" (Tracks and Trails – what it takes (2026), 34:20), which fits the upper end once extras are added. One finished S54 Touring was weighed on corner scales: 3,606 lb (1,636 kg) with a full tank, roof rack, spare tire and an E36 M3 muffler, 48/52 front/rear, cross-weight 49.66% with the driver, and a center of gravity 21.25 in (540 mm) off the ground on stock M3 springs and 245/40-17 tires (NAM3 – Black & Tan 332iT #25 (2023)). With a lighter battery it read 3,550 lb (1,610 kg) at 48.5/51.5, about 781 kg front and 829 kg rear (#52).
  • The door label binds the finished car. BMW: "Approved axle loads and approved gross vehicle weight must never be exceeded" (manual, p.162). Read your own door-pillar label in Phase 0; the 2004 manual's ratings are very likely the 2003's, since the curb weights match. The swap uses about 60–90 kg (130–200 lb) of the Touring's 520 kg (1,146 lb) payload (our estimate).
  • The front axle has little to spare when loaded. At curb it has 128–140 kg in hand. Loaded the way BMW loads a non-M E46 for ride height (68 kg in each front seat, 68 kg on the rear seat and 21 kg in the cargo area), it carries about 844–856 kg against its 900 kg rating: only about 45–55 kg (100–120 lb) to spare. The rear then carries about 965–982 kg against 1,210 kg. These are our estimates, with assumed seat positions.
  • Not for towing (our recommendation). BMW gives the M3 no trailer load (BMW AG's data table in the Flow PDF), and the US Sports Wagon manual has no towing section (manual).

Use the M3's parts at both ends. Only the rear spring needs choosing for the Touring.

Part numbers are from ETK: Touring front, M3 coupe front, M3 convertible front, M3 spring pads, M3 coupe front bar, M3 convertible front bar, Touring rear, M3 coupe rear, M3 convertible rear, Touring rear bar, M3 rear bar, levelling.

  • Front: M3 coupe parts. Your car's front axle load is within 1–3% of an M3 coupe's (our estimate), so the coupe's struts, springs, top mounts and pads should stand it at about M3 coupe height. A convertible's front springs were picked for about 856 kg, so on your car they would probably stand the nose high (our inference). With a convertible donor, order coupe springs from a dealer against a coupe VIN, or fit M3 coilovers. Don't put non-M springs on M3 struts: the M3's upper spring pocket and pad differ.
  • Rear springs: about 7–9% stiffer than an M3 coupe's. Your rear axle carries about 824–842 kg (our estimate), between the coupe's 770 kg and the convertible's 859 kg. To sit and ride like a coupe, it needs about 7–9% more spring rate and preload (our estimate). Moved-over M3 coupe springs and dampers sat Tenza's Touring so low that the wider rear tires rubbed its unflared fenders and the bumper (Tenza – coilovers (2022), 00:40, 01:20). The rear spring pads and the lower control arm that carries the spring are common to the Touring, the sedan and both M3s, so any E46 rear-drive barrel spring fits: choose by rate and height. One S54 Touring ran stock M3 springs on Koni dampers with 6 mm spring spacers to sit "more to ZHP height", then fitted late (ZCP) M3 springs, which set it 2 mm higher in front and 9 mm higher at the rear than the early springs with spacers; the early springs were marked with yellow stripes, the late ones blue (front) and green (rear) (NAM3 – Black & Tan 332iT #150, #598 (2026)). On another, Eibach M3 coilovers at full height still sat about 1 cm lower than the owner wanted (NAM3 – #12). In order of preference:
    1. The heaviest M3 rear spring, 33532283137, which fits the convertible and is also one of the coupe's choices (our inference from FCP Euro's fitment notes), checked against your measured heights.
    2. M3 coilovers with a rear spring about 10% stiffer than the kit's (see Coilovers for the M3 axles).
    3. M3 coupe springs with added height, from a height-adjustable perch or BMW's European rough-road upper pad (14.5 mm, 33531094754, with adapter 33531091598; our inference). The rate stays the coupe's, so the rear still sags more under load.
    4. Your Touring's own "reinforced" or "heavy duty" rear springs (Lesjöfors 4208445 and 4208446). They fit the M3 rear arm, which carries the spring on the same lower arm and pads, but their rates aren't published, so judge them by measured ride height (FCP Euro).
  • Order springs by VIN. ETK lists no spring numbers for any of these cars: BMW picks springs from a spring table by each car's weight and options, through its own parts catalog (FCP Euro). Before you order, ask a dealer for the front and rear spring numbers against an M3 coupe VIN and an M3 convertible VIN. FCP Euro's fitment notes give the candidates: M3 coupe front 31332283130, M3 convertible front 31332282332, M3 rear 33532283135, 33532283136 or 33532283137 (the convertible takes 33532283137, the heaviest), and for a manual 2003 325i Touring front 31331093068 (standard) or 31331093082 to 31331093085 (sport) (FCP Euro, FCP Euro, FCP Euro). BMW publishes no rates. No maker sells springs for an M3-axle Touring: H&R 29419, Eibach 2067.140 and Vogtland 951069 are for the non-M Touring's axles (springrates), while Ground Control's M3 coilover kit takes any Eibach rate (Ground Control). Before teardown, photograph the paint marks on the donor's springs and the symbol on each front strut, which BMW's repair instructions match to the suspension version (BMW ST056).
  • Rear dampers and top mounts. Fit M3 dampers on M3 top mounts with the M3 trailing arms. BMW says the M3's rear shock-mount hole pattern "is the same as on the standard parts" (BMW ST041), and ETK lists the M3 mount 33526779670 on every non-M E46 convertible too, cars that run the Touring's own dampers (ETK). Both mounts take the same self-locking M8 collar nuts 07119905374, new, at 28 Nm (21 ft-lb), and a new M10×1 rod nut 33526773882 at 14 Nm (124 in-lb) (Flow p.17, ETK). The convertible's damper (33522282267) was built for a rear axle load close to your car's, the coupe's (33522283105) for 770 kg (our inference: BMW publishes no valving). Bilstein's replacements show why your Touring's own dampers don't suit the M3 arm: its B4 for every non-M E46 rear (19-103150) runs 370–618 mm, its B4 for the M3 (19-199511) 377–597 mm, both with a 12 mm lower eye and a stem top (ShockWarehouse: M3, ShockWarehouse: non-M). A non-M damper bolts on but extends 21 mm further, and the rear damper is also the rebound stop, so use M3 dampers. The same Bilstein and Sachs parts serve both M3 rear numbers, 33522283105 and 33522282267 (FCP Euro).
  • Rear damper tops sit behind the cargo-area trim on the Touring (Tracks and Trails – M54 removal (2025), 08:00).
  • Anti-roll bars. Keep the M3's 26 mm front and 21.5 mm rear bars. The convertible's 27 mm front bar is BMW's own bar for a heavier M3, and an OEM way to add understeer if the rear-heavy Touring feels loose (our recommendation).
  • No self-levelling. No E46 Touring had it, US or European: ETK's Touring rear axles list no level-control parts, and BMW's level-control training covers only the E34 and E39 Tourings and the X5 (ETK: European 330d Touring, BMW ST056).

  • Mind the lowering. Set fully down, the M3 kits with published ranges sit 30–58 mm (1.2–2.3 in) below a stock M3, and Massachusetts allows no more than 50.8 mm (2 in) up or down from your Touring's original height (Massachusetts). Set the height against your Phase 0 baseline (below), not by the kit's range.
  • What builds used: KW coilovers (Sloan), Bilstein PSS10s (BaT car), BC Racing coilovers set "a little bit softer on the rear" (Autoalex – finished car (2025), 15:40), Bilstein struts with Eibach springs (Tracks and Trails – Touring rear end (2025), 00:20), ECS Tuning coilovers, which fixed Tenza's low stance (Tenza – coilovers (2022), 01:40), Eibach coilovers with Ground Control camber plates (NAM3 – puma1824/M3Projekts (2022)), Eibach coilovers later swapped for TCK-valved Konis (NAM3 – Kaiv's first S54 Touring), Koni dampers on stock M3 springs (NAM3 – Black & Tan 332iT), Ground Control coilovers (NAM3 – Redshift's S54T) and Moton 4-way coilovers (Built for Backroads listing). None of them published spring rates, and only one published measured heights (above). Check a coilover kit's height range against the Touring's weight before you buy.

Ride height: BMW's method and figures

How BMW measures. Ride height runs from the lower edge of the wheel rim to the lower edge of the wheel arch, read on a metric tape with 1 mm divisions. The front figures are in TIS group 31 and the rear in group 33 (BMW ST056, BMW ST503). TIS for the E46 M3 says: "attach tape measure to bottom middle of rim flange and measure to lower edge of wheel arch" (BMW TIS screenshots on NAM3 (2024)). Bounce each corner and roll the car a few feet first, on a level floor with the tires at placard pressure.

Which load. BMW measures ride height in "normal position": it unloads the car, then puts in its DIN load (TIS 32 00). The load depends on the model:

Model BMW's normal-position load
E46 M3 Full tank; 68 kg (150 lb) on each front seat, seats in their middle position; 14 kg (31 lb) in the middle of the trunk (TIS 32 00, M3)
Your 325i Touring Full tank; 68 kg on each front seat; 68 kg in the middle of the rear seat; 21 kg (46 lb) in the middle of the cargo area (TIS 32 00, non-M E46)

BMW's US training manuals say M3s are "usually … measured without any weight" (ST056) and call the car without added weight the "normal position" (ST503). The E46 workshop manual itself, TIS issue 12/2007, loads the M3 as above, so follow TIS. A person makes a good 68 kg; bags of known weight make the rest. For each US gallon short of a full tank, add 3.2 kg (7 lb) in the cargo area, BMW's allowance in ST056.

BMW's M3 figures, from TIS 31 00 and 33 00, at the M3 load (TIS 31 00, M3, TIS 33 00, M3; the NAM3 screenshots above are these pages, and the Bentley manual's 605 mm front figure, quoted in the same thread, agrees). On 18-inch wheels that's about 359 mm front and 341 mm rear from the hub center to the arch edge (our arithmetic):

M3 wheels Front Rear Tolerance
18-inch 605 mm (23.8 in) 587 mm (23.1 in) ±10 mm (0.4 in); left and right within 10 mm of each other
19-inch 619 mm (24.4 in) 600 mm (23.6 in) The same

BMW's figures for your Touring, from TIS 31 00 and 33 00, at the Touring load, ±10 mm with left and right within 10 mm (TIS 31 00, Touring, TIS 33 00, Touring). The label on each front strut gives your row: "6Z Serie" for standard suspension, "6Z Sport" for the lowered sports suspension (TIS 32 00):

Touring wheels Standard, front / rear Sports suspension, front / rear
15-inch 576 / 542 mm 561 / 526 mm
16-inch 589 / 555 mm 574 / 539 mm
17-inch 604 / 570 mm 589 / 554 mm
18-inch 617 / 583 mm 602 / 567 mm

A 2003 US 325i Touring came on 16-inch wheels as standard and on 17-inch wheels with the Sport Package's sports suspension, so expect 589/555 mm or 589/554 mm (our reading of BMW USA's fitments). BMW also publishes the 325i Touring's overall height: 1,409 mm (55.5 in), or 1,444 mm (56.8 in) with roof rails (2004 Sports Wagon manual, p.161). Sport suspension sits about 15 mm lower (BMW ST043).

  • Rim size changes BMW's number, not the car. BMW's figure starts at the rim, so a bigger rim raises it by about 12.7 mm (0.5 in) per inch of rim diameter with the body where it was. Record hub-to-lip too, from the hub center up to the same arch edge: it doesn't depend on the rim. Your Touring's Phase 0 and Phase 12 readings won't compare either way, because the wheels and the arches both change; compare body points measured from the floor instead (Massachusetts ride-height baseline).
  • M3 tires lift the body. Unloaded tire radii: 205/55R16 316 mm, 225/45R17 317 mm, 225/45R18 330 mm, 255/40R18 331 mm. The M3's 18-inch tires alone raise the body about 14 mm (0.6 in) at the same suspension position (our arithmetic).
  • M3 suspension holds the body lower on the hub. The M3 coupe and the 330Ci coupe are both 1,372 mm (54.0 in) tall on tires 12–14 mm larger in radius, so the M3's hub-to-body height is about that much less (our inference). Set to M3 heights, your car should stand within about 10 mm of a standard-suspension Touring's roof height, or about 15 mm above a Touring that left the factory with sport suspension (our estimate). Both are well inside Massachusetts' limit of 50.8 mm (2 in).

Targets for the mock-up and the bushed joints

Mock-up targets (Phase 6) combine the donor's measured heights with BMW's figures; Measure and mock up before you cut has the steps:

  1. In Phase 1, measure the donor on its own BMW 18- or 19-inch wheels, loaded to the M3's normal position (above, with the fuel allowance if the tank isn't full): BMW's ride height at each corner, plus its hub-to-lip and hub-to-body. On other wheels BMW's figure doesn't apply, so refit M3 wheels to measure.
  2. If it reads BMW's figure ±10 mm, with left and right within 10 mm, it stands as BMW built it: copy its hub-to-body.
  3. If not (tired or aftermarket springs, or damage), set each hub so that BMW's ride height, read on your Touring with the M3 wheels fitted, matches BMW's figure. The two cars' arch openings sit at about the same height (Measure and mock up before you cut), so that puts your hubs about where an M3's sit.
  4. If your springs or coilovers will set the car higher or lower than an M3, use your own target, and write it on the worksheet.

Don't load the stripped shell to ride height: it weighs far less than the finished car and rides high. Support the body on stands, take the springs out (or leave coilovers loose), jack each hub to its target, and check full bump and symmetry; at the front, also check the tires at full lock both ways. These positions decide where the rear arches are cut and welded. While the axle is in, also note how far each rear hub rises from its target height to full bump. That rise, taken from the hub-to-lip the new lip is marked at, gives the full-bump hub-to-lip that the loaded check in Phase 12 uses.

Rear bushed joints (Phase 7). Torque the trailing-arm through-bolts to 110 Nm (81 ft-lb), the control-arm bolts at the subframe to 77 Nm (57 ft-lb), the damper lower bolts to 100 Nm (74 ft-lb) and the anti-roll bar's brackets and links to 22 Nm (16 ft-lb), with each corner at its target hub-to-lip: the height the finished car will sit at in the M3's normal position. Either:

  • jack each rear hub until hub-to-lip equals its target, with the body still on its stands; or
  • wait until the car is complete on its wheels and loaded to the M3's normal position.

Don't jack until the body starts to lift. Without the engine and gearbox the car is lighter than when finished, so that leaves the suspension a little extended. Pass: hub-to-lip within 5 mm of target at each corner as you tighten (Card 7c).

Front bushed joints (Phase 12). Only the anti-roll bar clamp nuts, 21 Nm (15 ft-lb), wait for ride height, with the car on its wheels at the M3 load. The control-arm bracket bolts, new, at 59 Nm (44 ft-lb), are torqued on stands in Phase 8.

Massachusetts ride-height baseline

Massachusetts bars a car raised or lowered "by more than two inches above or below the original manufacturer's specified height" (c. 90 §7P) and publishes no way of measuring one. BMW's ride heights for your Touring (above) are the manufacturer's specified height, but they're measured to the arch edge, and the arch lips can't stay the reference: the rear ones are replaced and the front fenders change. So in Phase 0, before anything changes, load the car to BMW's normal position for your Touring (above), set the tires to placard pressure, and record:

  • BMW's ride height and hub-to-lip at each corner, against BMW's figure for your suspension; the arch work uses them too;
  • the roof height at marked points front and rear, or at the roof-rail tops. BMW publishes 1,409 mm (55.5 in), or 1,444 mm (56.8 in) with rails, for a 325i Touring;
  • the height of each of the four jacking points;
  • the door-pillar label and the label on each front strut.

After the build, measure the same points the same way, at the same load. Pass: the roof and every jacking point within 50.8 mm (2 in) of Phase 0. Our target: within 25 mm (1 in), to leave room for load and measuring error. Expect the M3's 18-inch tires alone to add about 14 mm. Keep the readings and BMW's published height in the car's file.

After the build: settle, check and align

  1. Settle the springs with 5–10 miles (8–16 km) of driving, then load the car to the M3's normal position and measure BMW's ride height. Pass: BMW's M3 figures in the table above, ±10 mm, or within 10 mm of your own target if you chose one; left and right within 10 mm; the tires clear the lips and inner arches at full lock both ways. Then load it as in Phase 0 and check the Massachusetts baseline above. Fail: springs wrong for the axle load, most often at the rear: adjust the perches, change springs, or trim the rear with the pad.
  2. Loaded check (our recommendation, not a BMW figure). Load the car as you'll use it fully loaded, staying under the door-label ratings (a public scale settles any doubt), and set the fully loaded tire pressures (Wheels, track and offsets). Pass: static rear hub-to-lip at least 30 mm above its full-bump figure from Phase 6; no tire contact when you bounce the rear; headlights still aimed in range (xenon cars level themselves). Fail: stiffer or longer rear springs, or more rear preload on coilovers.
  3. Align to BMW's E46 M3 values in Wheel alignment, after the ride-height check, in BMW's design position: the M3 load, then extra weight near the struts until each corner is within 2 mm of BMW's ride height. BMW aligns M cars only this way and bars the alignment rig's ride-height-input (no-load) mode for them, so tell the shop (TIS 32 00 150, TIS 32 00 155). If the car sits more than 10 mm below the M3 heights at that load, fix the springs first. A corner that already sits within 2 mm of BMW's figure, or up to 10 mm below it, can't be brought up by weights: have it aligned at the M3 load as it sits (our inference). Every geometry part is M3: knuckles, arms, offset top mounts and trailing arms. Set the toe roughly at home first: Tenza's first setup was undriveable, and the car went to the alignment shop on a trailer (Tenza – wagon lessons (2021), 03:20). The adjustments are limited: front camber moves only about ±0.5°, and caster not at all (BMW ST056). So a caster reading inside the M3 window is good evidence that the right parts are fitted and the body is straight (our inference).
  4. Then calibrate the steering-angle sensor (Session 7) and aim the headlights at ride height.

Brakes and bleeding

Which DSC unit, booster and master cylinder you run is decided in DSC, brakes and steering angle, which recommends keeping your Touring's MK60, booster and master cylinder. This section covers the brake hardware for that route and for the M3-MK60 alternative, the booster's vacuum, the parking brake, bleeding the brakes, clutch and power steering, and a brake run before the inspection.

What each DSC route needs:

Part Keeping your Touring's MK60 Fitting an M3 MK60 (09/2002-on)
Brake booster Yours (34336779682) Yours. The M3's (34332282622) only if the M3 master cylinder doesn't suit yours, which nobody has checked
Booster check valve The M3's (34331161300), in a new grommet (34336765316) Same
Master cylinder Yours (34336785666, the same part as a 330i's) The M3's (34317838638)
Front brake pipes Yours; an MK60 M3 uses the same four pipes (34326759218, 34326755801, 34326752405, 34326752407) Same
Front brake hoses The M3's (34322229723); yours are 34326766966 The M3's (34322229723)
Rear pipes and hoses Same part numbers on both cars (rear hose 34301165174) Same
Calipers, carriers, rotors, pads, parking-brake shoes The M3's, with the corners and trailing arms The M3's

Sources: ETK for the Touring's master cylinder, booster, front pipes and rear pipes, and for the M3's master cylinder, booster, front pipes from 09/2002 and rear pipes; BimmerWorld for the 330i master cylinder. An M3 built before 09/2002 has the MK20 and different front pipes, including 34322282275 and 34322282277 (ETK); you don't need them with an MK60.

On the default route nothing between the master cylinder and the wheels changes except the two front hoses. The DSC unit sits on the left under the master cylinder, and the circuits are split front and rear (BMW ST056). BMW's photos suggest the front circuit (pressure sensor "V") leaves the master-cylinder outlet nearest the booster and the rear circuit ("H") the forward one; the left rear brake is fed by the single long pipe 34326752409, the right rear by 34326755704, a union and the crossover 34326766825 (our reading of BMW's photos and ETK's drawing) (TIS 34 31 505, ETK). Option B opens those joints: label both pipes before you undo anything.

Pedal feel with your master cylinder. BMW publishes no bore sizes. One forum post gives the 330i's master cylinder as 23.8/22 mm and the M3's as 25/20 mm, with front caliper pistons of 57 mm (330i) and 60 mm (M3) (e46zone, a single post), and BimmerWorld sells your 325i's front caliper kit as 54 mm (BimmerWorld). Working from those sizes, the front circuit on your master cylinder needs about 10% more pedal travel than on an M3's to move the M3 pistons, and about 10% less pedal force for the same pressure (our estimate). A tandem master cylinder gives both circuits the same pressure, so the front-to-rear balance comes from the calipers, rotors and pads and from the DSC's electronic brake-force distribution, not from the master cylinder (our inference). Expect a slightly longer, lighter pedal than an M3's, not a dangerous one. M346's 2004 Touring with M3 brakes had a pedal "nice and firm" after a manual bleed and INPA's routine; which master cylinder it ran isn't stated (M346 Projects – Pt 16 (2024), 09:20).

Fitting the M3 brakes. Values are from Flow pp.23–28 and Department 69.

  1. The calipers, carriers and rotors come with the M3 corners and trailing arms, rebuilt on the bench in Phase 3. Front caliper carrier, on the M3's M12×1.5×41 bolts: 110 Nm (81 ft-lb). Rear carrier: new micro-encapsulated M10 screws (34203414763), 65 Nm (48 ft-lb). Caliper guide bolts: 30 Nm (22 ft-lb); Department 69 gives 25–30 Nm. Rotor screw: 16 Nm (142 in-lb). Dust-shield screws: 9 Nm (80 in-lb). Bleed screws: 3.5–5 Nm (7 mm) or 12–16 Nm (11 mm).
  2. Fit the new M3 front hoses between your pipe ends at the strut brackets and the calipers: 19 Nm (14 ft-lb) at the caliper, and 14 Nm (10 ft-lb) at the pipe union, BMW's figure for the E46-based Z4, since TIS gives no E46 row (TIS 34 32 1AZ). Never twist a hose. At the rear your own hoses, the same part as the M3's, go to the M3 calipers.
  3. Fit the pad-wear sensors: the front one at the left front, the rear one at the right rear (manual).
  4. Check every hose at full lock both ways and at full droop for rubbing or tension before you fill the system.
  5. Option B only: if you change the master cylinder, fit new self-locking nuts (07129906196) at 26 Nm (19 ft-lb).

The booster's vacuum. The S54 feeds the booster from a suction jet pump, which the DME switches through an air shut-off valve to add vacuum when the A/C is on, when you're in gear with the clutch up, and below 70 °C (158 °F) (BMW ST055). On the M3 the hose meets the booster from the other side (Tenza Motorsports – 5 things they don't tell you, part 1 (2021), 07:40), so:

  1. Fit a new grommet (34336765316) in your booster. It's the same part on both cars (ETK).
  2. Push the donor's check valve (34331161300) into it, in place of your non-return valve and elbow (34331160183, 34336751108). BMW fitted this check valve to your booster part on M52 cars, the 323i Touring included (ETK, ETK). Blow through it first: air must pass only from the booster toward the engine.
  3. With the engine in (Phase 10), connect the donor's hose from the jet pump. Shorten or re-route it to reach, and clamp it with 11151726340. Three builds did the same. Tenza cut the hose and moved its connector (same video). Import Modify cut an S54 hose that was "clearly too long" at its U-bend (Import Modify – S54 swap, transmission and wiring (2018), 11:04). An M3 converted from MK20 to MK60 had its longer line shortened and crimped onto the MK60's check valve (NAM3). Keep the jet pump, the air shut-off valve (11617833212) and its DME wiring working: they're the S54's own vacuum supply (ETK).
  4. Check. At first key-on, the DME's valve test clicks the valve (manual, step 29). Once the engine runs: engine off, pump the pedal until it's hard, hold it with about 110 N (25 lb), and start the engine. The pedal must drop slightly. That's the inspection's booster test (540 CMR 4.04(4)(c)2).

Parking brake. The M3 trailing arms carry their own shoe kit (34416761293), springs and adjusting screw inside the rear rotor's drum. Your cables (34411165020/021), lever and switch are the same parts on both cars, so they stay (ETK). Set it up from scratch:

  1. Free the cables. Loosen the cable nuts at the lever inside the car, with BMW tool 34 1 030 or with the console out (E46 workshop manual).
  2. Adjust the shoes before the cables, on both sides. Take out a wheel bolt and turn the adjuster through its hole, blind: up on the left side, down on the right, until the rotor won't turn. Then back it off 10 notches, as BMW's E46 procedure and BimmerWorld both say (TIS 34 10 014, BimmerWorld).
  3. Set the cables. With the cable nuts hand-tight, pull the lever hard five times, about 400 N (90 lb), with the button pressed. Then pull it to the 2nd tooth and tighten the cable nuts evenly until braking just begins (TIS 34 10 014).
  4. Check: released, both rear wheels turn freely and the red brake lamp is off; at the 1st tooth, no braking (the lamp may light); at the 2nd tooth, braking starts and the lamp is on. Readjust whenever the lever travels more than 10 teeth (TIS 34 10 014). The lamp checks need the battery connected; if the car is still dead, do them at power-up.
  5. Bed in the shoes. BMW's own run-in: at about 40 km/h (25 mph), pull the lever until you feel it brake, pull it one more notch and drive about 400 m (440 yd); let it cool and repeat if needed (TIS 34 10 014). BMW's drum limits are 160 mm, runout under 0.1 mm and lining at least 1.5 mm (TIS 34 41). For new shoes or rotors, ECS's procedure for its BMW rotors with built-in drums: using only the parking brake, make 10 light-to-medium stops from about 30 km/h (20 mph) to a near stop, driving about 500 m (550 yd) between stops to let the shoes cool. Then make 10 medium-to-heavy stops the same way, and park without the parking brake until everything is cold (ECS).
  6. Check before the inspection: in first gear at 1,200–1,300 rpm, the applied parking brake holds the car; and from 32 km/h (20 mph) the parking brake alone stops it within 24.4 m (80 ft), about 0.17 g (540 CMR 4.04(4); our arithmetic).
Safety

Your brake lights don't come on when you slow down with the parking brake. Bed the shoes in, and test the parking-brake stop, on an empty road.

Bleeding the brakes.

  1. Fluid: DOT 4 low-viscosity, BMW 81220142156. BMW's bleeding instructions say every DSC car without a pre-charge pump "must be filled with the new DOT4 low-viscosity brake fluid" (BMW TIS, 2005 issue, unverified), and the MK60 has no pre-charge pump (BMW ST056). BimmerWorld agrees: cars with DSC take the low-viscosity type (BimmerWorld, brake fluid types). Have about 1.5 L (1.6 US qt) on hand: one INPA bleed of an MK60 used about 1.25 L, on a Z4 M (z4-forum).

  2. Pressure bleeder: no more than 2 bar (29 psi). BMW's E46 procedure: "Charging pressure should not exceed 2 bar" (TIS 34 00 050). The bleeder needs an airtight reservoir cap (50sKid – pressure bleeding (2015), description).

  3. Flush each wheel in turn, right rear, left rear, right front, left front, until the fluid runs clear and bubble-free (TIS 34 00 050; NAM3).

  4. Then bleed BMW's way for the work you did.

    • Calipers and hoses only, with the master cylinder and DSC unit kept full (the default route): BMW bleeds the rear circuit with its tester's routine, and the front by pumping the pedal fully at least 12 times per side, then holding it down while you close the bleed screw, right front then left front (TIS 34 00 048). INPA's MK60 routine is the tester at home, so the rear-circuit routine waits until INPA can talk to the DSC (Phase 11; manual).
    • The master cylinder, the DSC unit or the pipes between them opened, or the unit ran dry: run the routine at every wheel in turn, right rear, left rear, right front, left front, each with its bleed screw open. Restart the routine for every wheel, and after each run press the pedal to the floor five times: the fluid must come out clear and bubble-free (TIS 34 00 050). This too waits for Phase 11.
    • Then bleed the clutch (below).

  5. Set the level to MAX, and check the rubber seal in the cap (TIS 34 00 050).

  6. Prove it without air. Don't blow air through the filled system: air that reaches the DSC unit makes the routine at every wheel necessary. Instead:

    • Press the pedal with about 560 N (125 lb) for 10 s. It must hold its height, with at least 20% of its travel left: the inspection's test (540 CMR 4.04(4)(c)1).
    • Wedge the pedal down hard overnight with a length of wood against the seat, and check every union for weeps in the morning (NAM3).
    • Once INPA talks to the DSC (Phase 11): both brake-pressure readings in its DSC status are under 5 bar (73 psi) with the pedal released (BMW ST056) and rise together when you press it (our suggested check). Then BMW's leak test, engine off: pump the pedal about 10 times to empty the booster, then press until INPA reads about 36 bar, roughly 500 N (110 lb) on the pedal, and hold it there. In 2 minutes the reading may fall no more than 8%, to about 33 bar. With the engine running, about 200 N (45 lb) on the pedal should give 75–90 bar (TIS 34 00).
    • The red brake lamp is off with the parking brake released.

    Air-test only new, dry hard lines, before they're filled: on one MK20-to-MK60 conversion the new lines held 1.4 bar (20 psi), losing about 0.03 bar (0.4 psi) in 22 hours (same NAM3 thread).

  7. Drive only with a firm pedal. ABS works above 12 km/h (7 mph) (BMW ST056): check it with a careful hard stop on a quiet road, and bleed again after the first few drives (NAM3).

Bleeding the clutch. E46 clutches are notoriously hard to bleed after a dry install.

  1. Bleed it after the brakes, at the slave cylinder's bleed screw, ideally with the pressure bleeder still connected. Keep the reservoir topped up.
  2. If the pedal stays soft, take the slave off the gearbox with its line attached. Hold it with the bleed screw at its highest point, open the screw, push the piston in by hand, close the screw, release the piston, and repeat about ten times (M3Post, car not stated, unverified). Refit the slave at 22 Nm (Flow p.70).
  3. Turner sells an E46 slave-cylinder bleeder tool that holds the piston compressed while you bleed (listing via ECS, unverified). BMW's procedure is in TIS group 21 52.

Power steering. Use ATF (Dexron III type), not Pentosin CHF 11S, and don't mix the two. BMW's catalog fits the same reservoir (32416851217) to both cars and pairs it with a label, 71246798132, whose own catalog page gives the fluid as "ATF" (ETK: reservoir, ETK: label). FCP Euro says BMW filled its cars without active steering or hydraulic suspension with ATF Dexron III until the N-engine generation, that mixing in CHF 11S shortens an older system's life, and that a replacement cap now says CHF 11S whatever the car (FCP Euro). BimmerWorld lists CHF 11S for no E46 model (BimmerWorld). M346's 2004 Touring with an M3 pump took ATF (M346 Projects – Pt 13 first start (2024), 08:00). If the donor's reservoir holds green fluid, someone has converted it: flush the whole system to one fluid. No capacity was found; fill to the mark.

Fill the reservoir before the first start: M346's pump rattled dry until the ATF went in (same video). Then bleed it as BMW describes (TIS 32 13 006; the printout doesn't name a model, so check the E46 version in TIS):

  1. With the engine off, fill the reservoir to about 25 mm (1 in) below its edge.
  2. Start the engine and top up the rest, pouring evenly.
  3. Turn the steering wheel to full lock each way, twice. Don't hold it at full lock: the M3 rack has no hydraulic end stops, so the pump runs at its 120 bar limit there (BMW ST041; our inference).
  4. Switch off, check the level against the mark on the lid, and top up.
  5. Check: no foaming or groaning after a short run; no weeps at the hollow bolts or the rack banjo; the level steady after a drive.

If the lines have been in storage, check them for kinks; Tracks and Trails found one and replaced it (Tracks and Trails – first drive (2026), 1:05:20).

Before the inspection: a brake run. Massachusetts tests more than the 9.1 m (30 ft) stop (540 CMR 4.04(4)). Run the same tests yourself, on an empty road, with a helper and a tape measure:

Test Pass
Light stops at 6–13 km/h (4–8 mph) No pull to either side
Service brake from 32 km/h (20 mph) by GPS, about 22 mph on the M3 cluster Stops within 9.1 m (30 ft) of where the brake goes on. That needs about 0.45 g; with M3 brakes expect roughly 4.5–5 m (15–17 ft) (our arithmetic)
Parking brake applied, first gear, 1,200–1,300 rpm The car doesn't move
Parking brake alone from 32 km/h (20 mph) Stops within 24.4 m (80 ft), about 0.17 g
Stopped, about 560 N (125 lb) on the pedal for 10 s The pedal holds, with at least 20% of its travel left
Engine off, pedal pumped hard and held at about 110 N (25 lb), engine started The pedal drops slightly
Lines and hoses No leaks, chafing, cracking or swelling; all fastened
Lamps Red brake, yellow brake, ABS and DSC lamps all out

BMW's red brake lamp means low fluid or the parking brake on; ABS and DSC faults light the yellow brake lamp and the ABS and DSC lamps (BMW ST056). Massachusetts rejects a lit "brake failure warning light", so get them all dark (Massachusetts).

Fuel system

The S54 uses a 5-bar regulator built into the fuel-filter assembly under the left front floor. It is referenced to engine vacuum "via a hose connected to the external air distribution pipe", the idle-air rail that feeds the throttle bodies (BMW S54 module). Your M54 runs at 3.5 bar from a one-piece filter-regulator whose hose is an atmospheric vent, not a vacuum reference (e46fanatics). This plan assumes an M54 Touring with a plastic tank and a return line. A US 325i with the M56 SULEV engine has a metal tank, no return line and a pump control unit, so the plan doesn't apply as written (ETK: control unit, tank, lines); confirm your engine code in Phase 0.

In short: move the donor's whole in-tank set into your tank, then fit the M3 pipe set, the three M3 lines, the M3 filter-regulator and the M3 front purge line. Keep your tank mounts, filler parts, canister and leak-test pump, and prove the system at 5 bar before the rear axle goes in.

Build date doesn't matter here. ETK lists the same fuel, line and EVAP parts for Tourings built in February and March 2003, so the MS43-to-MS45.1 change at 03/2003 doesn't touch this work. May 2005 Tourings list the same pump, tank, line and filter parts. The one 03/2003 change near the fuel system is the filler-flap actuator, and that stays with your body. US M3 lists match from 2003 to 2006, coupe and convertible alike (ETK: Touring, Feb 2003, Mar 2003, M3).

Choose the pump route

Either car's delivery unit fits either tank, as the builds below show; ETK explains why, since both use the same flange seal (16111184084), lock ring (16116762417) and plug housing (61138352390) (ETK: Touring, M3). BMW pairs the M3 unit with a baffle and its own jet pump: "The baffling has been modified for the E46 M3 fuel pump pickup in the right hand side of the fuel tank to maintain fuel supply during aggressive cornering", and "A Syphon jet is required… linked to the fuel return line" (BMW ST041 Part 2, p.24).

Route In your tank Pipe set and lines Use it when
A. The donor's in-tank set (recommended) M3 delivery unit 16142229684 (pump and right sender), baffle 16112229656, jet pump 16142282208 and left sender 16142229683 M3 pipe set 16112283288 and the three M3 lines By default. It's BMW's own pump, baffle, jet pump and sender combination, it arrives with the donor, and it mates with the M3 pipe set with no adapter
B. The donor's whole tank Donor tank 16112229736 with its set The same The donor's tank is clean inside and its vent nipples are intact. Every mounting and filler part is the same number as yours (ETK)
C. Your own pump (fallback) Your delivery unit, jet pump and left sender; no baffle Your pipe set 16117175998 with an adapter to the M3 rear feed line, or your rear feed line with an adapter at the M3 filter's inlet. Neither joint is documented Only if your pump delivers 1.3 L or more in 30 s at 5 bar (our margin, test T3 below) and you accept one undocumented joint

Keeping your own pump saves no parts and adds a joint nobody has documented (our inference). Every documented Touring build fitted either the M3 tank or the M3 pump in its own tank, most of them with M3 lines; none kept a 325i pump:

  • Kalim moved the M3 pump, baffle, transfer pipe and left sender into a 2003 325i sedan's tank, the same part as yours: "remove the old transfer pipe and install the M3 one into the baffle" (e46fanatics, ETK). Of two other owners, one says the M3 unit needs a sleeve in a non-M tank, and another found the M3 pump body smaller in diameter (e46fanatics, page 2). Both tanks take the same pump-flange seal (16111184084), O-ring and screw cap (16116762417), so the opening is the same; the "sleeve" is most likely the M3's own baffle, which sits under the pump (ETK, BimmerWorld). Fit the pump and baffle together. When you move the M3 jet pump and left sender, check that the transfer hose is latched: one M3 stalled with 9 L still in the left half when that hose came off at the left sender (NAM3 (2024)).
  • Project BMW swapped both in-tank units of a 325i Touring through the two access openings, with the tank lowered (Project BMW – Day 5 (2021), 03:20). Tracks and Trails put a new M3 pump in his Touring's tank: "Plug at the back. Easy peasy" (Tracks and Trails – Touring rear end (2025), 27:20).
  • ThaChileanDude, yavz on a UK 318i Touring and M3Projekts on a US 2003 325iT fitted the M3 tank (ThaChileanDude – Building an e46 m3 Wagon in 10 days (2024), 17:00, PistonHeads, NAM3). Tenza fitted one in place of an M56 SULEV car's sealed tank, which is a fit check rather than a method to copy (Tenza – No more SULEV (2021), 00:20, Registration and legal).

Why the margin is thin. The delivery floor for every E46 engine is at least 1.12 L (1.2 US qt) in 30 s at 12 V, about 134 L/h (35 US gal/h) (Bentley, quoted on e46fanatics); a trade magazine gives the same E46 figure as 2.25 L a minute (the bimmer pub, March 2013). Whatever the engine doesn't burn returns to the tank and drives the jet pump that moves fuel from the left half to the pump's side (BMW ST055). Our estimate for a pump that only just meets the floor:

Engine Power Fuel used at full power Return flow left
S54 (US M3) 333 hp (248 kW) 90–100 L/h (24–26 US gal/h) 34–44 L/h (9–12 US gal/h)
M54B25 (your 325i) 184 hp (137 kW) 50–55 L/h (13–15 US gal/h) 79–84 L/h (21–22 US gal/h)

These are our estimates, not BMW figures: they assume 0.27–0.30 kg of fuel per kWh at full load and 0.745 kg/L, with power from BMW (BMW ST041) and BMW USA's 2003 sheet (BMW USA). We found no factory flow rating for either pump. On those numbers the S54 at full power leaves the jet pump roughly half the flow an M54 leaves it with the same pump. A turbine pump also flows less at 5 bar than at 3.5 bar, so a Touring pump that met the floor on your M54 may not at 5 bar (our inference). That fits BMW's "high output fuel pump… to match the fuel supply demands of the S54 engine (5 Bar)" (ST041 Part 2, p.33), and one 330i that starved near a quarter tank under hard driving until its owner fitted the M3 pump (e46fanatics).

Handling the tank.

  • In Phase 7 the tank is out, so do the in-tank work on the bench. In the car, BMW's access plates are under the rear seat: the passenger side reaches the pump and its sender, the driver side the left sender and the jet pump (BMW ST041 Part 2, p.40).
  • Don't drop or carry a tank by its vent hoses: Tenza snapped both plastic vent nipples on an M3 tank, and they aren't sold separately (Tenza – M3 rear end (2021), 06:40).
  • The straps don't change. ETK gives both tanks the same straps (16116756583), bolts (07119905532) and nut (07146760121) (ETK: Touring, M3). The double-width strap bracket Redish describes belongs to the non-M convertible's V-brace pick-up, not to the tank (Redish – Touring build part 1 (2022), 08:00), and a 2003 car has the later brackets anyway.
  • Your tank is 16116766940 in today's catalog. A 2003 car most likely left the factory with 16111184899 or 16116762962, both superseded by it (our inference from ETK's date ranges), so read the label rather than trusting a number (ETK).

Fuel parts by car

"Same" means the same part number on the US 325i Touring (M54) and the US M3 (S54). The Touring column is today's catalog, from the February 2003 lists.
