Sources: ETK for the Touring, February 2003 build (pump, tank, lines, filter-regulator, EVAP, covers, filler), and for the US M3 (pump, tank, lines, filter-regulator, EVAP, cover, filler: coupe, convertible, engine feed pipe, purge valve).

Filter-regulator and vacuum reference

Filter-regulator. Fit a new M3 filter (13327831089) with the donor's regulator housing (13537830368) and regulator (13531404089) in place of the 325i's one-piece unit (13327512019). Both use the same bracket (13321435583) and filter cover (13328230397); the M3 adds a sealing element (13327830949) at the cover (ETK: M3, Touring). The donor's test in Phase 1 proves its regulator: 5.0 ± 0.2 bar, then 20 minutes later no more than 0.5 bar lost and still 4.5 bar or more, as in test T2 below. Buy a new regulator only if the donor couldn't be tested, or if test T2 below traces a bleed-down to the regulator.

  1. Fit a new filter with its flow arrow toward the engine. The rear feed line clicks onto its rear inlet.
  2. Fit the donor's housing on the filter's front end with a new copper ring (07119963129). BMW's fuel module says sealing rings in the fuel system are always replaced "with new COPPER rings only" (BMW ST055). The housing carries the regulator, the front-feed outlet, the return outlet and the threaded test fitting, TP1 (BMW ST041 Part 2, pp.25, 46).
  3. Fit the donor's regulator with new O-rings (13531720251, 13531720252) and a new lock ring (13531736234). M346's regulator leaked at the first start on bad O-rings and was replaced (M346 Projects – pt 13 (2024), 05:40).
  4. Refit the cover with the M3 sealing element once the tests are done.

Fit all of this before the first start; Tracks and Trails fitted it only after the car cranked and wouldn't start (Tracks and Trails – first drive (2026), 1:14:00).

Vacuum reference. Your M54's regulator line is a vent. BMW's E46 training says the non-M line "no longer connects to intake manifold vacuum, but is routed to the crankcase cyclone separator (in case of regulator diaphragm leakage)" (BMW ST034, p.32); that's written for the M52TU, whose regulator design the M54 carries over (our inference). The S54's regulator is "influenced by engine vacuum via a hose connected to the idle air distribution pipe" (BMW ST041 Part 2, p.25). Fit the donor's set: blue hose 11747797082, white hose 64111368684 and hose 11727837591, the corrugated metal sleeve 12517508831, cable tie 61131367599 and four clamps 61131365412 (ETK). Route it forward from the regulator's nipple along the feed line, away from the exhaust. Keep the metal sleeve: it's BMW's answer to the heat along that run, so don't swap it for plain hose (our inference). At the engine it goes to a small nipple on the S54's idle-air pipe, which is most likely the regulator's port (our inference from the ETK drawing; ETK).

Lines and the pipe set

The pump never meets the rear feed line. On both cars a short "fuel pipes set" of two hoses joins the pump flange to the floor lines: a feed hose from the pump to the rear feed line, and a return hose from the return line to a nipple on the tank. Your Touring's set (16117175998) is clamped at both ends. In BMW's drawing, the M3's set (16112283288) has a moulded push-on end at the pump and a quick-connector that takes the M3 rear feed line's angled male end (ETK: Touring, M3; drawings: Touring, M3). Nobody has documented the M3 pipe set on a Touring pump, which is why route A moves the M3 pump with it.

The joints. Along the floor, the M3's feed path is all quick-connectors: pipe set to rear feed, rear feed to the filter inlet, and the regulator housing to the front feed. Its return is hose and clamps. Your Touring's plain tubes are joined by short 8×13 mm hoses (13537563456) and clamps throughout (same drawings). The quick-connector size isn't documented, so measure before you buy any adapter.

The M3 lines fit as they are. Four Touring builds fitted M3 fuel lines and reported no routing problem. Project BMW found "a lot of room right here for all these fuel lines… it is the same" (Project BMW – Day 5 (2021), 03:00); the others are yavz (PistonHeads), ThaChileanDude (ThaChileanDude – Building an e46 m3 Wagon in 10 days (2024), 02:20) and Renner's car (Larry Chen – Renner's E46 M3 Touring (2025), 21:00). M3Projekts' US 2003 325iT shows "new fresh fuel lines" (NAM3). ETK gives both cars the same pipe clips, brackets, brake-pipe bracket and sealing; the M3 adds two tubing supports (16122282049, 16131177494). Clip the M3 lines to your existing points and add the supports.

  • Where they run. The lines run along the left floor past the filter and end at the tank ahead of the rear subframe, so the subframe-mount plates don't touch them (our inference). The parts that do pass the right rear subframe, the axle carrier panel and the wheelhouse are the EVAP vent lines, the canister lines and the filler pipe. After welding, check that every EVAP clip stud and route is still clear.
  • Feed and return. Label both ends of each before anything comes apart. Swapped at the filter, they gave one swap a no-start (NAM3). With M3 lines they're harder to mix up, since the feed joints are quick-connectors and the return is hose and clamp; label them anyway.
  • Engine end. The M3 front feed meets the S54's feed pipe (13317831683), which takes a new O-ring (13641730767) at the rail (BimmerWorld). The joint between them is probably a quick-connector, as on the M3 (our inference). Until the engine is in, cap the front feed's engine end with a quick-connect plug rated for at least 5 bar.
  • Purge line. ETK gives the M3 its own front purge line (16132229652), to the S54's purge valve (13907831770) and its hose (13907837663), which ends in a quick-connector (ETK, drawing). Project BMW found that the 325's line was "not going to work with this motor" and fitted the M3's (Project BMW – Day 5 (2021), 00:40). Fit the donor's front line. Whether it mates with your rear line (16136751175) isn't documented; if it doesn't, fit the M3 rear line (16132229417), which you need anyway with the M3 floor's canister mount.
  • If you keep your own pump (route C). Your pipe set doesn't take the M3 rear feed line. Adapt between your pipe set and the M3 rear feed's male end, or keep your rear feed line and adapt at the M3 filter's quick-connect inlet. Neither joint is documented, and any adapter has to hold 5 bar.

Filler and EVAP

At the filler, only the flap changes. The filler pot (51718208646), filler pipe (16117177490), pipe seal (16116755071), cap pin (16111184156), flap spring, rubber boot and sleeve are the same parts on the US 325i Touring and the US M3, and so is the 03/2003 actuator split (ETK: Touring, M3, filler pot). Only the flap differs (yours 51178208246, the M3's 51172695524), and the hinge on a coupe donor (51172695527); a convertible donor's hinge (51178151955) is your Touring's part. BMW fits the same pot and the same rigid filler pipe to both bodies, so the pot stays where it is and the M3 skin's filler surround is grafted around it (our inference; M346's method, M346 Projects – Pt 14 (2024), 36:40). After the arch graft (Arch graft step by step), check that:

  • the pot seats in the M3 skin's opening;
  • the flap closes flush and the actuator locks it;
  • the filler pipe and its 40×47×170 mm hose (16117176011) sit unstrained, with both L42-48 clamps (07129952119) on.

Then prove it with the leak test (test T10 below).

EVAP: the same canister and leak-test pump, mounted two ways. The canister family and the heated, 4-pin leak-test pump (DM-TL, 16137193479) are the same on both cars, and both sit under the cargo floor (BMW ST041 Part 3, pp.63–64, ETK: Touring, M3). Your Touring mounts the canister fore and aft between the battery tray and the spare well, under covers 51718233265 and 51718233266. The M3, which has no spare well, mounts it crosswise in holder 16132229735, under its own cover 51717893604, with its own vent pipes and rear purge line (Tenza – No more SULEV (2021), 01:20, ETK: M3 cover). Choose by the floor (Exhaust and the spare-wheel well):

Floor Canister mounting
Option 4, keep the well Your Touring's mounting, covers, vent pipes and rear purge line
Options 1 and 2, the M3 trunk floor Expect the M3 holder with its four nuts (07147153450), cover, vent pipes (16132283286, 16132229415) and rear purge line (16132229417), as Renner's Touring did: "the EVAP system is from the M3" (Larry Chen – Renner's E46 M3 Touring (2025), 22:40). The Phase 5 mock-up decides: under 25 mm (1 in) from the muffler or its right hanger, fit them; at 25 mm or more, either position works
Option 3, a flat panel A fixed mount and cover equal to one of these; no tested design exists

With the M3 floor in, check the Touring canister's clearance to the muffler at the mock-up, at full bump and rebound (Exhaust and the spare-wheel well). The M3 holder's four M6 studs may sit on the M3 floor or on the rear axle carrier panel, so find them on the donor before the floor is welded in. Route the vent hoses without kinks: there's little room by the subframe, and Tenza had to remake one (Tenza – No more SULEV (2021), 04:40). Either way the canister and leak-test pump must keep working, so the move relocates an emissions part and removes nothing: every hose connected, the leak-test pump wired as the manual describes (DM-TL leak-test pump), and the leak test passed.

The vapour separator is inside the arch graft. The liquid-vapour separator (ETK's "expansion tank", 16136752641, the same on both cars) sits "in the right rear wheel well behind the trim" (BMW ST041 Part 3, p.63), on a bracket (41148196386) that every E46 shares (ETK). Take it out with its vent hoses before you cut or weld the right arch. Protect the bracket if you keep your inner wheelhouse, or transfer it if you graft the donor's. Refit the separator and its hoses before the tank goes in, and let the leak test prove them.

Test the fuel system

Where the gauge goes. BMW's S54 test point is "a threaded fitting… at the fuel pressure regulator", taking adapter 13 5 220 (BMW ST041 Part 2, p.46). That's TP1, on the regulator housing under the left front floor. Remove the filter cover to reach it, with an 8 mm socket and a Phillips screwdriver (the bimmer pub, March 2013). An owner confirms that on the E46 M3 "the valve is next to the fuel filter under the car" (z4-forum), and the M3's rail has no test port (m3post, unverified). BMW names the same adapter for the threaded fitting on later non-M rails (BMW ST055), so one adapter should suit both cars (our inference). Before the engine is in, a gauge on the capped front feed line (TP2) works too, with a quick-connect adapter.

How to run the pump. Pull relay K96 behind the glovebox and fit a switch with a 15 A inline fuse across its socket's pins 6 and 2. WDS names pin 6 "Terminal 30", the load supply from fuse F54, and pin 2 the output to the pump (WDS: drawing, pin table); check them on WDS for your VIN. Leave pin 8 alone: WDS calls it "Terminal 87", but it's the relay coil's supply from fuse F3. BMW's own test bridges "pin 87b and 30 of the relay socket" (BMW ST041 Part 2, p.41). The US M3's pump-module socket has the same pin 6 and pin 2 (WDS), so BMW's 87b is pin 2 (our reading). Run the tests on the battery alone, without the charger, so the pump sees the 12 V that Bentley's figures assume.

Warning

Fuel spray, vapour and fire. Work outdoors or with the doors open, away from flames, sparks, heaters, grinding and trouble lights, with an extinguisher at hand, eye protection and fuel-resistant gloves. Relieve the pressure and put a rag and a container under a joint before you open it: BMW warns that "residual fuel pressure may be present". Never run the pump dry: BMW says not to run it unless it's installed and "submersed in the fuel" (BMW ST041 Part 2, pp.39, 46). Put at least 10 L (2.6 US gal) in the tank first (our figure). Never run it with the front feed line open: cap it or put the gauge on it. Collect fuel only in an approved container.

Phase 7, engine out. Record each result on the worksheet.

Test How Pass If it fails
T1 Static pressure Gauge on TP1; run the pump 30 s 5.0 ± 0.2 bar (72.5 ± 2.9 psi) (BMW ST041 Part 2, p.26; Bentley, quoted on e46fanatics) Low: regulator O-rings, filter, pump voltage (T4), then the pump. High: a kinked return or pipe-set hose, or the regulator
T2 Hold Switch off and wait 20 minutes No more than 0.5 bar (7 psi) lost; 4.5 bar (65 psi) or more (BMW; Bentley) Pinch the pipe set's feed hose at the tank with a hose clamp tool, then its return hose, to find whether the pump's check valve or the regulator leaks, as BMW's test does
T3 Delivery at 5 bar (our method) Disconnect the return line at the regulator housing and lead the outlet through a fuel hose into a graduated container of 2 L or more. Run 30 s, watching TP1 At least 1.12 L (1.2 US qt), with TP1 near 5 bar throughout. Keep a non-M pump only at 1.3 L (1.4 US qt) or more (our margin) Fit the M3 delivery unit (route A or B). With the M3 unit already in: the filter, a kinked hose, then the voltage
T4 Pump voltage Pump running: meter from the pump connector, under the right rear seat, to the battery posts Within 0.5 V of the battery on the feed; 0.5 V or less on the ground side (Luke Murray). Optional: 9 A or less, BMW's limit for passenger cars (the bimmer pub) Clean and tighten the pump plug and its ground; check F54 and the K96 socket. It matters more with an M3 pump on your 1.5 mm² feed (Fuel-pump control)
T5 Leaks After T2, look at the pump flange, the pipe-set joints, every quick-connector, the filter, the housing, the regulator's lock ring and the return clamps Dry Fix before the axle goes in

TIS 13 31's own collection point for the delivery test wasn't found; BMW's training says only that the volume must be tested, to check the pump's output and that the pump, lines and filter aren't restricted (ST041 Part 2, p.42). Collecting from the return line at the regulator measures the pump against 5 bar, the stricter case. Reconnect the return with a new clamp afterwards, refit K96 and the filter cover, and put the collected fuel back through a clean funnel.

Phase 12, first start. Leave the gauge on TP1, tied where you can read it.

Test Pass
T6 Key-on One prime; K96 clicks; 5.0 ± 0.2 bar
T7 Hot idle Vacuum hose on: below 5 bar (BMW's diagram shows 3.8 bar at part-throttle vacuum). Hose pulled: back to 5.0 ± 0.2 bar, and the hose dry inside; fuel in it means a leaking regulator diaphragm (our check)
T8 Fuel trims STATUS_LAMBDA_ADD_1 and _2 near zero (Session 6)
T9 Fuel gauge Against your Phase 7 litre log: Tool32 KOMBI46R.PRG → STATUS_AIF_TANKDATEN_LESEN shows the two senders' litres adding up to what's in the tank, the cluster's test 06 shows phase 1 (both sensors OK), and the reserve lamp comes on with about 8 L left (manual)
T10 Leak test After the arch, filler and canister work, with the tank 15–85% full: START_SYSTEMCHECK_DMTL, then LESEN_SYSTEMCHECK_DMTL, reports a "…DICHT" (sealed) result, not GROBLECK, FEINLECK or DECKEL_FEHLT; no "Check Filler Cap" lamp after refueling (manual)
T11 Under load (optional, on a dyno) At wide-open throttle the manifold vacuum is near zero, so the pressure should hold 5.0 ± 0.2 bar; a droop means the supply is short (our inference)

No build has published a 5-bar delivery figure or a pressure under load, with either pump. The only number is one S54 swap into an MS42 323i sedan, which also switches its pump relay from X60004 pin 10: a static 71 psi (4.9 bar) "at the valve on the FPR" with the non-M pump (NAM3).

Before the swap (optional). Your M54's pressure, taken now, tells you whether its pump is worth testing at 5 bar later: 3.5 ± 0.2 bar (51 ± 3 psi), and more than 3 bar after 20 minutes (Bentley, quoted on e46fanatics). Use the rail's threaded test fitting if yours has one. A pump that's weak at 3.5 bar won't pass at 5. On the donor, test at TP1 while it still runs (Phase 1): 5.0 ± 0.2 bar with the pump module bypassed (its socket's terminals 30 and 87b: pins 6 and 2 of plug X10157, through the same fused switch), then 20 minutes later no more than 0.5 bar lost and still 4.5 bar or more. That proves its pump, regulator and check valve before you move them.

Pump trigger. Which DME output switches your pump relay is a wiring question, covered in Fuel-pump control. Never connect the US DME's PWM pump output to a relay.

Cooling and oil cooler

The M3's radiator, fans, oil cooler and expansion tank go in, and your Touring keeps its heater box: heater core, evaporator and expansion valve. The front panel, the radiator supports and every radiator mounting part are the same part numbers on both cars, so the M3 radiator, shroud and oil cooler bolt in (ETK: M3, ETK: Touring). Only the expansion tank needs new brackets on the body.

What comes from where.

Sources: ETK for the M3's radiator, fan, pusher fan, expansion tank, thermostat, hoses and oil cooler, and the Touring's radiator mounting, fan, fan shroud, expansion tank and thermostat. The M3 radiator's missing drain plug: Blankowski.

Fans: what changes on a manual Touring. Your manual 325i Touring has no viscous fan. ETK lists the mechanical fan and its coupling for the US 325i Touring only "for vehicles with Automatic transmission" (ETK). A manual car's fan is a 390 W electric fan inside the radiator shroud (17117561757), and WDS shows its power stage and its plug, X82, on that shroud (WDS, ETK drawing). The M3 has two fans: a viscous fan behind the radiator, rated to switch on at 92 °C (198 °F) and off at 60 °C (140 °F) (Flow p.61), and an electric pusher fan in front of the condenser. The DME drives the electric fan from X60004 pin 4 on both cars, so nothing is re-pinned. But X82 now has to reach the pusher fan at the front: compare the plugs, check that the lead reaches, and extend or re-route it if it doesn't (manual).

BMW's catalog doesn't settle whether manual Tourings also carry a pusher fan. ETK lists one for the US 325i Touring (64546988913) with no gearbox note (ETK), but the DME has only one fan output, so we infer that it belongs to automatic Tourings, which have the mechanical fan; owners treat the non-M pusher as automatic-only too, so a manual Touring almost certainly has none. In one manual-Touring swap the M3 pusher "bolted right into the touring's rad support and plugged right in" (NAM3 – Non-M electric fan fitment (2023)), and WDS calls X82 the "auxiliary-blower motor" connector, so the plug probably matches; the lead may still need lengthening (WDS). The Touring's own shroud fan fits behind the M3 radiator only after trimming, and an S54-Touring builder who tried it went back to the M3 layout (same thread, page 2). The pusher needs the M3 bumper's ducting: one Touring could fit it only once it had an M-Tech II bumper (NAM3 – Kaiv's first S54 Touring #20). If you keep the non-M belly pan, support the bottom of the radiator duct as the M3 pan does; it sits about ¾ in lower (NAM3 – Black & Tan 332iT #289). Check your car in Phase 0:

  1. Behind the front bumper, in front of the condenser: is there a fan?
  2. In the radiator shroud: is there a fan motor, with X82 at the shroud's upper edge?
  3. Which plug does the 0.5 SW/GN wire from X60004 pin 4 reach? Photograph it, and measure from X82 to the front of the condenser.

Recommendation: fit both M3 fans, as BMW did. One S54 Touring build replaced both with a single electric fan (Tracks and Trails – Attempting to Drive my BMW E46 M3 Touring (2026), 1:02:40); this guide's checks assume BMW's pair. The DME drives the electric fan by PWM from the radiator-outlet temperature, its calculated catalyst temperature, road speed, battery voltage and the A/C pressure the climate control reports (BMW ST055, MS S54, p.86). Owners' reverse-engineering, not BMW, adds that it runs the fan at 60% when the climate control's data is missing, so a fan stuck at a steady 60% with the A/C on suggests the cluster isn't passing that data (MSS54-XDFs wiki).

The viscous fan's coupling has a left-hand thread: undo it clockwise with a 32 mm fan wrench while you hold the pulley (FCP Euro – S54 rod bearings (2022), 07:13, ECS Tuning – S54 valves and VANOS (2025), 02:31). Refit it at 40 Nm (30 ft-lb), and the fan to the coupling at 10 Nm (89 in-lb) (Flow p.61).

Expansion tank. Fit a new M3 tank (17112283344, which superseded 17112228944); the plastic gets brittle with age (BimmerWorld). It sits on the right of the engine bay, the other side from the Touring's (Blankowski), on holder 17112229108, which also carries the M3's secondary-air pump (ETK: tank, ETK: air pump). The only M3-only body brackets there are the "secondary air pump bracket, front" 41147894115 and "rear" 41147894116 on the front of the right strut tower, which your Touring's body lacks (ETK: M3, ETK: Touring); they're about $15–17 each new (BMWPartsDeal). Measure and photograph their positions on the donor, then weld copies or the new parts in. Builders cut them off the donor and welded them in (Tracks and Trails – first drive (2026), 22:40), or bought copies made for welding and fitted them with rivnuts so they can come off (M346 Projects – pt 13 (2024), 00:05). The 2.0 bar cap (17117639022) and the level switch (17137553919) are the same parts on both cars; extend or re-route the switch's lead to cluster pin 26 (Harness and re-pinning).

Heater valve and its pump. Every E46 M3 except the CSL, European cars included, has the "Water valve with additional water pump" 64118369807, whose pump your Touring's harness doesn't wire. The CSL and your Touring have the plain valve 64118369805 (ETK, ETK). Either way, the S54's engine-side heater hoses replace your Touring's: those are M54 parts, and the Touring's return hose runs to the M54's expansion tank, which goes. The heater core, its pipes and the valve's bracket (41148209658) are the same on both cars (ETK: M3, ETK: Touring, ETK: heater core).

Option 1: your plain valve, as on the CSL Option 2: the M3 valve and its pump
Valve 64118369805, your Touring's 64118369807, the donor's
Hose, engine to valve 64216902678, the donor's 64216902678, the donor's
Hose, valve to heater core The CSL's 64212282548, bought new (ETK). Your Touring's 64218363198 joins the same two parts and may fit, but nobody has tried it 64216902679, the donor's
Hose, heater core to engine 64216902680, the donor's 64216902680, the donor's
Wiring and coding None: your climate control is already coded for this valve Two wires, and ZUSATZWASSERPUMPE = aktiv in the climate control (manual)
Bleeding The engine's own pump does the venting (our inference); allow two heat cycles BMW's fill procedure runs the pump to vent the heater circuit

Recommendation: option 1. BMW built the CSL this way with the same engine-side hoses, it needs no wiring or coding, and owners running the plain valve on M3s report "No notable difference" (NAM3). If you keep the M3 valve, wire its pump before you fill: one swapper who left it unwired found his cooling system hard to bleed (UNRIVALED – before you S54 swap (2021), 02:32).

Oil cooler. The S54's oil cooler sits "directly under the water radiator", "very low at the front" (MotoIQ), clipped under a long air guide (Flow p.57) and held up by two side screws (Blankowski). A thermostat in the oil-filter housing sends oil through it from 95 °C (203 °F) (BMW ST041). Every part of it is M3-only (ETK). Fit new O-rings 17222245358 (4). The pipe unions take 25 Nm (18 ft-lb), the M8 flange screws 20 Nm (15 ft-lb) and the M6 bracket bolt 6 Nm (53 in-lb) (Flow p.57). The cooler breathes through the M3 bumper's lower opening, which is why the front end goes on before the first drive; with a ZHP bumper, one builder had to cut away a scoop behind it (Front end on a 4-door body).

Sensor leads. The washer-level leads may need extending to reach the M3 parts, and the radiator-outlet sensor lead has to reach the M3 radiator's sensor; only a Euro 318d diesel conversion has reported extending it. Add X82, which has to reach the pusher fan (Harness and re-pinning).

Fill and bleed the cooling system

Coolant. About 9.3 L (9.8 US qt) including the heater: BMW's US owner's manuals for the 2002 and 2003 M3 give 9.3 L, printed as 9.9 and 9.8 US qt (2002 manual, 2003 manual). The M54 in your Touring takes about 8.4 L (8.9 US qt) (2003 US sedan manual), so buy for the S54. Earlier manuals print other figures, so fill to the level mark, not by volume. Mix BMW antifreeze 82141467704, sold in 1 US gal jugs (ETK), 50/50 with distilled water. BMW sets the concentration at 50% all year (BMW ST054, engine cooling); distilled water is DIY practice (Blankowski). Two jugs cover a fill and the top-ups. The cap is rated 2.0 bar (29 psi) on both cars, and the M3 thermostat opens at 80 °C (176 °F) (ETK, BMW ST041).

Where these steps come from. BMW's S54 fill-and-bleed instructions (TIS 17 00) haven't been read. The steps below combine BMW's general fill rules from its training (BMW ST054, engine cooling), the level check in the M3 owner's manual (2003 manual) and one M3 owner's write-up (Blankowski); the order is ours. BMW's rules:

  • Before filling, switch the ignition on, set the blower low and the heat to maximum. The heater valve then opens fully, and the M3 valve's pump runs.
  • Fill slowly.
  • Don't fill past the mark: the coolant overflows, and the pump has to be able to move coolant to vent the circuit.
  • Check the level only with the coolant at 30 °C (86 °F) or below.

Some owners call the S54's cooling system "self-bleeding" (NAM3). BMW nonetheless fits a bleed screw (17111712788, 2.5 Nm) in the radiator-feed hose 11537830716, so bleed it after any drain (Flow p.60).

In Phase 10: engine cold, ignition off. The ignition stays off until the Phase 11 power-up. The heater valve rests open without power (BMW ST054, outputs), so the first fill works without it.

  1. Check that the S54 block drain plug (13 mm) is in, with a new 14 mm washer, at 24 Nm (18 ft-lb), one owner's figure, and that the lower radiator hose is on (Blankowski).
  2. Mix about 10 L (2.6 US gal) of 50/50 coolant.
  3. Park the car level or nose up, as owners of other BMW sixes do (z4-forum, on the Z4's M54, unverified).
  4. Take off the intake ducting over the front of the engine to reach the vent screw in hose 11537830716, and open the screw (Blankowski).
  5. Fill the expansion tank slowly. Expect about 7.5 L (2 US gal) to go in before coolant runs from the vent screw (Blankowski).
  6. When it runs without bubbles, fit the vent screw at 2.5 Nm (22 in-lb). It's plastic: don't overtighten (Flow p.60).
  7. Top up to the cold mark: the top of the red float level with the filler-neck rim, and no more than 2 cm (3/4 in) above it (2003 manual).
  8. Pressure-test it, still cold. Fit the tester to the tank neck and pump to 2.0 bar (29 psi), the cap's rating. Never go higher. Hold 15 minutes: no drop, and no seepage at the hoses, the heater hoses or the valve. Then test the cap on the tester's adapter: it should hold, and relieve at 2.0 bar. The 15-minute hold is BMW's practice on a later model (BMW SI B17 03 16); no E46 test pressure from TIS has been read.

In Phase 12, before the first start, with the car powered up in Phase 11:

  1. Battery on a charger. Ignition on, engine off. With automatic climate control (IHKA): temperature at maximum, blower low but on, A/C off. With manual climate control (IHKR): blower at position 1, since at 0 the valve is energized shut, and the temperature dial fully right (BMW ST054, IHKR). With the M3 valve, you should hear its pump.
  2. After a few minutes, top up, and crack the vent screw until coolant runs without bubbles. Refit it at 2.5 Nm.

First start and heat cycles:

  1. Start the engine and let it idle for about one minute with the cap off. Top up to the mark and fit the cap (BMW ST054, engine cooling).
  2. Let it warm up until the thermostat opens. Watch the coolant temperatures in Tool32, not the gauge: the M3 cluster's gauge shows oil temperature (manual). In MSS54DS0.PRG, STATUS_MOTORTEMPERATUR reads the engine and STATUS_KUEHLW_AUSL_TEMPERATUR the radiator outlet (SGBD documentation). The outlet should climb steadily once the engine passes about 80 °C (176 °F). Look for leaks.
  3. Switch off and let the coolant cool to 30 °C (86 °F) or below. Crack the vent screw: a hiss of air means another heat cycle, steps 11 to 13. Expect two (Blankowski).
  4. After the first drives, check the level again, cold.

Cooling checks and pass values

Check How Pass
Leaks Pressure tester on the tank neck, engine cold Holds 2.0 bar (29 psi) for 15 minutes with no drop and no seepage
Cap The tester's cap adapter Holds, and relieves at 2.0 bar
Level Cold, at 30 °C (86 °F) or below The top of the red float at the filler-neck rim, up to 2 cm (3/4 in) above
Air Vent screw cracked with the coolant cold No hiss, usually after two heat cycles
Thermostat Tool32: radiator outlet against engine temperature, warming up The outlet rises once the engine passes about 80 °C (176 °F); no fault 96 (0x60)
Viscous fan By hand, engine off Bearing tilt play within ±0.65 mm, measured at 120 mm diameter. BMW rates the coupling on at 92 °C (198 °F) and off at 60 °C (140 °F) (Flow p.61)
Electric fan Tool32 STEUERN_E_LUEFTER; then the A/C on at idle Runs on command; runs with the A/C on at a standstill, faster as the refrigerant pressure rises (manual)
Overheating Never test it on purpose The overheat lamp lights at 120 °C (248 °F), and the electric fan then runs on (BMW ST054, IHKA)
Oil cooler Feel its pipes after a hard drive Warm once the oil passes 95 °C (203 °F)

Fault 96 (0x60), "Plausibilisierung Kühleraustrittstemp." (radiator-outlet temperature plausibility) is the MSS54's check of the radiator-outlet reading against the engine's. BMW's job file lists "temperature rise too small, or radiator warmer than engine" among this fault's types (SGBD documentation), so we infer that a thermostat stuck open, or a radiator-outlet sensor that's unplugged or reading the wrong hose, would set it. Related faults: 43 (0x2B), the radiator-outlet sensor's circuit; 78 (0x4E), the engine's coolant sensor; and 53 (0x35), the electric fan.

Air conditioning

Your Touring keeps its A/C system. The condenser, receiver-drier, refrigerant lines, pressure sensor, expansion valve and evaporator are the same part numbers on the US M3 and the US 325i Touring. The S54 brings its own compressor and bracket, and only one line changes: the pressure hose from the compressor to the condenser (ETK: M3, ETK: Touring).

Safety

Never open an A/C line until a shop with Section 609-certified staff has recovered the refrigerant. Nobody may vent it (EPA). The rules are under A/C, odometer, title and insurance.

What changes.

Part US E46 M3 US 325i Touring Do this
Compressor 64526910458 to 09/2002, 64526916232 from 09/2002 64526910458; check yours The donor's, on the S54
Compressor bracket 64551432237 64551432237, or 64557512556 from 09/2002 The donor's
Compressor belt 11287830946 (5 ribs, 829 mm), tensioner pulley 11281433571 11281437450 (5 ribs, 863 mm), or 11287512762 (4 ribs, 863 mm) from 09/2002 The donor's pulley and a new belt. Count the donor's pulley grooves first: Denso lists 4 for 64526916232, while ETK gives the M3 only the 5-rib belt (spareto)
Pressure hose, compressor to condenser 64536902681, M3 only 64536984883 The donor's
Condenser 64538377614 Same Keep
Hose, condenser to receiver-drier 64536904013 Same Keep
Receiver-drier 64538377330, in bracket 64536917658 Same A new drier on the day of the charge; keep the bracket
Hose, drier to evaporator; double pipe at the evaporator 64536909448; 64536908907 Same Keep
Suction pipe 64536923956, with cover 64538385711 Same Keep
Pressure sensor 64539181464 (was 64539141957) Same Keep
Expansion valve; evaporator 64503452759; 64119135744 Same Keep, in the heater box
Service-valve cores and cap 64509177579 (low side); 64509177577 or 64538391215 (high side); cap 64538387437 Same Inspect; caps on
O-rings in the lines 64508374959 (4), 64508375741 (3), 64508363041 (1), 64538375742 (2) Same New at every joint you open
Flange screws 07119905720 (M8 × 30): 20 Nm (15 ft-lb) Same —
Compressor relay K19 61368373700 Same Keep

Sources: ETK for both cars' condensers (M3, Touring), receiver-driers (M3, Touring) and evaporators (M3, Touring); the M3's compressor, bracket and belt; the Touring's belt and later bracket. Flange-screw torque: Flow p.63.

Why not keep your Touring's compressor? One S54 sedan swap kept the 325i's compressor with its lines connected, so its refrigerant circuit was never opened; it needed a different belt (e46fanatics). In this build the donor's compressor is simpler. Your Touring's system stands open for months anyway. From 09/2002 the Touring's compressor runs a 4-rib belt where the S54's drive takes 5 ribs, so its pulley may not suit the S54. And the M3's pressure hose is the one made for the S54.

The job, phase by phase.

  1. Phases 0 and 1: before teardown. Photograph both cars' underhood A/C labels, which give the refrigerant charge and the oil. Run BMW's quick check on each car: windows and doors shut, engine at 1,500–2,000 rpm, blower on medium, maximum cold, A/C on for more than 3 minutes. The centre vent should blow at least 11 °C (20 °F) colder than the outside air; BMW's reference conditions are 32 °C (90 °F) and 50% humidity (BMW ST054, A/C service).
  2. Phases 2 and 4: recovery. A shop recovers each car's refrigerant before any line is opened. Ask it to write down how much refrigerant and how much oil came out of each car: BMW puts the recovered oil back in at the charge (BMW ST054, A/C service).
  3. Phase 4: keep your Touring's old compressor. When the M54 comes out, unbolt the compressor, cap its ports and keep it until the A/C is charged. BMW sets the oil in a replacement compressor by what the old one held (same source).
  4. Phase 10: fit the lines. The donor's pressure hose 64536902681 goes between the compressor and the condenser; your Touring's other lines stay. Fit new O-rings at every joint you open, wetted with the system's oil, and tighten the flange screws to 20 Nm (15 ft-lb). Leave the old drier in place and keep the system capped: the new one goes in on the day of the charge. The M3's header-to-A/C-line heat shield bolts to three studs on the M3's frame rail that a non-M rail lacks; a non-M car with an MK60 has only the center one, for the brake line. One S54-Touring owner stud-welded the missing studs, though most swaps skip the shield (NAM3 – Black & Tan 332iT #158, NAM3 – Trent's swap). Weld the studs while the engine bay is empty (Phases 4 to 8), or fit rivnut studs later, and fit the shield before the A/C is charged.
  5. Phase 12, after the first start: the charge. Give the shop the brief in Shop briefs. On the day, BMW's steps (BMW ST054, A/C service):
    • Fit the new receiver-drier 64538377330. BMW replaces it whenever a system has stood open for more than 24 hours.
    • Set the oil (below).
    • Evacuate for at least 30 minutes, then close off and hold for 5 minutes. A change of more than 7 kPa (2 inHg) means a leak.
    • Charge by weight to your Touring's underhood label.
    • Run the new compressor in: A/C off, every vent shut, engine idling, blower at 75% or more; then A/C on for at least 2 minutes at idle.

Charge and oil.

  • Refrigerant: R-134a, by weight, to the underhood label. Expect about 0.74 kg (26 oz). MAHLE's fill-quantity handbook, a vendor source, lists 715–765 g for every E46 petrol engine, the S54 included (MAHLE), and one E46 M3 owner reports 710–765 g (25–27 oz) (NAM3). The label decides.
  • Oil: PAG, about 150 ml (5.1 US fl oz) for the whole system (MAHLE). Use the type on the label; the NAM3 owner names PAG 46. Both OE compressors, 64526910458 and 64526916232, are Denso 7SBU16C units, filled with 160 ml of Denso ND-8 PAG when new (spareto: DCP05014, DCP05039).
  • Where the oil goes, by BMW's rules: a replacement compressor gets the amount of oil that came out of the old one, plus 10 g. We apply that rule to the donor's compressor: drain it, then refill it with the amount drained from your Touring's old compressor, plus 10 g. Add back the oil recovered from your Touring's system, plus about 30 ml (1 oz) for the new drier, and about 60 ml (2 oz) more if you fit a new condenser or evaporator. Hoses hold little oil. The total should come to about 150 ml (MAHLE).

Can you do it yourself? Small cans of R-134a, 0.9 kg (2 lb) or less with a self-sealing valve, can still be sold for DIY use; larger containers are sold only to technicians certified under Section 608 or 609 (EPA). The refrigerant has to come out through certified recovery equipment before the system is opened (EPA), and an empty system needs a vacuum pump and a charge by weight. Give the recovery and the charge to a shop.

Climate-control coding. Keep your Touring's. Its coding carries engine and compressor settings, and both cars are six-cylinder petrol, so never code it from the M3's vehicle order. The checks are in the manual's A/C section.

A/C checks and pass values

Check How Pass
Compressor engages Snowflake button on, blower at 1 or more In MSS54DS0.PRG, STATUS_DIGITAL, both STAT_AC_EIN and STAT_KO_EIN read 1; the clutch pulls in; the idle holds
Electric fan A/C on, car standing The fan runs, faster as the refrigerant pressure rises (manual)
Efficiency, BMW's test Outside air at 20–30 °C (68–86 °F). Heat the cabin first: recirculation, air to the footwells and windscreen, maximum heat and blower, 2,000 rpm to operating temperature, then idle. Switch the A/C on when the cabin reaches 50 °C (122 °F) The evaporator reads 15 °C (59 °F) or less within 3–4 minutes: Tool32, IHKR46 or IHKA46, STATUS_ANALOGEINGAENGE, STAT_TVERDAMPFER_WERT
Pressures Gauges on both ports, engine at 1,500–2,000 rpm Low side 1–2 bar (15–30 psi), up to about 3 bar (45 psi) on a hot day. High side 10–15 bar (150–225 psi), roughly 2–2.5 times the outside temperature in °F, read as psi
Vent temperature Thermometer in the centre vent 4–20 °C (40–68 °F), and at least 11 °C (20 °F) below the outside air

The values are BMW's (BMW ST054, A/C service). If the evaporator test fails, BMW's next step is to recover and weigh the charge. If the compressor never engages, work through the manual's A/C section, which starts with the climate control's coded compressor lock.

Deep dive: electronics and coding

The S54 brings its own engine computer (the DME) and engine harness. Your body wiring, keys, light module and body modules stay. Five things change: the engine harness and a few body-side pins, the fuel-pump trigger, the immobilizer handshake, the instrument cluster and, if you choose, the stability-control unit. Figure 18 maps the modules involved. This chapter explains each choice and the order of work. Pin tables, continuity checks and button-by-button coding sessions are in the Wiring and coding manual.

Decide these before you strip the donor. They set which donor parts you harvest and which of your own you keep.

Decision Recommended Alternatives Details
Engine wiring The complete M3 engine harness and DME, with your body-side plugs re-pinned in the E-box A plug-in swap harness Harness and re-pinning
Fuel-pump trigger Leave your pump relay wiring as it is and accept one stored fault code Fit the US M3's pump module, or have the fault suppressed Fuel-pump control
Immobilizer An EWS-delete flash of the donor DME, with your VIN written in A used DME matched to your EWS, by a vendor or virginized for you to sync; the donor's EWS and keys Immobilizer (EWS)
DME software A manual donor's US software, unchanged apart from the delete and your VIN An SMG donor's DME needs US manual ("HS") software: from the delete vendor, ECUWorx's tool or a WinKFP flash Manual, Session 2
Cluster The M3 cluster, set to your VIN and true mileage by a vendor or by fitting a new memory chip Keep your Touring's cluster Instrument cluster and mileage
Stability control and brake hydraulics Keep your Touring's MK60, booster and master cylinder, coded as they are The M3's MK60 (donors built from 09/2002), coded from a session vehicle order with M3 values set by hand DSC, brakes and steering angle

Order of work. The coding jobs depend on each other, so do them in this order:

  1. Back up first (the manual's Session 1). Set up the laptop and cable and prove them on your unmodified Touring. Then save the vehicle order, every module's coding, and the memories of the cluster and light module. These files are your way back (manual).
  2. DME during bench work (Session 2). Have it EWS-deleted with your VIN written in (Phase 3).
  3. Wire, then check. Re-pin, prove every moved wire with a meter, then power up and let the DME's status jobs prove the electronic parts at the ends of those wires (manual).
  4. EWS check (Session 3). After a delete there's nothing to sync; confirm that your EWS reads the key and the clutch input.
  5. Cluster before DSC (Session 4). The DSC checks its VIN against the cluster's. In one 330Ci the DSC and yellow BRAKE lamps went out only once the M3 cluster carried the car's VIN (e46fanatics), and an M3 owner's MK60 "complained that the vin was not a match" with the cluster (NAM3). Session 4 also checks which vehicle order the cluster holds. A chip-route cluster brings the donor M3's, and that's the one to keep: BMW's coding data accepts an M3 cluster only with an M3 order, so your car's order stays in the light module (ALSZ), the source for every other module (manual).
  6. DSC, then the first start (Sessions 5 and 6). Initialise the DSC and run its compensation routines (an M3 unit is coded first), then start the engine with its adaptations cleared and let the throttles relearn (manual).
  7. Alignment, then the final steering-angle calibration (Session 7).
  8. Options last (Sessions 8 and 9): M Track, units and lighting, each tested on a running car. Code only the modules each change touches, one at a time. Never use Code Car on this car: it re-codes every module from the vehicle order and wipes the hand-set cluster and DSC values (NAM3).

Harness and re-pinning

Use the complete M3 engine harness and its DME. Your MS43 or MS45.1 and the M3's MSS54 or MSS54HP use the same five-plug Siemens connector, X60001 to X60005, but the pin assignments differ throughout (BMW ST055, WDS). X60004, the 40-pin "vehicle interface", belongs to your body harness and stays. The other four plugs come with the M3 harness, along with its E-box branch, fuse carrier and gearbox-module harness. Keep the donor's DME and harness together. The coil pin order differs between DME families, and one 330Ci owner damaged a DME by mixing MS43 and MS45 coil harnesses during an M54 swap (e46fanatics). The M3 harness's part numbers change at 09/2003, about when the MSS54HP arrived (ETK), but BMW's diagrams wire an HP donor like an MSS54 of the same build date (manual).

Find out which DME you have first. US 325i Tourings built to 02/2003 have an MS43, and those built from 03/2003 an MS45.1 (ETK). Read the label in the E-box. Kassel's chart and most forum posts call the MS45.1 "MS45". BMW's wiring-diagram tables headed "MS45" are drawn for the M56 SULEV car, and the pinout workbook's "MS45.1" tab is a 3.0-litre table, so don't wire your car from either. The manual lists the other ways to tell (manual).

What moves. Most X60004 circuits sit on the same pins on all three DMEs and don't move: the pedal, CAN, EWS, terminal 15, diagnosis, the A/C and secondary-air relays, the electric fan, road speed, the cruise buttons, the radiator-outlet sensor and the fuel-pump relay on pin 10. These change, from BMW's Wiring Diagram System (WDS); each wire's color, size and drawing are in the manual (manual: MS43, manual: MS45.1):

Circuit MS43 Touring (to 02/2003) MS45.1 Touring (from 03/2003)
Leak-test pump heater Body X6011 pin 7 → X60004 pin 18 X60004 pin 2 → pin 18
Secondary-air sensor — Take the wires out of X60004 pins 5 and 15
E-box fan — Take the wire out of X60004 pin 19, if there is one
Brake-light switch, test contact X60004 pin 28 → pin 34 Same
Clutch signal X60004 pin 23 → body X6011 pin 7, once the heater wire is out X60004 pin 23 → body X6011 pin 7, with a new terminal
Oil-pressure lamp Body X6011 pin 3 → X60004 pin 11 Add a wire: X60004 pin 11 → cluster pin 13
Charge lamp Body X6011 pin 4 → X60004 pin 1 Add a wire: X60004 pin 1 → cluster pin 2
Oil level Body X6011 pin 5 → X60004 pin 21 Add a wire: X60004 pin 21 → cluster pin 17
Start feedback to the cluster Body X6011 pin 6 → X60004 pin 2 The same move, only if your X6011 pin 6 holds a wire
DME ground Add a wire: X60004 pin 5 → ground point X1108 (recommended) Same, once pin 5 is clear
Sport button (optional) Add X60004 pins 15 and 16 from the switch center Same, once pin 15 is clear
Clutch-switch module Fit the M3's, 61319122700 Same
Cluster coding Code its three lamp switches to the wires, not CAN Same

In X6011 the clutch wire meets the M3 harness's gray wire, which runs through the gearbox's gear switch to X60002 pin 20. The leak-test pump's own wires, on pins 20 and 30, don't move on BMW's drawings; test them before you change anything. Work in the order of the manual's tables, wires out before wires in. On an MS45.1, tag pins 2 and 15 before you pull them: both are black with red (SW/RT).

Where other sources differ. The tables follow BMW's drawings. You'll meet these other versions:

  • Kassel's swap chart puts the oil-pressure lamp on cluster pin 14, which is the K-bus. WDS, BMW's ISTA as a swap shop quoted it, and owners' working cars use pin 13 (Kassel, NAM3). The chart also prints the brake wire BR/GN where WDS has BR/GR (brown with gray), and its MS43 and MS45 columns leave out the clutch, the heater and some of the lamps.
  • A forum mapping sends X6011 pin 6 to X60004 pin 6. WDS puts that wire, the start feedback, on pin 2 (e46fanatics).
  • Forum advice to swap pins 20 and 30 on MS45.1 cars follows BMW's table labels, which call the two pins pump and valve the other way round from the MSS54's. Every drawing wires them to the module the same way, and one builder who swapped still had a leak-test fault (e46fanatics). Test before you swap.
  • X60004 pin 5 is a ground on every M3: a 0.35 mm² BR/SW wire to ground point X1108, under the driver's-seat carpet. On an MS45.1 the cavity holds the secondary-air sensor's wire, which must come out. No source shows what the DME uses this ground for, and the one builder who added one saw no change (WDS, NAM3). Fit it anyway: it's one wire, and it matches BMW's wiring.
Note

A widely quoted e46fanatics list moves four wires (oil pressure, oil level, charge lamp and start signal) from X60004 into X6011. Its author posted it from memory, about an earlier MS42-to-MS43 M54 swap in a 1998 323i (e46fanatics). For an S54 in an MS43 Touring, the same wires move the other way, into X60004; an MS45.1 Touring adds them.

Why the lamps matter. On an MS43 Touring the oil-pressure switch reaches the cluster through X6011 without touching the DME, and on an MS45.1 the lamps arrive over CAN. The M3 routes all three through the DME: the oil-pressure switch comes in at X60003 pin 26, and the lamp goes out at X60004 pin 11. A 2001 325iT with an S54 showed neither its oil nor its battery lamp until this was fixed (e46fanatics), and an S54-swapped 2003 330i ZHP (MS45.1) needed the pin-11 wire added and the cluster recoded (NAM3). Prove the lamp at key-on before the first start, and prime the oil with a gauge anyway (see Phase 12).

The E-box plugs. Besides X60004, the M3 harness meets your body harness at two E-box plugs, X6011 (black, 8 pins) and X6021 (black, 4 pins), and the battery feed to the DME relay comes in at X64101/X64102. After the moves, X6011 carries only the starter wire, terminal 15 and the clutch wire, on pins 1, 2 and 7. X6021 pin 1 carries the US M3's pump-module signal and has no mate in a manual 325i, so it stays unconnected (Fuel-pump control). X6053 and X6054 (X60531 and X60541 on an MS45.1) join the engine harness to the gearbox-module harness within each car's own set, so use the M3's sections together. Mixed halves put the M3's throttle-actuator lines on the Touring's injector feed: a 330i swap got injector "circuit low" faults on all six that way (e46fanatics). Older forum posts describe a 3-pin E-box plug with the reverse-light wires and the DME-relay feed; BMW's drawings for these cars put those on X6021 and X64101/X64102 (manual). Compare every cavity on both halves before you join a plug. While the donor is still whole, trace its circuits: Tenza's builder understood Kassel's re-pin instructions only after tracing them on his donor (Tenza Motorsports – M3 Touring build finally runs (2021), 08:36).

Power, grounds and fans. The DME relay (K6300), the injector and secondary-air relays, the E-box and the engine ground cable are the same parts on both cars, so the M3 harness meets your car's power layout unchanged (manual). Add the X60004 pin-5 ground above. The electric fan's DME wire doesn't move (X60004 pin 4). But on a manual Touring the fan the DME drives sits in the radiator shroud, with its plug X82 on the shroud, while the M3's electric fan is a pusher in front of the condenser: compare the plugs, then extend or re-route X82's lead if it doesn't reach (one manual-Touring swap plugged it straight in) (Cooling and oil cooler, manual). If your E-box has no blower (BMW fits one only to automatic, SMG and hot-climate cars), leave the M3 harness's E-box fan plug unconnected, as Tenza did (ETK, Tenza Motorsports – 5 things they don't tell you, part 2 (2021), 02:05).

Re-pin, don't splice. One swapper's advice: "Learning to de-pin is faster, neater, and less prone to error" (e46fanatics). Use depinning keys and BMW pre-crimped repair leads. X6011 and X60004 take different terminals, so a wire that moves between them needs a new terminal of the target's type. Nobody publishes which terminal fits which cavity, so pull one from the cavity you'll use and match it in the manual's terminal table before you order (manual). Switch the ignition off whenever you plug or unplug the DME; BMW warns that arcing can damage it (BMW ST055).

A swap harness instead? Redline's adapter ($265) and Race German's ($304.88, made to order, no refunds) are sold per DME family, with new connectors and pedal, pump-relay and Sport-button wiring, and both need an EWS-deleted DME (Redline, Race German, October 2026). Neither publishes its circuit list, so ask whether it covers the cluster lamps, the brake-switch move, the leak-test heater, the clutch move and keeping X6021 pin 1 off the pump relay. Don't fit the M3's whole body harness: the one build that did had to move the Touring-only circuits into it (PistonHeads).

Body-side jobs (wiring in the manual):

  • Sport button (optional). It switches the DME's throttle map. Fit the M3's console switch unit (61316925520 on coupes, 61316925521 on convertibles) and wire its plug X1869: pin 17 to X60004 pin 15 for the button, pin 18 to X60004 pin 16 for its LED. One non-M swap did exactly that, and it worked (e46fanatics). A base Touring with only a DSC button also lacks the switch center's terminal-30 and terminal-R feeds and its K-bus wire, on X1869 pins 7, 22 and 23 (manual, M346 Projects – E46 M3 SMG Touring build, part 2 (2023), 20:45). Watch: Tenza Motorsports – 5 things they don't tell you, part 2 (2021), 08:45.
  • Cruise control needs the brake-switch move, the clutch chain through X6011 pin 7 and the gear switch to X60002 pin 20, and the M3's clutch-switch module, 61319122700. The module is required, not optional: the M3's sends +12 V with the pedal up, and your Touring's (61319231129) doesn't (NAM3). Two S54 builds cured no cruise with it (e46fanatics, NAM3). The 420G's gear switch is 23142229113 (ETK).
  • Keep the start interlock. The clutch module's fourth wire to EWS pin 8, fitted to US and Japanese cars, stays as it is (e46fanatics).
  • Sensor leads that may not reach the M3's parts: the coolant-level sensor (the M3 expansion tank sits on the other side), the washer pump and level sensor (the M3 tank sits low), and the radiator-outlet sensor (e46fanatics, Tracks and Trails – Attempting to drive my E46 M3 Touring (2026), 22:40). Add the electric fan's plug X82, which has to reach the M3's pusher fan (manual).
  • Heater valve. Every E46 M3 except the CSL has a valve with a small electric pump (64118369807) that your Touring's plain valve lacks. Either fit your plain valve (64118369805) on the S54 with the CSL's valve-to-heater-core hose 64212282548, with no wiring or coding (recommended), or keep the M3 valve and wire and code its pump. One builder who left the pump unwired found his cooling system hard to bleed (manual, UNRIVALED – Watch this before you S54 swap (2021), 02:32). See Cooling and oil cooler.
  • A/C. Both climate controls send the A/C request over the K-bus to the cluster, which passes it to the DME over CAN. A/C with the S54 is confirmed on cars with automatic climate control (IHKA). Nobody has reported first-hand on manual climate control (IHKR), but BMW describes the same messages, so it should work; test it early (manual, e46fanatics). Keep your Touring's climate-control coding, which carries engine and compressor settings. If the compressor never engages, check the climate control's coded compressor lock first (same manual section).

Fuel-pump control

Your Touring and a US M3 switch their fuel pumps differently (WDS, WDS, BMW ST041, ETK):

Car What switches the pump DME output
Your 325i Touring (M54, MS43 or MS45.1) Relay K96 (white-green, 61368373700) behind the glovebox. The DME grounds its coil through a black/violet (SW/VI) wire X60004 pin 10
Euro M3 Relay K96 X60004 pin 10
US M3 A pump module (EKP, 61357892976) that slows the pump at idle and part load, in a coupe's trunk above the right rear wheel or behind a convertible's right rear side trim (e46fanatics) X60002 pin 11, a 0–120 Hz PWM signal, out through the E-box plug X6021 pin 1

On the US M3's drawings X60004 pin 10 is "not used", a Euro-only output. Builders report that US software drives it anyway: swap shops run K96 from it (e46fanatics, e46fanatics). BMW's drawings put K96 on pin 10 on both of your DMEs, the MS45.1 too; the workbook tab that lists pin 10 as unused is the M56 layout (manual).

Recommended: leave your pump wiring as it is. The MSS54's pin-10 output then switches your K96 relay. A swap shop that does this on non-M E46s: "I don't modify anything in the fuel pump wiring system, this DOES leave a shadow code for the Fuel Pump Relay (shows in ISTA/INPA but not on a generic scan tool) but does not set the CEL", and the car "will pass an OBD2 plug in emissions test" (e46fanatics). Kassel's swap chart lists no pump changes for any E46 (Kassel). Three checks, all part of the manual's checks before first power-up:

  1. Pin 10 reaches K96's coil. Continuity from the X60004 pin-10 cavity to pin 4 of the relay's socket. Then, at key-on, the pump primes once, and Tool32's STEUERN_EKP makes K96 click; the click proves your software drives pin 10.
  2. The PWM wire stays off the relay. On a manual 325i the body side of X6021 pin 1 is empty, so the M3's pump-module wire connects to nothing (WDS). Keep it that way. A relay coil can't follow a 0–120 Hz signal and would likely chatter; nobody has reported trying it (NAM3).
  3. Expect the stored fault: location 1 (0x01), "Relais Kraftstoffpumpe", because US software misses its pump module. It shows in INPA, ISTA and PA-Soft, not on a generic scanner, and doesn't light the check-engine lamp; INPA prints it as 1. Don't confuse it with 130 (0x82), the immobilizer fault. A real pump fault carries the same number, so tell them apart by the car: with one prime at key-on, 5.0 bar and a running engine it's the expected fault; with no prime and no pressure it's real. BMW's files don't say exactly what sets the fault. One untested lead: the MSS54 learns which pump control is fitted, and Tool32 can read that value, STAT_EKP_CFG_VERBAUT_WERT; that it has anything to do with the fault is our inference. Read it if you're curious, and write nothing to the DME (manual).

If your state reads manufacturer fault codes, or you want a clean fault memory, you have two alternatives:

  • Fit the M3's EKP module. It takes five wires where the relay takes four, and its signal needs a terminal and a new wire in your side of X6021 pin 1 (manual). Kalim suggests rewiring the socket behind the glovebox for it (e46fanatics). It brings back the slow-running pump and BMW's documented crash cut-off. Nobody has documented it in a Touring.
  • Have the DME vendor suppress the fault. One swapper planned to have it "coded out" (e46fanatics), and Kassel's "Engine Swap Coding" ($349) includes "any and all options" for a swap (Kassel); ask before you order.

Don't flash Euro DME software to get rid of the fault. It drops the functions the pin tables mark "USA only", including the DM-TL leak test you need for inspection (our reading of the pinout sheet).

With the relay, your pump runs at full speed whenever the engine runs. That sends more fuel back to the tank's jet pump and makes more pump heat and noise; no failures have been reported from it. Your K96 feeds the pump through a 1.5 mm² wire, where the US M3's module uses 2.5 mm² (WDS, WDS), so with an M3 pump check the voltage at the pump connector: within 0.5 V of the battery (test T4 in Test the fuel system). An E46 has no wire from the airbag unit to the pump: the airbag unit sends a crash message on the K-bus, the cluster passes it on over CAN, and the DME switches the pump off (BMW ST034). The MSS54 has the function, but whether US software also drops its pin-10 relay output after a crash isn't documented (manual). All of this assumes an M54 Touring with this relay. The M56 SULEV engine has its own pump controller and a returnless metal tank, and a manual gearbox doesn't rule it out, so check your engine code (BMW B11 75 02, Check your own Touring first). The pressure and delivery tests, the M3 filter-regulator and the fuel lines are in Fuel system; the pins and checks are in the manual.

Immobilizer (EWS)

How it works. Your EWS reads the key's transponder through the ring antenna and checks the clutch input. It then releases the starter and sends a rolling code to the DME. If the code matches, the DME enables injection and ignition; if not, the engine cranks but won't start (BMW ST051). The DME burns the code table into its memory the first time it pairs with an EWS: "once a DME is 'Married' to the vehicle it will not work in any other vehicle", and BMW's alignment job only resets the table to its first code (same source). So:

  • Cranks but won't start, with fault 130 (0x82, "EWS manipulation") stored: the DME isn't accepting your EWS.
  • Won't crank: the cause is upstream of the DME. Check the key, ring antenna, EWS, and the clutch input at EWS pin 8.
  • Cranks, fires once or twice, never runs: treat it as the immobilizer too. A builder of S54 Tourings: "Key to EWS blocks/enables cranking. EWS to DME blocks/enables starting. EWS to DME issues generally manifest as a brief fire or no fire at all." On one M3 the cause was a delete that hadn't taken; once the DME carried a working delete it started (NAM3 (2025)). Have the vendor re-check the delete.
  • Runs for a few seconds, then dies: not the immobilizer. Look elsewhere, starting with the throttle system and the pump hold (manual).
Route What it involves Cost (October 2026) In Tourings
1. EWS delete (recommended) A vendor or a licensed tool sets the donor DME to skip the rolling-code check; your VIN goes in at the same time $100–$300, plus $20 for the VIN at Kassel The usual route; your keys, locks and start interlock stay
2. Used DME matched to your EWS A vendor programs the used DME to your car's EWS and key, or clears it for you to sync yourself About $300 at RPM, plus shipping both ways None in a Touring. A vendor-hosted review reports a running S54 in a 2001 330i after RPM matched its used DME "to the EWS and key" (RPM). A DIY sync is still undocumented: two failures in Tourings, and two more DIY-virginized MSS54s failed (route 2 below)
3. Donor EWS and keys Fit the M3's EWS with its DME and use its key Parts from the donor Cleared the EWS fault in one 325iT, which still didn't start; you carry two keys

Route 1: the delete. It's one setting in the DME's data, changed by the vendor or by a licensed tool (ECUWorx, Kassel). Afterwards, "the EWS module is now simply looking for a proper matchup with the key transponder" (NAM3): your EWS still checks the key and the clutch and still controls the starter, and that's the only immobilizer layer left. Fault 130 (0x82) may stay stored unless the tampering fault is deleted too; one owner "confirmed that the engine can start" with it (same source).

Vendor Service and price (October 2026)
Kassel Performance EWS delete $109; VIN recode $20; "Engine Swap Coding" with all swap options and a consult $349; optional $429 core charge
DUDMD Bench flash $215; remote flash with a cable you keep $225 (needs a Windows 8 or newer laptop)
Severn Tuning MSS54 and MSS54HP delete, $100, or $200 with its "Shipping" option; listed "for off-road use only"
RPM Motorsport "Ready to start" delete, $300, 1–2 business days after arrival
Poverty Built Tunes from $220, with immobilizer and swap configuration on request

You can also read the DME yourself, have the file done remotely and flash it back, as Tracks and Trails did (Tracks and Trails – Attempting to drive my E46 M3 Touring (2026), 1:12:40), or run ECUWorx's licensed tool yourself (manual). When you order:

  1. Read and save the DME's identification, VIN slots and fault memory before you ship it, and check that the vendor supports its hardware number (manual).
  2. Order the delete with your Touring's full 17-character VIN. If the donor was an SMG car, ask for manual-gearbox software too. SMG software left in place kept one swapped sedan in limp mode (UNRIVALED – Watch this before you S54 swap (2021), 02:02).
  3. Decline the secondary-air, rear-O2, catalyst-efficiency and EVAP deletes on these vendors' menus. They're illegal on a road car.
  4. When the DME comes back, read your VIN out of it.
Key point

Keep the clutch-start interlock. Leave the clutch switch's wire to EWS pin 8 in place and the EWS parameter PARK/NEUTRAL_EINGANG at aktiv (e46fanatics). A popular swap video recodes it to nicht_aktiv to get a car to start (ShopLifeTV – Starting the S54 swap car for the first time (2015), 01:08), which lets the engine crank in gear. If the car won't crank, find the fault instead.

Route 2: a used DME matched to your EWS. If a vendor does the matching, as RPM's used-DME EWS programming does, you get the DME back ready for your key; that has worked once, in a 2001 330i (above). If you sync it yourself, only a DME whose immobilizer memory has been cleared can learn your EWS (BMW ST051). That's a vendor job, done through the DME's programming port: RPM Motorsport offers used-DME EWS programming for $300, and in October 2026 Kassel listed virginizing only for the M54's MS43 (RPM, Kassel). The Tool32 sync sequence that circulates worked once, on one owner's CSL-clone MSS54: a DME converted in hardware to run CSL software, whose immobilizer code (ISN) he had written in through its BDM programming port. He wasn't sure it works on a virgin DME (NAM3). INPA's keys for an MSS54 sync aren't documented: Kassel's widely shared "Shift + F6, F1" clip syncs an M54's MS43 (KasselPerformance – MS43 EWS sync in INPA (2015)). Two other MSS54s virginized with a DIY flasher failed too: one wouldn't sync ("Error_SG_Rejected" in INPA) and one was bricked (NAM3, NAM3). Two Touring attempts failed:

  • A 2002 325iT with its donor's DME, not virginized: INPA refused the job, Tool32 reported success but the sync status stayed invalid, and fault 130 (0x82) remained (e46fanatics).
  • A 325xi wagon built in 03/2001, with a Kassel-virginized 2003.5 MSS54: "start value not understood" (e46fanatics). A member blamed the older car's ZCS coding. That's unlikely: BMW keeps the rolling code separate from ZCS coding, and the MSS54 isn't coded from the vehicle order at all (BMW ST051, SGBD documentation). A partly cleared DME, the wrong INPA script or low voltage fit better.

Route 3: the donor's EWS and keys. In the 2002 325iT above, fitting the donor's EWS and key and re-running the Tool32 sync cleared the EWS fault, but the car still cranked without starting, with a fuel-pump relay fault and all six injectors disabled, and the thread ends there (e46fanatics). The route also leaves the car needing the donor key's transponder at the ring antenna as well as your own key in the lock, unless a locksmith re-keys the cylinders; your tailgate and rear-glass locks have no M3 equivalent. The donor EWS and its key transponders carry the donor's VIN, which forum members say takes a dedicated key programmer to change (e46fanatics); the EWS's job file reads it with FGNR_LESEN (SGBD documentation). On a car built from 09/2001 the EWS holds a VIN but no vehicle order, so it's no backup of your options (Instrument cluster and mileage). An SMG donor's EWS may expect a neutral signal rather than your clutch switch, so match its coding to your saved EWS file. Use this route as a test or a fallback.

If your state checks DME software. Since July 2021 California's Smog Check fails software that doesn't match an OEM or CARB-approved configuration (BAR), and a swap shop reports California failing cars for detected tunes (e46fanatics). If your state checks software, ask whether a VIN-matched EWS delete passes before you choose a route. See Registration and legal.

Instrument cluster and mileage

The M3 cluster brings a tachometer with an 8,000 rpm redline and warm-up lights, and an oil-temperature gauge; with the MSS54 they all work (e46fanatics).

Why it needs work. The cluster and the light module (LCM) both store the VIN and mileage and compare them at every key-on. A mismatch lights the "tamper dot" (e46fanatics), and until the VINs match the DSC and yellow BRAKE lamps can stay on too (e46fanatics). A used M3 cluster carries the donor's VIN and mileage, and neither can be rewritten over the OBD port: PA-Soft can read the cluster, but its VIN and mileage areas are write-protected, and NCS Expert can't write a used cluster's VIN (NAM3, e46fanatics). BMW's own rule explains why: "The VIN is entered in the cluster through coding and will only be accepted when the cluster mileage is zero", and the light module passes its mileage to the cluster only when the VINs match and the cluster reads zero (BMW ST052). That's why the routes that work start from a zero-mileage chip, and why a dealer "can program a 'brand new' cluster, but not a used one" (NAM3).

The light module is the master record. It holds your car's VIN and true mileage, and its mileage can only go up (BMW ST052). On cars built from 09/2001 it also holds a copy of the vehicle order (FA), the option list that NCS Expert codes every module from (e46fanatics). Make the cluster match the LCM, never the reverse. One swap video advises "realigning" the LCM to a donor cluster (ShopLifeTV – What parts are needed for an S54 swap (2016), 03:14); with a donor cluster, that rewrites your car's mileage record.

The cluster brings the donor's vehicle order with it. The cluster holds the other copy of the order, in its own memory; BMW's E46 coding data names no third, so the EWS is no backup on your car (SGBD: KOMBI46R, BMW's E46 coding data, via ncsx). A new chip written from the donor's file therefore carries the donor's order: "the VO is brought back onto the new Chip" (NAM3). After the chip route your cluster holds the donor M3's order, coupe or convertible, and your LCM still holds your Touring's; anything coded from the cluster's copy would be coded as the donor. Leave it there all the same: BMW's coding data accepts an M3 cluster (index 22, 23 or 24) only with a vehicle order that has an M3 type key (engine S54B32) and a build date from 09/2001 (BMW's rule: PU01 AND S54B32), so your Touring's order (EN33, M54B25) makes NCS refuse the cluster, and writing it in would very likely be refused too (BMW E46SGVT.000, SP-Daten V32). Note on your coding sheet that the cluster holds the donor's order, and use the light module (ALSZ) as the source of your car's order for every other module (manual).

Two ways to set the cluster to your VIN and true mileage:

  1. A cluster service. Send the cluster with your VIN and the mileage your LCM shows. Kassel set Tenza's M3 cluster "to reflect the mileage of the actual wagon" and added the rear-door warning lights that M3 clusters lack. Tenza budgeted about $1,000 in 2021 for Kassel's DME and cluster work, including shipping (Tenza Motorsports – M3 Touring build finally runs (2021), 02:17, Tenza Motorsports – 5 things they don't tell you, part 2 (2021), 06:07). Huggins Racing lists a used-cluster correction to "your car's VIN, Mileage, and build specification" at $125 (October 2026) (Huggins). Owners also name Fixels and RPM Motorsport (e46fanatics, NAM3). Ask the service to keep the M3 coding and to leave the donor's vehicle order in the cluster: NCS codes an index-23 or 24 cluster only with an M3 order. Turn down coding "from the factory vehicle order", which one service lists as standard (ECUswap): from your order, that default-codes an M3 cluster.
  2. A new memory chip, fitted yourself. Save the cluster's EEPROM with PA-Soft. Prepare a copy with the odometer cleared and your VIN set, and write it to a new M35080 chip, either in a programmer such as the R270 or by soldering in a blank chip and writing it with PA-Soft. With the VIN matching, the refitted cluster reads your true mileage from the LCM within seconds. One S54 wagon owner did exactly this (e46fanatics). It needs hot-air desoldering, and the gauge needles come off and must be reset. The chip also brings back the donor's vehicle order, which is the one the cluster needs, as above. The steps are in the manual.

Cars built before 09/2001 store their options in the older ZCS format, and the light module may not pass the mileage to a new cluster. One 2001 Touring owner had the true reading written straight into the chip (e46fanatics); a cluster service can do the same.

Coding. Keep the M3 cluster's own coding index. The redesigned clusters from about 2003 (index 23 or 24) are the only ones that properly support the M Track light and the brake-force display (e46fanatics). If your Touring was built in 09/2002 or later, its cluster must be from 09/2002 or later too: ECUswap calls that "zwangsweise", compulsory (ECUswap). A 2003–06 donor's cluster qualifies.

Code the cluster only from a complete coding file made from its own read-out, with just the lines you mean to change edited. Never default-code it in this car: no empty coding file, no plain coding from the vehicle order, no "Code Car". With your 325i Touring's order loaded, NCS Expert should refuse the cluster outright, by BMW's coding data (a harmless read with your ALSZ order shows it), and one owner who default-coded a cluster whose index had been altered got a tach stuck at 9,000 rpm until he wrote back his EEPROM backup (e46fanatics, as above). The options that matter:

  • The three lamp switches: with the lamp wires in place, code CAN_OELDRUCKSCHALTER, GENERATOR_UEBER_CAN and TOG_UEBER_CAN to nicht_aktiv, on an MS43 or an MS45.1 Touring. The oil-pressure, charge and oil-level lamps then come from the wires, whatever software the DME runs. BMW's coding data has the three switches on cluster indexes 07 and 08 (non-M) and 23 and 24 (M3) only. A US M3 leaves the factory with oil level over CAN aktiv and oil pressure over CAN nicht_aktiv, and the charge lamp over CAN aktiv only if built from 03/2004 (BMW E46CVT.000, SP-Daten V32). On one index-24 cluster an MSS54HP didn't light the oil-pressure lamp over CAN even with the cluster coded for it (NAM3, manual).
  • Fuel-gauge curve: TANK_KENNLINIE = 60_l_literskala, BMW's coding rule for both the M54 and the S54, so a donor cluster coded from its own M3 order already reads it. On index 23 and 24 clusters metalltank, for the M56's metal tank, is a different curve, while dad_tank_diesel is the same as 60_l_literskala (BMW E46CVT.000, KMBE46M3.C24, manual).
  • Oil-level readout: leave it off. The trip computer's oil-level display (OELNIVEAU_M3) works only on an MSS54HP running the Euro-only CSL software, and this build keeps stock US software. The low-oil warning lamp is set by the DME and works without it (NAM3).
  • M Track light: optional; the mode works without it (ECUWorx). It's one cluster value, ANZEIGE_HOCHLADEN, set in the cluster's coding file alongside an M3 DSC unit coded for M Track (liam821). Keep the M Track option code, $7MA (the Competition package's), out of your stored vehicle order (manual).

Touring details.

  • M3 clusters have no rear-door lights. Solder them in, or have the service add them (e46fanatics); Huggins Racing's mod for M3 clusters in non-M cars adds them for $100 (October 2026) (Huggins).
  • The backlight feed changed at 09/2002: a cluster from an earlier car fitted to a car built from 09/2002 needs a backlight wire to cluster pin 7 (same source). A cluster from a 2003-on donor avoids this.
  • The speedometer over-reads by about 8.9% by design. The M3 cluster's correction table is set to 49/45, against about 5.7% on non-M clusters (e46fanatics), so it isn't caused by the differential. Check it against GPS; an edit to the cluster's memory can correct it.
  • Move the M3 left sender with the M3 delivery unit, as the fuel plan recommends (Choose the pump route), and the cluster reads BMW's own M3 sender pair in a tank of the same 63 L (16.6 US gal); with your Touring's senders, nobody has reported the reading. Either way, check the gauge, the range and Tool32's KOMBI46R.PRG → STATUS_AIF_TANKDATEN_LESEN against a measured fill before you rely on them; STATUS_TANKINHALT_LESEN belongs to the older clusters' job file. It matters beyond the gauge: the DME takes the fuel level from the cluster for its leak test (manual).
  • Nobody has documented what an M3 cluster shows when a Touring's tailgate or rear glass is open. The cluster takes its check-control warnings over the K-bus (BMW ST052); it has one rear-lid symbol and nothing to code for doors or lids, while the body module (GM5) reads the tailgate and rear-glass contacts separately (KOMBI46R, ZKE5). Open each in turn after fitting it and note what it shows; if a symbol stays dark, check the input in Tool32 ZKE5.PRG → STATUS_DIGITAL (manual).
  • Keeping your Touring's cluster also works with the S54; one 323i swapper's stock cluster did (e46fanatics). You lose the M3's tach and warm-up lights.
Safety

Federal law lets you replace an odometer if the replacement shows the same mileage (49 U.S.C. §32704), so the M3 cluster keeps your Touring's true mileage and nothing else. Program it to that mileage, photograph the cluster and LCM readings first, and keep screenshots before and after. Never write a donor cluster's reading into the light module. The federal written mileage disclosure on sale no longer applies to model-year 2010 and older vehicles (49 CFR 580.17), but altering mileage is still illegal and your state may require disclosure.

DSC, brakes and steering angle

Which units you have.

  • Your Touring: a Teves MK60 on most US 325is, though BMW's catalog also lists ASC-only units for the US 325i Touring, with no steering-angle sensor, so check the hydraulic unit's label (ETK, e46fanatics). From 09/2001 the Touring's MK60 (hydraulic unit 34516765453, which superseded 34516759046 in June 2003, and control unit 34526765455; read your own unit's label) uses a 47-pin plug and a yaw-sensor cluster that talks over CAN; earlier MK60s use older analogue sensors (ETK, e46fanatics).
  • The M3: a Teves MK20 (34512229827, 43-pin plug, separate pre-charge pump) on cars built before 09/2002, then an MK60 (34512282558, or 34512282421 on Competition cars from 12/2004) with the same 47-pin plug and yaw sensor as your car (ETK, ETK). The MK20 won't plug into your harness.
  • The parts around the unit are shared. From 09/2002 BMW lists the same wheel-speed sensors (front 34526792896/897, rear 34526752683), yaw and lateral sensor cluster (34526764018) and steering-angle sensor (32306793632) for the M3 as for your Touring, and the same brake pipes (ETK, Brakes and bleeding).

Option A (recommended): keep your Touring's MK60, booster and master cylinder. Its VIN already matches your car, so after the build it needs only the VIN and steering-angle initialisation and the compensation routines (manual, Session 5). It's also the documented fix: one S54 wagon never cleared "VIN not initialized" with an M3 MK60, and refitting its own 325i unit cured it (e46fanatics). Non-M MK60s work with the MSS54 once the cluster, steering-angle sensor and DSC share the car's VIN (e46fanatics). One sedan swapper's sequence was NCS Expert reading the vehicle order from the light module (ALSZ), then SG_CODIEREN on the MK60, then a Tool32 steering-angle calibration; mixing MK20 and MK60 wheel-speed sensors upset his DSC (NAM3 – Trent's swap #57 (2023)).

  • Brakes: the M3 calipers, with the M3's front hoses (34322229723, an M3-only part) on your own pipes. No pipe changes: from 09/2002 the M3 uses the same front pipes as your Touring, and the rear pipes and hoses are the same parts on both cars. The M3 pipes 34322282275/277 belong to M3s built before 09/2002, with the MK20 (ETK, Brakes and bleeding).

  • Pedal: your master cylinder is the 330i's. Forum-reported bore sizes point to a front-circuit pedal about 10% longer and lighter than an M3's (our estimate). M346's 2004 Touring with M3 brakes had a "nice and firm" pedal after a manual and an INPA bleed, though which master cylinder it ran isn't stated (Brakes and bleeding).

  • What you give up. The unit stays coded for a 325i: M54 engine, 325i brakes and rack, open differential. You lose M Track, and coding can't turn the unit into an M3 one. A non-M MK60's coding options (from a dump of one at coding index C05) include no M3 body type (coupe_m) and no M3 rack curve (wert_05). Its body types are coupe, touring, sedan, convertible and roadster, plus "_s" versions such as touring_s. It does offer the M3's brake-pressure models. So "M3 values" on your unit means editing its brake and intervention parameters by hand, not changing its body type (manual, Session 5). There's no tire-size setting either: after fitting the M3 wheels, set the pressures and reset the flat-tire warning, if it's on (Tool32 RPA_RESET). The two mismatches, as we read them (our inference; nobody has tested either):

    • Rack. Your unit's steering-angle curve suits your own 13.7:1 rack. With the M3's 15.4:1 rack and knuckles (Front axle and steering), it assumes about 12% more road-wheel angle than the car gets. The touring_s setting and the ZHP curve (wert_02) that forum posts suggest are for quicker racks, not the M3's slower one (e46fanatics, liam821), so leave the rack setting as it's coded.
    • Brakes. Its brake-pressure models assume 325i brakes. Against your 325i's front brakes, the M3's bigger front pistons and rotors give roughly a third more braking torque per bar (our arithmetic from forum-reported piston sizes), so its interventions may bite harder than it expects. These are the values that could be set to the M3's by hand.

    Our recommendation: leave your unit as it's coded and run the three routines. It's a safety system, and nobody has documented hand-set values in a Touring with M3 brakes and rack (manual, Session 5).
