Option B: the M3's MK60 (donors built from 09/2002). Another S54 wagon ran on both units and was "much better with m-track mode and M3 settings" (NAM3). It brings:

  • The M3 master cylinder (34317838638 from 09/2002) and perhaps the M3 booster (34332282622 from 09/2002), in place of your own (ETK); both cars' numbers are in Brakes and bleeding. Nobody has documented whether the M3 master cylinder suits your booster. In a 330Ci swap the M3 booster's bolt holes didn't line up with the firewall and had to be slotted (DBO – Full M3 swap into a 330Ci, part 1 (2019), 08:44). Whichever booster you use, the S54's vacuum hose reaches it through the M3's check valve, as in Brakes and bleeding.
  • Coding from a session order. NCS Expert codes every MK60 from one rule file that picks M3 values when the vehicle order says S54B32 (liam821). BMW's coding data admits the M3 unit (coding index C06) only with an M3 type key and a production date from 09/2002, so NCS won't code it from your Touring's own order (M54B25, TOUR) at all (SP-Daten V32, manual, Session 5). Coded from a session order with the donor's type key, it takes the M3's values: check them, and set the rack curve and brake models for the parts you fitted. Its coding has no Touring body type, only coupe and convertible, so leave it at coupe_m (ECUWorx).
  • A late enough vehicle order. An M3 MK60 codes only from a vehicle order whose production date suits its coding index: use 09/2002 or later for the coding session, then run INPA's VIN and steering-angle initialisation. Read that order from your light module (ALSZ), not the cluster, which keeps the donor's order, give it the donor's M3 type key and that date for the session only, and don't write the changed order back (no FA_WRITE). Once the unit is coded, keep its final coding file and never run Code Car or write a blank coding file to it: either wipes the hand-set M3 values (manual, Session 5). The S54 wagon whose M3 unit never cleared 5EF1 (5E1F in BMW's job file), "VIN not initialized", had only written a blank coding file and reset the steering-angle sensor in PA-Soft. In a parallel M3 case, the unit coded and initialised once the session's date was late enough (e46fanatics, NAM3, NAM3). If it still won't initialise, refit your own unit. Nobody has documented an M3 MK60 coded into a Touring step by step; the steps are in the manual's Session 5. One S54 Touring has run an M3 MK60 with M Track since 2022, with $7MA ("brake bias, m-track, steering rack") in its vehicle order, but its owner hasn't posted the steps (NAM3 – Black & Tan 332iT #185).
  • On a Touring built before 09/2001, the later yaw-sensor cluster and its wiring as well (e46fanatics).
  • M Track, switched on by coding and worked by the existing DSC button. A cluster with the M Track symbol is optional (ECUWorx). Set it in the MK60's and the cluster's coding files and keep $7MA, the Competition package's code, out of your stored vehicle order (manual, Session 5).
Tip

Whichever you choose, keep your Touring's MK60, booster, master cylinder and cluster until the car has passed inspection, with the rest of the hold list in Space, storage and logistics. They're your fallback.

Wheel-speed sensors. An M3 built before 09/2002 has the MK20, with inductive sensors and gray plugs: they don't plug into your harness, and an MK60 isn't made to read them. From 09/2002 BMW lists the same active sensors with blue plugs for the M3 as for your Touring, and says the MK60 uses the MK20's pulse wheels (ETK: front, ETK: rear, BMW ST056). So your own sensors plug in and read the M3 hubs and half-shafts. Tenza's ABS lamp isn't evidence against that:

  • That 2004 Touring had a 2002 donor, an MK20 car, so the donor's sensors wouldn't plug in, and the Touring's own went into the M3 hubs (Tenza Motorsports – 5 things they don't tell you, part 2 (2021), 03:20).
  • The lamp came on at the first start, with the car standing and the brakes not yet bled (Tenza Motorsports – M3 Touring build finally runs (2021), 07:18, 09:27).
  • Three months later the builder had "not had any issues with this yet", after 0.5–0.6 km (0.3–0.4 mile) of driving (5 things, part 2, 04:00), and his October 2021 update mentions only body damage (Tenza Motorsports – Building an E46 M3 wagon is far more complicated (2021), 01:00).

On a 2003 xi Touring the M3 sensors' plugs mated with the xi's harness (e46fanatics). The xi's Bosch sensors use the same blue housings, so that proves the plugs fit, not how the sensors read (BMW ST056). Never splice an MK20 donor's sensor leads onto your harness. If an ABS lamp stays on after the build, the likeliest causes are faults stored while parts were unplugged, a sensor not fully seated, or a damaged pulse wheel (our inference). The DSC fault number tells them apart: see the manual's Wheel-speed and pad-wear sensors.

Lamps. BMW's red brake lamp means low fluid or the parking brake on. DSC and ABS faults light the yellow brake lamp, the ABS lamp and the DSC lamp, and the DSC unit drives the ABS lamp directly. If the fluid-level switch in the reservoir cap opens, the DSC switches off its traction and stability functions, while ABS and normal braking carry on (BMW ST056). Massachusetts rejects a lit brake warning lamp, so get them all dark before the inspection (Brakes and bleeding).

Coding and VIN. Once the cluster carries your VIN: with Option B only, write your VIN into the M3 unit with PA-Soft and code it. Then, with either unit, initialise the VIN and steering angle in INPA, and run the other two compensation routines, for the pressure sensors and the lateral-acceleration sensor, with the wheel straight, no brake pressure and the car level (e46fanatics, written on a non-US 2002 318i whose INPA pages are the same; NAM3). The steps and the fallbacks (Tool32, a scan tool) are in the manual's Session 5. Watch: LM Auto Repairs – E46 MK60 coding and VIN (2016), 04:47 for the PA-Soft VIN write (filmed on a 2003 E46 diesel), and 50sKid – E46 DSC unit replacement and coding (2016), 33:47 for the initialisation.

Steering angle after the alignment. Calibrate the steering-angle sensor again after the wheel alignment, with the wheel dead straight. The calibration takes the wheel's position as zero, and a calibrated sensor should read 0 with the wheel straight (Evan Goyuk – Calibrate the steering-angle sensor (2020), 03:19), so a sensor zeroed before the toe was set reads off-center afterwards. Use INPA's MK60 page, or Tool32 if your INPA lacks it, as some 5.0.x builds do (e46fanatics). In Tool32 the job is lenkwinkel_dsc_abgleichen in DSC_MK60.PRG (SGBD DSC_MK60); the `test_lenkwinkel` that some guides give belongs to the xi's Bosch unit (manual, Session 7). Then turn to full lock each way: with 3.0 turns lock to lock, expect about 540° either side of zero (our arithmetic). See Wheel alignment.

Bleeding and testing. After caliper and hose work, BMW flushes each wheel, bleeds the rear circuit with its tester's routine and the front by pumping the pedal (TIS 34 00 048); INPA's pump routine is the home equivalent. If the master cylinder, the DSC unit or the pipes between them were opened or ran dry, the routine runs at every wheel (TIS 34 00 050, Brakes and bleeding). Drive only once the pedal is firm, and bleed again after the first few drives (NAM3). Then check the DSC hardware (BMW ST056 for the lamps and the button, SGBD DSC_MK60 for INPA's status readings):

  1. Key on: the ABS, DSC and yellow brake lamps light, then go out after the start or within the first few metres. Expect them to stay on until the faults stored during the build are cleared.
  2. Read the DSC fault memory and note every fault; clear it, drive above 20 km/h (12 mph), and read it again (manual).
  3. In INPA's DSC status, the brake-light switch, the parking-brake switch, the DSC button and the brake-fluid level switch each change state as you work them, and all four wheel speeds agree when rolling.
  4. DSC button: a short press, under 2.5 s, lights the DSC lamp; a long press, over 2.5 s, lights the DSC lamp and the yellow brake lamp. Another press puts them out.
  5. ABS works above 12 km/h (7 mph): make a careful hard stop from above 30 km/h (20 mph) on a quiet road. The pedal pulses and the car stays straight.

If your car turns out to be a 325xi, it has a Bosch DSC 5.7 instead (e46fanatics). Converted to rear drive, it needs more than Option B's unit: the whole MK60 system, with its sensors, sensor cluster, master cylinder, reservoir, pipes and an adapter loom, because the xi's front sensors don't fit a rear-drive hub and MK60 sensors don't work with the Bosch unit (BMW ST056). Kept all-wheel drive, it keeps its own DSC 5.7: there, Option A is the only option. Both are in 325xi: rear drive or all-wheel drive.

Inspection readiness

  • Keep every emissions function. Order the DME flash as an EWS delete only. Keep the secondary-air pump, all four O2 sensors and the DM-TL leak-test pump, wired to the MSS54's pins 18, 20 and 30 (Kassel, manual).
  • Write your full VIN into the DME. State testers read the VIN stored in the DME, and BMW issued a bulletin for E46s whose DME held only the last seven digits (BMW SI B12 09 13). California's test reads it from the OBD port (e46fanatics). So a DME with your full VIN written should report it to the tester. Nobody has confirmed that every US MSS54 answers a generic scanner's VIN request (mode 09), and no rule required it before the 2005 model year: California's OBD rule asks for the VIN only from MY2005, while the rule for 1994–2003 cars asks only for the calibration ID and a software check (13 CCR 1968.2, 13 CCR 1968.1). So a 2001–03 MSS54 may not report a VIN at all: check the donor with a generic scanner in Phase 1, and yours with INPA as well as a scanner.
  • What the federal OBD check passes. A car with stored codes passes if the check-engine lamp isn't commanded on, and a model-year 2001-or-later car may pass with one monitor not ready. It fails if the lamp is commanded on but not lit, or doesn't light with the key on and the engine off (40 CFR 85.2222), so check the bulb with the M3 cluster fitted. States add their own limits: New York fails a 2001-or-later car with more than one monitor not ready (NYVIP3). Massachusetts doesn't emissions-test a 2001–05 car in 2026 (Massachusetts).
  • Expect stored faults: location 1 (0x01), the pump fault, which doesn't light the check-engine lamp (Fuel-pump control explains it), and possibly 130 (0x82) after the EWS delete. Nobody has documented whether a leftover 130 (0x82) commands the lamp, so check STAT_MIL_EIN and a generic scanner rather than guess, and ask for the tampering-fault delete with the EWS delete.
  • The EVAP leak test is the hard monitor. The MSS54 runs its DM-TL test only with the engine off, after at least 20 minutes of driving that followed at least 5 hours parked, with the tank 15–85% full, the air between −7 and 35 °C (20–95 °F) and the battery between 11.5 and 14.5 V, and only every second time those conditions are met (BMW ST041). EVAP is the monitor reported "not ready" on an MSS54 swap (e46fanatics).
  • The cluster feeds the leak test. The DME takes the fuel level, the outside temperature and the parked time from the cluster over CAN (SGBD documentation). An M3 cluster that misreads your Touring's tank senders can keep the test from ever running, so check the fuel gauge against a measured fill first (manual).
  • One bank, and purge under EVAP. The S54 has one bank of six cylinders, so a scanner shows one set of catalyst and O2 results, not two. A generic scanner doesn't list the purge check on its own; it reports it as part of the EVAP monitor (manual).
  • Readiness resets when codes are cleared or the battery is disconnected (NYVIP3). Lazy pre-cat O2 sensors can stop the secondary-air monitor completing (e46fanatics, unverified); BMW does judge the secondary-air system by those sensors' response (BMW ST041). The drive plan is in the manual.
  • The DME's system checks test parts, not readiness. Tool32's secondary-air, leak-test and purge checks report pass or fail. The readiness mask is a separate value that the monitors set while you drive, so we infer the checks never set a monitor to ready; BMW doesn't say (manual). Use them to prove the hardware, then drive.
  • Software checks: see Immobilizer (EWS) and Registration and legal.

Troubleshooting

The full trees and tables, with tool jobs, pins and expected readings, are in the manual. INPA prints fault numbers in decimal and BMW's job documentation in hex, so this guide gives both: 130 (0x82) is the immobilizer fault, and 1 (0x01) the pump fault.

Symptom Likely cause Where to look
Won't crank A flat battery, which stopped Tenza's first attempt (Tenza Motorsports – M3 Touring build finally runs (2021), 03:55); the key not recognized; no clutch signal at EWS pin 8 Won't start, Immobilizer (EWS)
Cranks, won't start, or fires once or twice and never runs; 130 (0x82) stored The DME isn't released: the delete wasn't done or hasn't taken, or a virgin DME's sync failed. "EWS to DME issues generally manifest as a brief fire or no fire at all," as a builder of S54 Tourings puts it (NAM3 (2025)) Immobilizer (EWS)
Cranks, won't start; no prime at key-on X60004 pin 10 not reaching K96, fuse F54 or F3, or the E-box plugs Fuel-pump control
Cranks, won't start; primes, but pressure low Feed and return swapped at the filter-regulator (NAM3) Fuel system
Runs for a few seconds, then dies Not the immobilizer. A throttle-system (EML) fault that shuts the engine off within about 3 seconds is one documented cause (MotoIQ) Won't start
Fault 1 (0x01) stored, but the pump primes and the engine runs Expected with US software on the relay Fuel-pump control
Injector "circuit low" on all six Mixed X6053/X60531 halves Harness and re-pinning
No oil or charge lamp at key-on Lamp wires not moved or added, or the cluster coded for CAN Warning lights
Yellow brake lamp, or fault 106 (0x6A) and no cruise The brake switch's test-contact wire still on X60004 pin 28 Harness and re-pinning
Cruise won't engage The non-M clutch module, the gear switch, the X6011 pin-7 crossing or the brake contacts Harness and re-pinning
Revs hang between shifts, or idle hunts on clutch-in Clutch-chain wiring first ("the most common rev hang"), then SMG software in the DME. In a non-M automatic-to-manual swap (2000 323Ci, MS42) it was a tune written for the automatic (e46fanatics) Manual
Limp mode or an SMG lamp An SMG donor's DME still running SMG software Immobilizer (EWS)
Tamper dot Cluster VIN differs from the LCM's, or the LCM's mileage is higher (NAM3) Instrument cluster and mileage
DSC lamp with "VIN not initialized" VIN and steering angle not initialised; or an M3 MK60 not yet coded from a late enough session vehicle order, or reset in PA-Soft instead of initialised in INPA DSC, brakes and steering angle, manual, Session 5
ABS lamp after the first drive Faults stored while parts were unplugged (clear them and drive), a sensor not seated, a damaged pulse wheel, mixed tire sizes, or an MK20 donor's sensors. The DSC's wheel-speed faults are 5D90–5DC5, one block per wheel; the last digit: 0 wiring, 1 or 3 seating, 2 pulse wheel, 4 or 5 tooth count or tire size Wheel-speed and pad-wear sensors, DSC, brakes and steering angle
Sport LED dark; fault 110 (0x6E) The wire from the switch center to X60004 pin 16 Manual
EVAP monitor never ready The heater not on pin 18, the pump and valve wiring not proven, a hose, the vapour separator in the right rear wheel well or the filler cap after the arch work, the fuel gauge, or the test conditions Inspection readiness
A/C won't engage The cluster not passing the request; the climate control's coded compressor lock (KOMPRESSOR_SPERRE); the refrigerant pressure; then the chain from the DME's pin 29 to relay K19 and the compressor clutch Manual
Fault 96 (0x60), radiator-outlet temperature plausibility, or a slow warm-up The radiator-outlet sensor unplugged or in the wrong hose; we infer that a thermostat stuck open sets it too Cooling checks and pass values
Speedometer about 9% high The M3 cluster's built-in over-read Instrument cluster and mileage

Deep dive: bodywork and fitment

Everything in the M3 front end bolts to the Touring except the front fenders. The rear arches are the big job: you graft M3 arch steel into the Touring's rear quarters around a mock-up of the final axle, wheels and tires. The graft moves the skin outward, not the opening: the arch opening is the same shape and height on both cars, and the M3 skin stands out from the Touring's by a profile that peaks over and behind the axle and fades out above and behind it (Flare profile). Set up the welder, and protect yourself and the car, as described in Welding settings and safety.

Front end on a 4-door body

Genuine M3 front fenders don't bolt onto a sedan or Touring: the coupe's front fenders are "an inch longer than those on the sedan and wagon" (Jalopnik). Builders describe the M3 fender as longer between the arch and the door and sitting further out; forced into place, its swage line drops, and its side gill sits further back than a 4-door fender's (Tracks and Trails – What it really takes (2026), 02:20, Calvin's Car Diary – PT9 (2020), 06:00).

The rest bolts on. "Basically the complete M3 frontend will fit on the Touring… the only thing that won't fit are the two front fenders" (M3projekts – Ep3 (2023), 08:00), and Redish found the M3 hood "fits straight on" (Autoalex Cars – Part 3 (2023), 05:00). The hood still needs M3-shaped fenders beside it, which is why one budget Touring kept a non-M front end (Tenza Motorsports – Wagon tour and plans (2020), 01:40). BMW's catalog lists the same front panel (51717111691) and front body brackets for the Touring, coupe and M3 (ETK), and the same M3 fender (41357894337) and hood (41617894223) for the M3 coupe, convertible and CSL, so a convertible donor's front panels are the same parts (ETK).

Option A: graft genuine M3 fenders. Keep a strip of your 4-door fender at the door gap and A-pillar, and weld the front of the M3 fender to it (NAM3); one builder describes "a slit off the sedan fender cut and welded on to the M3 fender" (e46fanatics). SOS Customz kept the factory fender's mounting points, door-gap section and front corner, tacked the M3 flare to it and spliced the M3 gill molding in so its line meets the headlight (SOS Customz – Building an E46 M3 Touring wagon (2023), 05:00, 12:00). Calvin's body man used the rear section of a standard Touring fender and moved the gill forward (Calvin's Car Diary – PT9 (2020), 07:00). A graft that joins the front half of an M3 fender to the rear half of the original, so the arch line stops short, looks wrong (Calvin's Car Diary – PT5 (2020), 07:20). On a bench:

  1. Bolt your 4-door fender to the car and mark a graft line a few inches ahead of the door gap, clear of the arch flare.
  2. Trial-fit the M3 fender with the hood, headlight and bumper mounted, so the front edges sit where they must. Mark the same line on it.
  3. Cut both fenders, leaving the M3 piece slightly long, then trim to a 1 mm butt gap.
  4. Clamp both pieces back on the car, check the door gap and the line along the hood, and tack-weld. If pushing the fender flush lifts its top edge, relieve it; one builder slit the top of the fender (Eurofed Automotive – Miki's M3 Touring (2025), 04:00).
  5. Remove the fender, finish with short stitch welds, alternating ends to keep heat down, and planish the seam.
  6. Seal the back of the seam and prime.

Option B: buy Touring fenders.

  • 2M Autowerks (steel). One owner's verdict: "The fit is ok. Not what I would call factory appearance." Thin mounting tabs broke, the line at the A-pillar "doesn't look right", it needed filler for "dimples and fixing some lines", and the M3 liners needed "a LOT of trimming" (e46fanatics).
  • M3Projekts (carbon). €1,400 before VAT; the maker says you can "simply bolt on" them (M3Projekts). They're moulded from a metal hybrid of sedan and M3 coupe fenders (M346 Projects – Pt 18 (2024), 02:20). Fit reports: "a few hours of fiddling" per side, with lines and door gaps close but one side tight at the front and open at the rear (Tracks and Trails – What it really takes (2026), 04:00); two days of alignment, a carbon tab ground shorter and the hood-hinge holes opened 2–3 mm (M3projekts – Ep4 (2023), 04:30); about five hours to fit the side-gill trim and modify its clips (M346 Projects – Pt 18 (2024), 07:00).

Before you commit:

  • Bumper supports. The M3 bumper mounts on fender supports 51118195295/96. Tourings built before 09/2001 have them; facelift cars use different supports and need these added (ETK, Garagistic). Early M3s (to 11/2001) share the Touring's bumper carrier; later ones use a lighter carrier (51117893527). Facelift Tourings with genuine M3 bumpers and headlights exist; the Sloan car is a 2004 (BMWBlog).
  • Brackets and liners. A Touring without the M Tech front bumper needs two more brackets for the bumper corners, and you need the M3's front and rear fender liners (M3projekts – Ep3 (2023), 09:30). The 2M fender owner also needed the M3 bumper carrier, lower headlight trim and M3 horn bracket (e46fanatics).
  • Airflow. Keep the M3 bumper's lower opening and ducting; the oil cooler depends on it. With a ZHP bumper, Tenza had to cut away a scoop behind the bumper so the M3 oil cooler got air (Tenza Motorsports – Front end with M3 parts (2021), 03:20).
  • Washer tank. The M3's washer tank sits low behind the bumper. Original M3 and ZHP bumpers leave room for it; aftermarket bumpers may not (Tenza Motorsports – 5 things (part 2) (2021), 01:00). Its pump and level-sensor leads need extending (M3projekts – Ep5 (2023), 04:30); see the Wiring and coding manual.

Rear arches and doors

How much wider. The rear hub faces sit in about the same place on both cars. The M3's rear track is 1,525 mm on Motorsport Australia's homologation form and 60.0 in (1,524 mm) on BMW USA's spec sheet, and the US 325i Touring's is 1,483 mm (Motorsport Australia, BMW USA: M3, BMW USA: Touring). Half the track plus the wheel offset puts each rear hub face about 788–790 mm from the centerline on both cars: 788.5 mm with the M3's ET26 wheel and an ET47 wheel on the Touring. So the extra rear width comes from the M3 wheel itself. Its ET26 offset moves the wheel about 21 mm further out per side, and the 9-inch rim and 255 tire add width on top. Treat the hub-face figure as good to a millimetre or two: neither source says which wheels its track was measured on (the form lists the M3's 19-inch ET27 rear wheels, which would give 789.5 mm), and BMW's MY2003 wheel and tire list puts the Touring's 8J × 17 wheel at ET47 and its 7J × 16 wheels at ET46 or ET47, depending on the style (BMW wheel and tire list: Touring).

The body follows, by a profile, not one number. BMW USA gives the M3 a width of 70.1 in (1,780 mm) and the 325i Sport Wagon 68.5 in (about 1,740 mm): 20.3 mm (0.8 in) more per side at the widest point (BMW USA: M3, BMW USA: 325 models). We scaled BMW's dimension drawing of the M3 coupe and a drawing of the Touring to BMW's published dimensions (M3 coupe drawing, Touring drawing). By our measurement the M3 skin stands:

  • about 21–23 mm (0.8–0.9 in) proud of the Touring's from 300 mm ahead of the axle to 100 mm behind it;
  • 25–32 mm (1.0–1.3 in) proud from 150 to 350 mm behind the axle;
  • about 10 mm (0.4 in) proud 500 mm behind the axle, fading out beyond;
  • blended in again 470–530 mm (18.5–20.9 in) above the hub, just under the shoulder crease at about 540 mm (21.3 in).

These figures come from drawings and are good to about ±5–10 mm, so the plan has you confirm them with templates on both cars. The station table and the seam lines are in Flare profile.

HARD Motorsport's M3-style rear flares are "Aprox 30mm wider" (HARD Motorsport), and an owner who fitted them measured "a solid 25-30mm" (e46fanatics). That matches only the rear half of the flare. We infer from BMW's drawings that from about 150–220 mm behind the axle rearward, below the bumper's top line, the arch edge you see is the bumper cover, not steel, on both cars. So much of the extra width behind the axle is probably the M3 bumper corner, and the steel and lip hidden behind it may move out less (Rear bumper, skirts and trim).

The opening stays put. BMW-style drawings of the M3 coupe, M3 convertible, non-M coupe and Touring all put the arch edge about 340–350 mm (13.4–13.8 in) above the hub at the top and 355–365 mm (14.0–14.4 in) ahead of it at hub height (our measurement, ±10 mm) (M3 convertible drawing, non-M coupe drawing). The M3's difference is sideways, not a bigger opening. The graft moves the skin and its lip outward and leaves the opening where it is.

Tires against the body. On the M3 wheel, the rear tire's widest sidewall sits about 892 mm from the centerline. That is about flush with the M3 flare's crown, at about 890 mm, and about 22 mm (0.9 in) outside an unflared Touring's widest point. These are our estimates, assuming a 255/40R18 measures about 260 mm across on a 9J rim. Motorsport Australia's recognition form gives the E46 M3's bodywork width as 1,787 mm at the rear axle (3-18-007), about 24 mm per side more than BMW's 1,739 mm for the Touring. On an unflared Touring with M3 axles, one owner found a 9J ET40 rear wheel with a 245/40-17 tire sat flush with the arch lip (NAM3 – Black & Tan 332iT (2023)); the M3's own ET26 wheel and 255 tire sit about 19 mm further out. Without the M3 flares the tires stand proud of the body, which matters at a Massachusetts inspection (Massachusetts).

Where the rear door meets the arch. The Touring's rear door has its own part numbers (41527034155/156; the sedan's are 41527034153/154), and its lower rear corner is cut around the wheel, so its trailing edge forms the front of the arch opening (ETK). It meets the arch on its forward upper curve, at about 10 o'clock on the left side and 2 o'clock on the right: roughly 300–350 mm (11.8–13.8 in) ahead of the axle and 150–250 mm above the hub. That is our estimate from a drawing without dimension lines, ±50 mm, so measure yours.

  • The M3 flare starts about 380–420 mm ahead of the axle, so the first 50–100 mm of its ramp falls on the door.
  • At the shut line the M3 surface would stand about 11–20 mm (0.4–0.8 in) proud of the stock door (our estimate).
  • That is the forward "nose" that builders have had to beat in and blend where it meets the door (M346 Projects – Pt 14 M3 body work (2024), 28:20), or carry onto the door. The choices are in Rear doors.

Where the steel comes from. Most conversions we found used welded steel. BMW's prototype arches "appear to be fully metal constructed" (Redish), and the Sloan car's "OEM metal fender flares were grafted on" (BMWBlog).

  • Petroyle's quarters are steel. BMWBlog lists Petroyle's carbon panels as the rear bumper, side sills, boot floor and front wings, and says "The quarter panels stay in steel" (BMWBlog – Petroyle E46 M3 Touring (2026)). Its rear quarters are "shaped and welded to match the BMW concept's arches, while the rear doors stay standard" (Perfects Auto).
  • Petroyle's "carbon wings" in Hagerty's video are those front wings (Hagerty – Petroyle's E46 M3 Touring (2026), 09:00). One video review calls the car's arches carbon (candyshowroom – The M3 BMW never built (2026), 15:40), which conflicts with both.
  • The inside of the arch changes too. BMW's changes for the M3 coupe included extra C-pillar reinforcement, modified inner side sections around the wheel arches, and a fuel-filler flap reshaped to the M3 quarter (BMW ST041). Expect to rebuild the inside of the arch, not just the skin.
  • Massachusetts. Welding steel from another car into your unibody may count as reassembling "the frames or unit bodies of two or more motor vehicles", which brings an RMV inspection and a "reconstructed" title. Ask the RMV first (Massachusetts), or use new BMW panels: see A new-steel route below.

What BMW's catalog shows:

  • Two M3 quarters. The coupe and CSL use 41217890689/690 (14.5 kg); the M3 convertible has its own, 41357894541/542 (11.5 kg) (ETK). The difference comes from the upper body, C-pillar and roof against the soft-top, as on non-M cars: a 325Ci coupe quarter weighs 15.2 kg and a 325Ci convertible's 10.3 kg (ETK).

  • The same arch, as far as BMW's drawings show. BMW gives both M3s the same rear track, the same 18 × 9 rear wheels and the same 70.1 in body width (BMW USA). The parts around the flare are also the same on both: filler flap 51172695524, the rear bumper and its side brackets, the side skirts and their intermediate pieces, and the M3-only "coverings" 51712695667/51717895936 (ETK). BMW's dimension drawings of the two show the same arch opening within 2–9 mm and the same flare within 3–7 mm, except perhaps 350–400 mm behind the axle, where the convertible's turns in about 10 mm sooner (M3 coupe drawing, M3 convertible drawing). That is our measurement from the drawings, so confirm it with templates.

  • The inner half of the rear wheelhouse (41148231757/758) is one part on the M3 coupe, the M3 convertible and the US 325i Touring (ETK). The extra width sits in the outer skin and the outer side of the wheelhouse. BMW draws one wheelhouse diagram for all three bodies. In it, the panel that meets the skin's lip is different on each:

    • the Touring's own outer half, 41218242355/356, a narrow flanged strip;
    • the coupe's interior side frame, 41217890677/678, an inner quarter panel with the wheel cut-out;
    • the convertible's inner lateral trim panel, 41217894553/554, together with its heavy interior side frame, 41217894557/558.

    That is our reading of BMW's diagrams (ETK: Touring, ETK: M3 coupe, ETK: M3 convertible), not a BMW statement. BMW gives the M3 its own part wherever this panel forms the outer wheelhouse: the non-M 325Ci convertible's 41217022593/594 becomes the M3's 41217894553/554 (both 4.8 kg), and the 325Ci coupe's interior side frame 41218242067/068 becomes the M3's 41217890677/678 (ETK, 325Ci convertible, ETK, M3 convertible). BMW's drawing shows 41217894553 as an inner quarter panel with the arched outer wheelhouse built in (drawing). An M3-only number on an otherwise identical panel suggests the M3 arch flange, but nobody has confirmed it: at about $128, buy one and check it against an M3 skin before you plan around it.

How the factory built the lip. The arch edge is a double skin. The quarter skin and the outer wheelhouse flange overlap in a nested U-channel, spot-welded and seam-sealed (NAM3, Redish – BMW E46 rear arches (2020), 01:00), and E46 arch rust starts in that channel. Redish puts the lip at about 15 mm (0.6 in) on most E46s and about 4 mm on the CSL, whose lip is bonded; its own bonded "CSL-style" lip is about 8 mm and gains about 7 mm of tire clearance (Redish). The skin itself is thin. Expect about 0.7–0.8 mm (0.028–0.031 in), the range I-CAR gives for typical outer panels (I-CAR), and measure yours at a cut edge. How to rebuild the lip is in Arch graft step by step.

A convertible donor yields the whole M3 outer skin from the door shut line back to the tail-light, with the full flare and the right-side filler opening and flap. It lacks only the C-pillar and roof section, which a Touring doesn't use. It also brings the same M3 trunk floor (41127895619), front fenders, hood, rear bumper, side skirts and filler flap as a coupe. The catch is cutting: the arch flange sits on the convertible's inner lateral trim panel and its heavy interior side frame (33.5 kg each, against 5.7 kg for the coupe's interior side frame), so you drill out more spot welds to free it (ETK). Builds with convertible donors:

  • M346 Projects cut both rear quarter sections and the trunk floor from a 2003 M3 convertible and welded them to a Touring, with no convertible-specific problem mentioned on camera (M346 Projects – Pt 1 (2023), 06:40, Pt 14 (2024), 58:00). M3Projekts, which built its own Touring from a convertible donor, says "Coupe or Cabrio/Vert doesn't really matter" (M3projekts – Ep7 (2023), description).
  • Two written build logs used convertible donors without saying where the arch steel ended up: the US 325iT built in Hungary by M3Projekts, which came back with welded steel arches carried onto the doors (NAM3), and a 2016 PistonHeads build that bought the rear half of a Cat C 2005 M3 convertible for its quarters and boot floor, then stopped before any bodywork (PistonHeads).

Steel sources. Prices were checked in October 2026 unless dated. BMW lists no section or arch repair part for the M3 rear quarter; its only E46 "section of rear fender" (41217057389/390) is for sedans (ETK).
